metadata.title: A single-cell time-series atlas of endothelial cell embryonic development
metadata.summary: The STED-EC atlas enables inter-organ and multi-time-point comparisons of gene expression in endothelial cells, revealing substantial transcriptomic variations across endothelial cells from different embryonic organs and facilitating investigation of previously unknown molecular mechanisms that govern organ-specific vascular development.
metadata.content: Skip to Main Content Skip to Main Menu Outline Download PDF Cite Share Set Alert Get Rights Reprints Previous article Next article Highlights • Time-series endothelial cell scRNA-seq atlas covering entire mouse embryonic development • Endothelial cells initiate organ-specific differentiation from mid-gestational embryo • Endothelial gene and pathway comparison in 26 time points and 8 organs • Endothelial Casz1 regulates growth, differentiation, and crosstalk of lung blood vessels Summary Endothelial cells (ECs) are essential components of the vertebrate circulatory system; however, a comprehensive atlas characterizing how ECs acquire organ-specific transcriptomic heterogeneity has not been established. Here, we generated a time-series endothelial resource covering the entirety of mouse embryonic development, including 26 time points and 8 organs. Time-series multi-organ comparison revealed emergence timing and lineage trajectory of organotypic ECs together with organ-specific genes and pathways. Using these resources, we found that most ECs showed distinguishable organ specificity before late gestation. The organotypic EC-enriched genes were associated with vascular function in the organs. Human and mouse pulmonary ECs underwent an evolutionarily conserved transcriptional transition. Endothelial-specific knockout of Casz1, a pulmonary EC-enriched transcription factor, resulted in impaired vascular growth, disturbed pulmonary endothelial organotypic differentiation, and deficient epithelial-EC crosstalk. Our work provides a powerful endothelial resource that reveals fundamental principles of organ-specific EC differentiation and uncovers previously unknown molecular mechanisms governing lung-specific vascular development. Graphical abstract Keywords endothelial cells embryonic development single-cell atlas angiogenesis vascular development organ-specific differentiation Casz1 lung development organotypic vessel interorgan comparison Introduction Endothelial cells (ECs) are one of the most fundamental cell types in vertebrates.1 This specialized cell population lines the inner side of the circulatory system, which is vital for nutrient transport, immune surveillance, and organ development.2 Extensive research studies have unveiled the common molecular mechanisms of angiogenesis,3,4,5,6,7 but the knowledge regarding organ-specific vascular development and multiorgan embryonic endothelial comparison remains largely unexplored.8,9 In the past, vascular ECs were categorized into arterial, venous, and capillary ECs based on corresponding molecular markers.10 Recent studies have uncovered previously unknown organ-specific heterogeneity within ECs of different organs.11,12,13,14 In adult mice, single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) revealed that ECs in different organs exhibit distinct organotypic characteristics at the transcriptomic level.15,16,17,18 However, it remains elusive whether this is a rapid developmental process or a time-consuming event that requires long-term crosstalk between ECs and tissue-resident cells. The key regulator governing organ-specific EC differentiation remains largely unknown, and it is unexplored whether endothelial loss of organotypic features influences the development and regeneration of corresponding organs. To address these questions, we established a time-series atlas of EC embryonic development at the single-cell level in mice. This atlas captured the dynamic differentiation from progenitor ECs to organotypic ECs across 8 organs during the process of embryonic development, facilitating the identification of key regulators in organ-specific EC differentiation. Results A single-cell and time-series embryonic developmental atlas of ECs To create this atlas, we collected cells from whole mouse embryos starting from embryonic day (E) 1.5, at 0.5-day intervals, continuing until E19.0 (Figure S1A). In the mid-gestational stage and afterward, the embryos were split using a tissue tag to label the head, trunk, viscera, and skin (Figure S1A). In all scRNA-seq captured cells, we utilized unsupervised clustering together with endothelial scoring to define ECs, which expressed typical endothelial markers such as Cdh5, Pecam1, and Kdr (Figure S1B).17 We obtained a total number of 70,915 ECs with a median gene number of 4,881, indicating high sequencing quality of this atlas (Figures S1C and S1D). The Cdh5+Pecam1+Kdr+ triple positive cells were detectable in E7.0 embryos, visualized in wild-type and Cdh5-mTnG endothelial reporter mice (Figures S1E–S1H),19 suggesting that ECs began to emerge at approximately E7.0, which is consistent with previous detection of ECs at E7.25 using Flk1-GFP reporter mice.20 Using the embryonic day tag, we constructed a time-series uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) plot of ECs from E7.0 to E19.0 (Figure 1A; Table S1), together with sampling tissue tags without dramatic batch effect or sex bias (Figures S1I–S1M). Figure 1 A single-cell and time-series embryonic atlas of ECs Show full caption Figure S1 Overall design and additional information of STED-EC atlas, related to Figure 1 Show full caption Next, we established an annotation workflow to check whether these ECs had developed organ-specific characteristics through combinations of tissue tags, unsupervised cell clustering, random forest classifier, and previously known molecular markers for adult organotypic ECs (Figure S2A). Repetition of this iterative process allowed us to categorize ECs in different organs as unorganotypic (UO) ECs (defined as ECs without organ specificity or arterial differentiation, UO ECs), central nervous system (CNS) ECs, pulmonary ECs, lymphatic ECs, endocardial ECs, hepatic ECs, gastrointestinal ECs, renal ECs, muscular and dermal ECs, UO arterial ECs, and endothelial-mesenchymal transitional ECs (EndoMT ECs) (Figure 1B). Embryonic ECs in our atlas shared some similar organ-specific markers, e.g., pulmonary EC-specific Scn7a, with their adult counterparts (Figures 1C, 1D, and S2B),9,15,22,23,24,25 although notable differences existed between embryonic and adult ECs within the same organ (Figures S2C and S2D). To validate the expression of these molecular markers in the embryonic organotypic ECs, we performed immunostaining in corresponding organs and another organ without expression of these markers as a negative control at E19.0 (Figure S2E; Table S3). Spatial RNA-seq by microfluidic indexing-based spatial-ATAC and RNA-seq (MISAR-seq) confirmed the expression of these markers in lung and heart in situ (Figures S2F and S2G).26 Projection of published endothelial scRNA-seq data into our atlas showed that these endothelial datasets from different organs unanimously projected into corresponding locations in the UMAP plot (Figures 1B and S2H).9,15,22,23,24,25 Therefore, experimental and analytical evidence supported the annotation of embryonic organotypic ECs, which, together with EndoMT ECs and arterial ECs, showed similar organotypic markers such as the pulmonary EC-specific marker Scn7a (Figures S2I–S2L). Figure S2 Annotation of organotypic ECs in the STED-EC atlas, related to Figure 1 Show full caption The EC percentage in all sequenced cells and the estimated total cell number in embryonic mice21 allowed us to predict the EC number change during embryonic development (Figures 1E, S1I, and S2M; Table S2). Together with vascular development, the diversity of organotypic ECs significantly expanded, and the proportion of organotypic ECs in different organs dynamically changed during embryonic development, e.g., hepatic ECs markedly increased after E11.5 together with expansion of the liver from this stage (Figures 1F and S2N).27 Together, we have established a “single-cell and time-series embryonic development endothelial cell atlas” (abbreviated as “STED-EC atlas”) covering 8 organs and all EC embryonic developmental stages, which is accessible on our public website (http://sted-ec.ccla.ac.cn). Organ-specific differentiation of ECs initiates from the mid-gestational stage of embryonic mice After establishing the STED-EC atlas, we explored how we could best implement this resource to expand our knowledge about vascular biology, especially in the field of endothelial organotypic differentiation. In the following sections, we demonstrated that the STED-EC atlas enabled us to improve our understanding of the following: (1) the initiation timing of endothelial organotypic differentiation, (2) the association between organotypic EC-enriched genes and vascular function in corresponding organs, (3) time-series human and mouse EC development comparison, and (4) prediction and validation of organ-enriched gene function. Although our STED-EC atlas, together with the previous scRNA-seq dataset, highlighted organ-specific EC differences at the transcriptomic level,15,16,17,18 one critical question remained: when do ECs differentiate to acquire organotypic transcriptomic profiles during development? To address this question, we used combinatory molecular markers of mature organotypic ECs to score the organ-specific differentiation level of ECs (Table S3). The comparison of maturity scoring with real developmental time points was highly consistent (Figures 2A and S3A). This scoring method could be used in public endothelial datasets to correctly predict endothelial maturity (Figure S3B).28 This evidence suggested that this gene set could effectively evaluate the organ-specific differentiation levels of ECs. We noted that maturity scores remained low and stable in early embryonic stages, but they increased irreversibly after certain time points in different organs (Figures 2B, S3C, and S3D, arrows). For instance, the scoring of pulmonary and CNS ECs increased continuously after E12.0 and E9.5, respectively, suggesting these time points marked the initial emergence timing of organotypic ECs in these organs (Figure 2B, arrows). This initial emergence timing was not exactly the same in different organs but largely fell into the time window of E9.0–E13.5, suggesting the mid-gestational stage was a critical period for the initiation of the EC organotypic profile. The onset of key markers was concomitant with this initiation timing and was nearly undetectable beforehand (Figures 2C and S3E). This was validated by immunostaining of these molecular markers in ECs at the relevant developmental time points, generating a timeline for the initial emergence of organotypic ECs in these organs (Figures 2D, 2E, and S3F), and achieving a combinatory display of real developmental time and organ-specific EC differentiation at each embryonic stage in the STED-EC atlas (Figures 2F and S3G). This analysis suggested that ECs differentiated to acquire organotypic features at the mid-gestational stage of mouse embryonic development. Figure 2 Organotypic differentiation of ECs during mouse embryonic development Show full caption Figure S3 The emergence and dynamic differentiation of organotypic ECs, related to Figure 2 Show full caption To predict the organotypic differentiation paths of ECs in different organs, we applied Moscot (an optimal-transport-based method) in the STED-EC atlas.29 In the application of this methodology, we started with the transcriptome of ECs in different organs at E19.0, tracing backward to identify the most similar cell population at the preceding developmental time (E18.5), and this iterative process was repeated sequentially back to E7.0. This method allowed us to predict the lineage differentiation paths of ECs within the STED-EC atlas (Figure 2G). We noted that the differentiation path of endocardial ECs was different from others, while ECs in other organs shared similar differentiation paths from E7.0 until E9.0 with divergent routes afterward (Figure 2G), further supporting that mid-gestation was a critical stage for the beginning of EC organotypic differentiation. But the differentiation path of ECs had almost no direct overlap with pericytes from E7.75 to E13.5 in head and trunk (Figure S3H). Next, we quantitatively compared the transcriptomic differences of ECs from various organs over time using Pearson’s correlation coefficient analysis (Figure 2H). At E12.5, the transcriptomic variances had become evident in endocardial, hepatic, and lymphatic ECs. By E15.5, the differences between CNS ECs and other organs became more pronounced, which was consistent with blood-brain barrier establishment at this time.30 Approaching E18.5, the transcriptomic differences of pulmonary and renal ECs became apparent, and the overall statistical variance gradually approached the levels in adult organotypic ECs (Figure 2H). This analysis suggested that ECs continuously expanded their organotypic variances in the late-gestational stage after acquisition of organotypic profiles in the mid-gestational stage. Additional Pearson’s correlation analysis of ECs in individual organs at different developmental time points revealed critical periods of EC differentiation within each organ. In the respiratory system, pulmonary ECs showed limited transcriptomic changes from E12 to E15 (lung pseudoglandular stage) with robust alteration from E17 to E19 (lung canalicular and saccular stages) during respiratory system development (Figure 2I).31 In other organs, ECs displayed their unique critical differentiation periods within corresponding organs (Figures 2I and S3I). In summary, STED-EC atlas analysis revealed that the mid-gestational stage is a critical period for the initiation of EC organotypic differentiation with increasing divergence afterward in embryonic mice. Organotypic genes in ECs are associated with vascular function in the organ Next, we took advantage of the multiorgan feature of the STED-EC atlas to compare the gene expression pattern and signaling strength in ECs across multiple organs. We began by analyzing the expression of key endothelial markers. In ECs, the expression level of most key endothelial markers remained weak at E7.0 and E7.5 (Figure 3A). The E7.0–E7.5 UO ECs form a unique cluster in all UO ECs (Figure S4A), with thousands of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) as well as higher expression of hematopoietic marker Runx1 and endothelial progenitor marker Etv2,32,33 suggesting the E7.0–E7.5 ECs remained immature (Figures S4A–S4C). After E7.5, key endothelial markers maintained constant expression (Figure 3A), but these markers were not expressed equally in different organs (Figure 3B). For example, tight junction protein claudin-5 (Cldn5) was relatively enriched in CNS ECs, consistent with its irreplaceable function to maintain blood-brain barrier integrity (Figure 3B).34 The low expression of Apln in endocardial ECs was previously proved by genetic lineage tracing (Figure 3B).35 These cases suggest key endothelial markers displayed organotypic expression pattern in the embryonic ECs from different organs. To systematically compare this organotypic gene expression variance in ECs, we analyzed the gene expression trend of all ECs and found that the transcriptomic pattern of ECs can be categorized into four modules based on activation and repression timing of genes during embryonic development (Figure 3C). Surprisingly, the proportion of genes in these four modules showed high variance across different organs. In endocardial, CNS, and hepatic ECs, module 1 constituted 35% to 40% of genes, while the fourth module accounted for 50% to 64% of genes in pulmonary, renal, and lymphatic ECs (Figure 3D). This analysis showed that gene activation and repression patterns have robust organ-specific differences in ECs, suggesting the existence of more organotypic genes in ECs in addition to the key endothelial markers. Figure 3 Multiorgan EC gene expression comparison over time Show full caption Figure S4 Multiorgan gene expression comparison in EC, related to Figure 3 Show full caption To explore these endothelial organotypic genes and their potential association with organ functionality, we identified a substantial number of DEGs when comparing ECs that initially acquired the organotypic feature (E13.5) with ECs at the late-gestational stage (E18.5) in the same organ (Figure S4D). An intersectional analysis of these DEGs and organotypic EC-enriched genes facilitated identification of a series of genes whose Gene Ontology (GO) or Reactome pathways were associated with the function of corresponding organs (Figure 3E). To further analyze the strength of different pathways over developmental time in different organotypic ECs, we used the GO and Reactome pathway database to collect signaling pathways and corresponding gene lists for scoring (Figures 3F and S4E; Table S4). This analysis revealed that organotypic EC-enriched signaling pathways showed high relevance to the function of corresponding organs. For example, cardiac chamber development, atrial septum development, and right ventricle morphogenesis (GO: 0003215, 0060413, 0003205, and 0003283) showed strong pathway scores in endocardial ECs because endocardial ECs lined the innermost side of the cardiac chamber (Figures 3F and S4E; Table S4). Abnormalities in signaling in endocardial ECs severely disrupt cardiac chamber formation.36,37 The solute carrier (SLC)-mediated transmembrane transport (Reactome pathway: R-MMU-425407), D-glucose transmembrane transporter activity (GO: 0055056), and other transmembrane transporter activities (GO: 0140359, 0008559, 0015172, 0022858, 0032328, 0015837, and 0089718) were enriched in CNS ECs because the SLC gene family, together with other transporters, was indispensable for material transfer across the blood-brain barrier (Figures 3F and S4E; Table S4).38,39 As a metabolic center, hepatic ECs were associated with the amino sugar catabolic process (GO: 0046348)40 and steroid hormone biosynthetic process (GO: 0006700)41 in the liver (Figures 3F and S4E; Table S4). The Wnt5a signaling (R-MMU-5140745) in hepatic ECs was reported to regulate fetal hematopoiesis and hepatocyte proliferation (Figures 3F and S4E; Table S4).42,43 The lymphatic ECs were linked to lymph node development (GO: 0048535),44 lymphocyte chemotaxis (GO: 0140131, 0010820, and 1901623),45 and antigen processing and presentation (GO: 0002579)46,47 (Figures 3F and S4E; Table S4), much more than canonical function as conduits for fluid and immune cell transport. A full list of GO and Reactome pathway scoring can be visualized in the webpage of the STED-EC atlas (http://sted-ec.ccla.ac.cn/). These data suggest that ECs in different organs have unique signaling pathways that are possibly relevant to their function in corresponding organs. Detailed gene expression comparison suggested similar linkage of organotypic EC-enriched genes with corresponding organ function. For instance, the expression of Gata5 was selectively high in early endocardial ECs because of its known interaction with NFATc in regulating endothelial-endocardial differentiation (Figure 3G).48 Foxl2, whose expression was experimentally validated in brain vasculature, was involved in midbrain-hindbrain boundary development (Figure 3G).49 Maf, a transcription factor enriched in hepatic ECs, was indispensable for the differentiation of zonated sinusoids in the liver (Figure 3G).9 The liver was also known as a major source of coagulation factor FVIII (F8), which was secreted from hepatic ECs but not hepatocytes (Figure 3G).50,51 The extracellular protein reelin (Reln) was reported to be released from lymphatic ECs for efficient organ repair after injury (Figure 3G).52 The inflammation and collagen deposition in lungs were promoted by endothelial-specific Foxf1 ablation,53 while Pbx1-deficient mice displayed abnormal blood vasculature in the kidneys (Figures 3G and 2C).54 Thus, the comparison of organotypic EC-enriched genes and existing literature supports that organotypic EC-enriched genes show a high possibility to be associated with their physiological functions in corresponding organs. The previous analysis suggested the potential to use the STED-EC atlas to search unknown organotypic EC-enriched genes. Indeed, some genes showed an organ-preferential expression pattern in ECs (Figure S4F). For example, although SLC gene family members were enriched in CNS ECs, other trans-endothelial transporters (Slc9a9, Slc28a2, and Slc45a3) could be detected in other organs. The expression of Cdh5 was ubiquitous in ECs, while other tight and adherent junctions (Cldn11, Cdh13, and Cdh11) showed an organ-preferential expression pattern. Some transcription factors (Lef1, Casz1, Hoxd10, and Hoxa10) were selectively enriched in some organs,9,53,55,56 which was supported by SCENIC analysis (Figures 3H, S4G, and S4H). EC-derived angiocrine factors, which included the interleukin family (Il1a, Il7, and Il33), stem cell factor (Kitl), Igf family (Igf1 and Igf2), pleiotrophin (Ptn), and BMP family (Bmp2 and Bmp6), displayed distinct expression levels in different organs (Figures 3I and S4I). The variance of angiocrine factor expression may partially explain the organ-enriched endothelial-epithelial or endothelial-mesenchymal crosstalk (Figures 3J–3L and S4J). Taken together, the STED-EC atlas provides a powerful resource to examine the endothelial gene expression levels and signaling pathways in multiple organs over developmental time. The genes and signaling pathways enriched in organotypic ECs are potentially relevant to endothelial function in the corresponding organ. Time-series human and mouse pulmonary EC comparison reveals a similar developmental path and endothelial subpopulation but different gene expression modules In previous analysis, we leveraged the STED-EC atlas to perform multiorgan EC gene expression analysis, but time-series comparisons of EC development between different species at the single-cell level are still rare. Therefore, we utilized another advantage of the STED-EC atlas with the entire embryonic time, taking pulmonary EC development as an example, to compare the dynamic EC development between mouse and human in the lung. We incorporated published human lung embryonic developmental scRNA-seq datasets, which included transcriptomic information of lung endothelial, epithelial, and mesenchymal cells with several time points from 5 until 22 post-conception weeks (pcw).57 Multiple data integration comparisons suggested harmony canonical correlation analysis (CCA) and SeuratV3 CCA as ideal methods (Figures S5A and S5B; Table S5).58 After integrating mouse and human datasets, the differences of endothelial, epithelial, and mesenchymal cells were clearly distinguishable (Figure S5C). Notably, the distribution of human and mouse ECs in an integrated UMAP plot showed remarkable similarities, comparing the real sampling time (Figures 4A and S5D). This prompted us to perform trajectory analysis of pulmonary ECs. Starting from the earliest time point, we observed highly similar trajectory paths for both species (Figure 4B). In mice, lung capillary ECs differentiate to Car4+/Tbx2+ and Plvap+ subpopulations,59,60 while human TBX2+ lung capillary ECs shared the highest similarity with the mouse Car4+ subset (Figures 4B and S5E). Furthermore, we aligned the developmental stages of lung endothelial, epithelial, and mesenchymal cells in two species for similarity and gene expression pattern analysis. Fetal lung development can be roughly divided into the embryonic stage, pseudoglandular stage, canalicular stage, and saccular stage,31 and all three cell types had similar alignment results (Figure S5F).61 Comparing the human lung EC transcriptome at different time points based on alignment results, we found robust changes in the EC transcriptome from 18 to 20 pcw, namely the canalicular stage (Figures 4C, 4D, S5G, and S5H), reminiscent of the critical transition period of mouse lung ECs (Figure 2I). These findings suggest a high similarity between human and mouse lung EC development in terms of trajectory paths, EC subpopulations, and critical differentiation time points. Figure 4 The time-series developmental comparison of pulmonary ECs between humans and mice Show full caption Figure S5 Human and mouse pulmonary EC comparison, related to Figure 4 Show full caption By contrast, we detected robust gene expression differences between human and mouse lung ECs. Following the previous method of analyzing gene expression modules (Figures 3C and 3D), we unexpectedly discovered that each of the four gene expression modules exhibited a substantial proportion of mouse-specific or human-specific patterns, with only 28.9% similarity in expression trends (Figure 4E). In addition, mouse and human pulmonary ECs only shared 35.7% similarity in expressed genes in the top 200 of pulmonary EC-enriched genes, including pulmonary EC-specific Scn7a (Figures 4F, S5I, and S5J).62 GO analyses of common genes indicated that these genes were primarily involved in vascular development and epithelial cell proliferation (Figure 4F). The gene expression differences might be associated with cell-cell communications, with increased percentages of ECs acting as a signal sender in humans as well as species-enriched crosstalk within these three cell types (Figures 4G, 4H, S5K, and S5L). Therefore, the time-series comparison of human and mouse lung ECs showed similarity in trajectories, EC subpopulations, critical differentiation periods, and discrepancy in gene expression trends, which suggests that genetic mouse models should be used to investigate common genes shared by human and mouse ECs to facilitate better understanding of human development and disease. Casz1 regulates vascular development and EC differentiation Finally, we showed that the STED-EC atlas could facilitate the identification and validation of organ-enriched gene function in combination with genetically modified animals. Through STED-EC atlas prediction, we identified Casz1 as a pulmonary EC-enriched transcription factor that was commonly expressed in humans and mice (Figures 3H, 4F, 5A, S6A, and S6B). To validate its expression pattern, we used the Casz1em1Zyliu knockin reporter mice, in which hemagglutinin (HA) was inserted into the Casz1 coding region.63 This strategy allowed us to detect endogenous Casz1 expression via HA immunofluorescence staining, which confirmed that Casz1 was expressed in pulmonary ECs but not in the ECs of the liver, heart, or brain (Figures 5B, S6C, and S6D). Consistently, Casz1 was detected in cardiac cells in the heart (Figure S6D).64 Figure 5 Casz1 is essential for vascular development and EC differentiation in the lung Show full caption Figure S6 Endothelial-Casz1 knockout influences pulmonary vascular development, related to Figure 5 Show full caption Previous research about Casz1 focused on its function in cardiomyocytes and neurons.63,64,65 To explore its function in ECs, we crossed the Cdh5(PAC)-CreERT2 mice with Casz1em1Cflox flox mice to generate tamoxifen-inducible EC-specific Casz1 knockout mice (Cdh5-CreERT2+/T Casz1F/F, Casz1iΔEC). Tamoxifen administration resulted in the deletion of exons 5 and 6, with approximately 60%–70% knockout efficiency in fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS)-sorted lung ECs (Figures S6E and S6F). At E15.5, we observed significant reduction in the lung vascularized areas visualized by Emcn and CD31 in Casz1iΔEC after tamoxifen administration (Figures 5C and S6G). No apparent vascular morphological abnormalities were detected in other organs of Casz1iΔEC at E15.5 (Figure S6H). At E18.5, we found a dramatic reduction of Car4+ capillary ECs in Casz1iΔEC mice, indicating abnormal differentiation of lung ECs (Figure 5D).59,60 The expression pattern of VEGFR2, lung EC-enriched Tbx3, and extracellular matrix collagen Ⅳ was influenced by endothelial Casz1 (Figures S6I–S6K). Similar pulmonary vascular defects were detected 12 h after birth and at postnatal day (P) 14 (Figures S6L–S6N). To understand the molecular mechanism of these vascular defects and identify endothelial downstream targets of Casz1, we combined 14 Casz1iΔEC and 8 littermate control mice at E18.5 to sort CD45−Ter119− cells for scRNA-seq (Figures S6O–S6Q). Subcluster analysis of lung ECs confirmed reduction of Car4+ lung ECs (Figures 5E, S6R, and S6S). Importantly, when the STED-EC atlas was used as a template to perform transcriptomic similarity comparison, control ECs, as expected, were more similar to E18.0–E18.5 (Figure 5F). Strikingly, the transcriptomic profile of ECs in Casz1iΔEC resembled ECs before E16.0, suggesting that the loss of Casz1 prevented the critical transition of lung ECs from the pseudoglandular to the canalicular stage (Figures 5F, 2I, 4C, and 4D). DEG analysis revealed that Casz1 disruption resulted in 120 to 470 DEGs in 4 subclusters of lung ECs (Figure 5G). An in-depth analysis of these DEGs identified key angiogenesis regulators (Vegfa, Kdr, Tek, Nrp1, Efnb2, Sox17, Vwf, and Jag1) (Figure 5H), various markers of Car4+ and Plvap+ lung capillaries (Tbx2, Car4, and Cemip2) (Figure 5I), and the top 50 pulmonary EC organotypic differentiation markers (Foxf1, Tmem100, Ace, Fendrr, Tbx3, and Ahr) (Figure 5J), suggesting that Casz1 played a profound role in influencing angiogenesis, lung capillary subpopulation formation, and pulmonary EC organotypic differentiation. GO analysis of DEGs in Car4+ lung ECs uncovered that the relevant genes were enriched in VEGF signaling, angiogenesis, epithelial tube morphogenesis, and lung development (Figures 5K and S6T). To investigate whether Casz1 controlled the expression of these genes through chromatin binding in ECs and check whether the binding positions overlapped with DEGs, we isolated CD31+ lung ECs from Casz1em1Zyliu knockin mice and performed Cut&Tag sequencing of the Casz1 (recognized by anti-HA) binding sites (Figure 5L). In freshly isolated lung ECs, Casz1 primarily bound to transcriptional start regions, with approximately 70% in promoter regions (less than 4 kb), around 12.2% in introns, and about 15.8% in intergenic regions (Figures 5M and S7A). Casz1 bound to chromatin regions of various DEGs involved in angiogenesis and lung EC differentiation, including Vegfa, Kdr, Tek, Foxf1, Tmem100, Tbx3, Tbx2, Car4, and Cemip2 (Figures 5N and S7B). To confirm that Casz1 affected gene expression and function in ECs, we overexpressed Casz1 in human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) (CASZ1 OE), which led to transcriptomic changes and over 240 DEGs (Figures 5O, S7C, and S7D). Casz1 knockout and overexpression resulted in a similar gene expression trend, including the top 50 markers in lung ECs (Tmem100 and Car4) as well as well-established functional genes (Flt1, Itgb1, Unc5b, Fli1, and Jag1) in ECs (Figure 5P). Casz1 overexpression reduced HUVEC migration capability and enhanced tube formation, while shRNA-mediated Casz1 knockdown produced the opposite effects in vitro (Figures 5Q and S7E–S7H). Casz1 influences organotypic endothelial-epithelial crosstalk during lung development Furthermore, we investigated whether endothelial abnormalities influenced lung epithelial cell development in Casz1iΔEC. At E15.5, we detected decreased Nkx2.1+ epithelial cell area and enlarged spaces between vasculature and epithelium in Casz1iΔEC mice (Figure 5C). The reduction of Nkx2.1+ epithelial cell number continued at E18.5 (Figure 6A), together with fewer Epcam+ epithelial cells, Sftpc+ alveolar type 2 (AT2) epithelial cells, and RAGE+ or Epcam+ Pdpn+ MHCⅡ− alveolar type 1 (AT1) epithelial cells66,67 (Figures 6B–6D; Table S6). 5-ethynyl-2′-deoxyuridine (EdU) incorporation assays showed reduced proliferation ability of lung epithelial cells in Casz1iΔEC mice (Figures 6E and 6F). Similar pulmonary epithelial defects were detected 12 h after birth and at P14 (Figures S7I and S7J). Figure 6 Endothelial Casz1 influences endothelial-epithelial crosstalk in the lung Show full caption To understand how endothelial Casz1 knockout leads to epithelial cell abnormalities, we analyzed the scRNA-seq epithelial cell dataset of Casz1iΔEC. Consistently, the proportion of Nkx2.1+ cells and epithelial cell cycle scoring were reduced together with a substantial number of DEGs in each epithelial cell subpopulation (Figures S7K–S7P). Because Casz1 was specifically knocked out in ECs, we analyzed the potential crosstalk between endothelial and epithelial cells. In Casz1iΔEC, crosstalk strength and communication amount for most of the endothelial and epithelial subpopulations reduced (Figures 6G and 6H). A detailed comparison of signaling from Car4+ endothelial to epithelial cells showed more enhanced pathways in control, in which we found ECs may release FGF1 to target epithelial cells (Figure 6I). The FGF family plays a crucial role in lung development.68 The STED-EC atlas showed FGF1, FGF3, and FGF12 expression in different organs of embryonic ECs, while FGF1 was the sole FGF family member enriched in embryonic pulmonary ECs (Figures 6J, S7Q, and S7R). In Casz1iΔEC mice, we detected a dramatic reduction of Fgf1 in ECs together with a robust binding of Casz1 in the Fgf1 chromatin region (chromosome 18: 38,971,726–39,062,525) (Figures 6K and 6L). FGF1 was reported to stimulate epithelial cell proliferation,69 a defect in Casz1iΔEC mice; therefore, we established an in vitro system to co-culture HUVEC and epithelial cells70,71 (Figure S7S). We found that shRNA-mediated CASZ1 knockdown in HUVECs resulted in reduced proliferation of co-cultured epithelial cells (Figure 6M). Adding FGF1 partially rescued the CASZ1 knockdown-induced epithelial proliferation abnormality (Figures 6N and S7T), suggesting that loss of FGF1 may, at least partially, explain the epithelial proliferation defect in Casz1iΔEC mice. This evidence suggests that endothelial knockout of Casz1 results in lung developmental deficiency through interfering in endothelial-epithelial crosstalk. Discussion In this study, we developed a comprehensive single-cell atlas of EC embryonic development termed the STED-EC atlas. This time-series atlas spans all mouse embryonic developmental stages together with 8 organs. Previous studies have utilized scRNA-seq to analyze ECs in several organs,9,14,15,22,23,24,25,72,73 but most studies predominantly focus on individual organs at discrete time points, thus constraining the possibility to perform time-series multiorgan comparison as we carried out in this work. The dataset in our atlas is captured in an unbiased manner within all organs, which minimizes sample processing-induced bias, facilitating gene and signaling comparison in multiple organs. Another advantage of our atlas is that the data cover the entire span of mouse embryonic development in 0.5-day intervals. This short interval allows us to identify precise developmental time points for the emergence of organotypic ECs in different organs and many other events during EC development. However, our atlas does not comprise all organs, e.g., bone marrow. This is most likely because these organs are very small in embryos or because they initiate organogenesis in late-gestational stages.72 We take advantage of the STED-EC atlas to perform human versus mouse EC time-series comparisons during lung development. This application of the STED-EC atlas may potentially be extended to other organs, such as the brain, liver, or heart, to identify common genes shared by human and mouse organotypic ECs, which make better use of genetically modified animals to investigate common genes (e.g., Casz1) to mimic human development and disease. Meanwhile, our STED-EC atlas provides a standard EC developmental template to facilitate understanding how gene manipulation disrupts the features of ECs. In this work, we make an attempt to compare pulmonary ECs at different developmental stages in the STED-EC atlas with deficient ECs in Casz1iΔEC, which suggests that removal of Casz1 results in the failure of pulmonary ECs to accomplish the transcriptomic transition in the canalicular stage and abnormal epithelial cell development. Additionally, the transcription information in the STED-EC atlas could be integrated into spatial RNA-seq, Cut&Tag-seq, and other sequencing technology to comprehensively understand the transcription, chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, histone modification, and metabolism of ECs. For biologists without programming expertise, we have provided a user-friendly interactive platform (http://sted-ec.ccla.ac.cn/) to check gene expression and pathway scores in multiple organs during whole EC developmental time points. For organ-specific ECs, their molecular profile, vascular barrier structure, and angiocrine function have been described in adults.1,11,13,15,74 However, the intrinsic and extrinsic mechanisms to induce organ-specific EC differentiation remain largely unknown. The precise timing for the emergence of organ-specific ECs was elusive. Although ECs in every organ take a long time to become fully mature, our work shows that ECs in most organs display organ-specific transcription heterogeneity before E14.5, suggesting that organotypic EC differentiation does not require time-consuming interactions between organ-residential cells and ECs. The transcription factor Maf is reported to influence hepatic EC differentiation.9 Our study reveals that transcription factor Casz1 is enriched in pulmonary ECs, controlling the expression of a series of lung-EC organotypic differentiation markers. This evidence may suggest the essential function of transcription factors during organotypic EC differentiation. Casz1 was reported to induce skeletal muscle differentiation in embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma,64 promote tube formation in zebrafish,75 suppress neuroblastoma formation,76 and be involved in otic neurogenesis.63 However, the function of Casz1 was not investigated using endothelial-specific knockout mice during lung development. The DEGs and chromatin binding region of Casz1 involve multiple key regulators of angiogenesis as well as another pulmonary EC-enriched angiocrine factor, FGF1, which at least partially explains the epithelial defects in Casz1iΔEC. Therefore, the STED-EC atlas provides a valuable platform to investigate molecular mechanisms regulating the organ-specific differentiation of ECs. To summarize, our study presents the STED-EC atlas as a powerful resource for EC embryonic development, which facilitates multiorgan and time-series EC comparison. The combination of STED-EC atlas analysis and genetically modified animal validation provides insights to understand the molecular mechanism and physiological significance of EC organotypic differentiation. Limitations of the study Although the STED-EC atlas covers 8 major organs, other organs (e.g., bone marrow, spleen, pancreas, lymph node, thymus, testis, ovary, and retina) are not included in our atlas. This is most likely because we use an unbiased rather than a rebalanced scRNA-seq sampling strategy; therefore, if the organs are too small in the embryonic stage, their ECs cannot be effectively captured. This sampling strategy also results in higher EC numbers in larger organs such as the CNS, skin, liver, and lung. Another limitation is that this manuscript focuses on the organotypic differentiation of ECs without in-depth analysis of other important aspects of vascular biology such as vasculogenesis, arteriovenous differentiation, tip-stalk EC development, hemangioblast identification, and endothelial-pericyte crosstalk. Our analyzing methods should be carefully evaluated to determine whether they are suitable for your dataset, and it’s necessary to perform multiple methodology comparisons, particularly interspecies integration. Finally, although the STED-EC atlas has a high sequencing depth, we cannot guarantee that it will capture all genes, especially those genes whose transcription level is relatively low. The technical limitations of current scRNA-seq may be resolved by advanced sequencing technology in the future. a new tab Experimental model and study participant details Animals C57BL/6N mice were used for all analysis of wild-type mice. Mice were mainly sacrificed between 8am and 10am. After overnight mating, female mice were examined in the following morning for the presence of a vaginal plug, which was counted as embryonic day 0.5 (E0.5). The developmental stage of embryos was assessed by plug date and morphological features. The developmental stages to sacrifice mice were indicated in figures and figure legends. Casz1iΔEC were analyzed at E15.5, E18.5, P0 and P14 as indicated in figures. Both male and female mice were used in the study and we did not observe any sex effect on the results. Littermates were randomly assigned to experimental groups based on genotyping results. Animals were housed in the animal facility of Guangzhou Institutes of Biomedicine and Health. Animal experiments were performed according to the institutional guidelines and laws, following the protocols (2021046, 2024028) approved by local animal ethics committees. Human scRNA-seq data We used published scRNA-seq dataset for mouse and human pulmonary development comparison (E-MTAB-11267). This manuscript did not involve any new human sampling or new human scRNA-seq dataset. Method details Genetically modified animal experiments Casz1 knockout mice (C57BL/6JGpt-Casz1em1Cflox/Gpt) were generated by GemPharmatech (Strain NO. T008505, Nanjing, China) and crossed with Cdh5(PAC)-CreERT2 mice91 to generate endothelial-specific Casz1 knockout mice (Cdh5-CreERT2+/T Casz1F/F, Casz1iΔEC). 1mg tamoxifen (Sigma, T5648) was i.p. injected for 4 consecutive days from E11.5 and analyzed at E15.5. 1mg tamoxifen was administrated for 5 consecutive days from E11.5 and analyzed at E18.5 or 12 hours after birth. 0.05 mg tamoxifen was administrated for 4 consecutive days from P2 and analyzed at P14. 20 mg/kg EdU (Thermofisher Scientific, A10044) was i.p. injected to pregnant female. Casz1em1Zyliu reporter mice (IMSR_JAX:039651) was generated and kindly provided by Zhiyong Liu.63 Cdh5(PAC)-mtdTomato-nGFP (Cdh5-mTnG) endothelial reporter mice used membrane tdtomato for EC labeling and was previously validated.19 Cryosectioning, immunostaining and confocal imaging Embryos were dissected and placed in ice-cold 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA-PBS) (Sigma, P6148) solution and fixed overnight. Fixed lung samples were dehydrated in 20% sucrose-PBS solution, and embedded in OCT (SAKURA, 4583) for storage at -80°C. Cryosectioning was performed on a Leica CM3050 cryostat with low profile blades to achieve sections in the thickness of 8 μm. For immunostaining, sections were rehydrated in PBS, permeabilized for about 15 min in 0.5% Triton X100-PBS solution and blocked for about 2 hours in PBS with 1% BSA, 2% donkey serum, 0.3% Triton X100-PBS (blocking buffer) at room temperature. Sections were stained with primary antibodies diluted in blocking buffer at 4°C overnight. Secondary antibodies were diluted in blocking buffer at room temperature for 2 hours. After that, sections were washed three times with PBS, mounted with Fluoromount-G (0100-01, Southern Biotech) and kept in 4°C for confocal imaging. The primary antibodies include EMCN (Santa Cruz, sc-65495, 1:100), HA (Cell signaling Technology, 3724, 1:600), NKX2.1 (Abcam, AB76013, 1:200), Car4 (R&D, AF2414, 1:100), VEGFR2(R&D, AF644, 1:100), Isolectin B4 (Vector, B-1205-.5, 1:100), Collagen IV (Bio-Rad, 2150-1470, 1:500), TBX3(Abcam, ab99302, 1:50), CD31 (R&D, AF3628, 1:100), RAGE (R&D, MAB1179-100, 1:500), SFTPC (Merck, AB3786, 1:500), VE-cadherin (Thermofisher Scientific, 14-1441-82, 1:50), Foxq1 (Proteintech, 23718-1-AP, 1:100), Meox2 (Novus, NBP2-30647, 1:200), Lyve1 (R&D, MAB2125, 1:100), Prox1 (Abcam, ab199359, 1:300), Foxf1 (R&D, AF4798, 1:100), CD36 (Proteintech, 18836-1-AP, 1:100), Pbx1 (Cell signaling Technology, 4342S, 1:100), Hand2 (Abcam, ab200040, 1:50), CD31 (Abcam, ab28364, 1:50) were used in this study. The secondary antibodies include Donkey anti-Rat Alexa Fluor 488 (Thermofisher Scientific, A21208, 1:200), Donkey anti-Rabbit Alexa Fluor 546 (Thermofisher Scientific, A10040, 1:200), Donkey anti-Goat Alexa Fluor 647 (Thermofisher Scientific, A21447, 1:200), Streptavidin, Alexa Fluor 405(Thermofisher Scientific, S32351, 1:200). Sections were imaged with laser scanning confocal microscopes (LSM800). Sections were imaged with the same microscope and imaging acquisition settings for quantitative analysis. For image quantification, we used Image J for analysis. The area was defined based on the intensity of image. Fluorescence intensity higher than threshold, which was automatically calculated by Image J, was defined as positive area. The area was calculated based on the resolution of images. The normalization process is that both control and CKO divided by the average of control group. “Normalized area” is normalization of exact area number of control and CKO mice divided by the average area of control mice. Thus, the normalized number of control mice should fluctuate around “1”, with the average normalized number equals to “1”. The normalization process does not have any influence to the p-value. Flow cytometry Lung was excised and minced for flow cytometry. The tissue was immersed in dissociation solution: 5ml 2% FBS-DMEM solution with 5 mg collagenase Ⅰ (Gibco,17100017), 0.1 mg DNase Ⅰ (Solarbio,D8071) and 25 U Dispase Ⅱ (Sigma-Aldrich,42613-33-2), incubating at 37°C for 30 min. Samples were filtered using 100 μm Nylon cell strainer (Biosharp, BS-100-XBS) to get single cell suspensions, and cell centrifugation was performed at 300 g for 5 min. Red Blood Cell Lysis Buffer were diluted in deionized water and incubated with cells on ice for 10 min. Cells were washed by 2% FBS-PBS solution and then incubated with primary antibodies on ice for 30 min. Cells were washed again and resuspended in 2% FBS-PBS for flow cytometry. The following primary antibodies were used in this study. CD45-Pacific Blue (Biolegend,30-F11,103126), Epcam- PE-Cy7 (Biolegend,G8.8,118216), Pdpn-PE (Biolegend,8.1.1, 127408), MHCII-APC (Biolegend,AF6-120.1, 116418), CD31-FITC (Biolegend,390, 102406). The sorting experiments were performed by BD AriaII (serial Number P07800188). We use Pureflo ZenFlo capsule (Cat log number 700031101 REV.01) with rating 0.2 μm to filter out bacteria and impurities. The filter includes Blue laser (780/60, 695/40, 616/23, 585/42, 530/30, 488/10), red laser (780/60, 660/20) and violet laser (530/30, 450/20). We use BD LSRFortessa (seria Number H647800L5015) with saline filter (BD, CA 2503, 343542) to analyze the endothelial cell embryonic development. The filter includes blue laser (710/50, 530/30, 488/10), yellow green laser (780/60, 710/50, 670/30, 610/20/, 586/15), red laser (780/60, 730/45, 670/14), violet laser (610/20, 525/50, 450/50) and UV laser (675/50, 450/50). All FACS samples were transferred to 5 mL tubes (Falcon, 352235) which has 35 μm filter to avoid cell cluster. All tubes are RNase/DNase free. Cells were resuspended in 2% FBS-PBS supplemented with 1 μg/ml DAPI to allow exclusion of nonviable cells when required. EdU was stained using Click-iT EdU Flow Cytometry Assay Kits (Thermofisher Scientific, C10634) following manufacturer's protocol. Cell culture The human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) (ATCC, Cat log. PCS-100-013) were cultured in ECM medium (ScienCell, 1001) with extra Endothelial Cell Growth Supplement (EGCS) (ScienCell, 1052) and grown in 5% CO2 at 37°C. A549 cell line was cultured in DMEM medium (Gibco, C11995500BT) with 10% Fetal Bovine Serum (FBS) (NEWZERUM, FBS-E500) and 1% penicillin/streptomycin (Thermofisher Scientific, 15070063). HEK293T/17 cells were seeded in 10% FBS-DMEM in 10 cm plates at 50% confluency. Recombinant FGF1 was purchased from MedChemExpress (HY-P700289). The HEK293T/17 cells were transiently co-transfection with lentivirus with pLL3.7-GFP-shCasz1/PAX2/pVSVG or Casz1-overexpression/PAX2/pVSVG to produce corresponding virus for infection. To co-culture HUVEC and epithelial cell, matrigel (Corning, 356324) was coated on the outer surface of transwell inserts (Corning, 3460) at 50 μL/cm² and incubated at 37°C for 1 hour. HUVECs stably infected with shCtrl or shCASZ1 were seeded onto the Matrigel-coated side at 1×10⁵ cells/well and adhered for 3 hours at 37°C. Inserts were then inverted into 12-well plates containing 1.5 mL complete ECM medium per well. A549 cells were seeded onto the inner surface at 8×103 cells/well and cultures maintained overnight. The following day, inner compartment medium was replaced with complete DMEM (10% FBS) containing vehicle or 50 ng/mL FGF1, and cells cultured for an additional 48 hours. EdU (20 μM) was added 12 hours prior to analysis, and EdU incorporation assessed by flow cytometry. Tube formation assay To perform tube formation assay, 50 μl of Matrigel (Corning, 354234) was spread evenly on 96-well plates and incubated at 37 °C for 30 minutes. 104 of shCtrl or shCASZ1 infected HUVECs were seeded on top of gel, resuspended in 100 μl ECM (ScienCell,1001), and incubated at 37 °C for 6 hr. Images were captured using an Olympus IX73 microscope with 4x and 10x objective lens. For analysis, the Angiogenesis Analyzer plugin in ImageJ was utilized to quantify tube network formation. Transmigration assays Transmigration assays were conducted using 24-well transwell inserts equipped with 8 μm pore-sized filters (Corning, 353097) and corresponding 24-well culture plates. A suspension of 2 × 10⁴ shCtrl or shCASZ1 infected HUVECs in ECM was placed in the upper chamber. The lower chamber was filled with 700 μL of ECM containing EGCS. After 12 hours of incubation, the cells attached to the upper surface of the filter membranes were carefully removed using cotton swabs, while the cells that had migrated to the lower side of the filter were stained with crystal violet. Images were captured using an Olympus IX73 microscope with 4x and 10x objective lens. For analysis, the migrating cells were counted by ImageJ interface. Cut&Tag-seq The CUT&Tag assay was performed utilizing the Hyperactive Universal CUT&Tag Assay Kit for Illumina (Vazyme, TD903). 105 FACS-sorted lung EC from Casz1em1Zyliu reporter mice were harvested and washed with 500 μL of wash buffer before binding to ConA beads for 10 minutes at room temperature. The cells were then incubated with 1 μg of HA-Tag (CST, 3724S) antibody at 4 °C overnight. Following this, anti-rabbit IgG was added and allowed to incubate for 1 hour at room temperature. The cells were then washed three times with Dig wash buffer and incubated with 0.04 μM pA/G–Tnp for 1 hour at room temperature. Following three washes with Dig-300 buffer, the cells were resuspended in Trueprep Tagment Buffer L and incubated at 37 °C for 1 hour. The tagmentation reaction was halted by the addition of proteinase K, Buffer L/B, and DNA extraction beads. After incubation at 55 °C for 10 min, cells were plated on a magnet and unbound liquid was carefully removed. The beads were gently washed twice with 80% ethanol, and DNA was subsequently eluted using double-distilled water. Library preparation was carried out using the 'TD903 Hyperactive Universal CUT&Tag Assay Kit for Illumina' and the 'TD202 TruePrep Index Kit V2 for Illumina' from Vazyme Biotech. After quality check, the library was used for sequencing. All raw sequence data were quality-trimmed using fastp v0.23.4. Reads were aligned to the mm10 mouse genome with Bowtie2 v2.5.4 and converted to BAM format using SAMtools v1.18. Bigwig files and heatmaps were generated with DeepTools v3.5.5. Peak calling was done with MACS3 v3.0.0a6, and motifs were identified through de novo motif search with Homer v4.11. ScRNA-seq sampling for STED-EC atlas Embryos were collected at 0.5-day intervals between E1.5. and E18.5, with an additional timepoint at E7.75 and at E19.0 (sample at birth). Embryos were imaged for record of developmental staging. Trypan blue staining solution was added to count cell number and assess cell viability. Single-cell samples were collected from mouse embryos at different timepoints by different protocols to enhance the efficiency of sampling and adequate coverage of cell types. For all stages, single cells were collected in PCR tube and resuspended in DPBS containing 0.04% BSA (Table S1). E1.5-E2.5: Zona-pellucida free embryos were placed to Ca2+-Mg2+ free DPBS and aspirated repetitively using a finely drawn, mouth-controlled glass pipette to dissociate into single cells. Cells were collected and washed once in M2 medium before transferred to PCR tube. E3.0-E4.5: Zona-pellucida free embryos were collected in M2 medium, then transferred to 100μl enzyme solution (10U/ml papain:accutase = 1:1 v/v) for 30 min. The embryos were dissociated into single cells by repetitive aspiration using a finely drawn, mouth-controlled, glass pipette. Cells were washed twice in M2 medium before transferred to PCR tube. E5.0-E7.5: Embryos were washed with cold DPBS twice, then incubated in 10U/ml papain for 10 min at 37°C in 5% CO2/air and pipetted gently every 5 min. The digestion was halted by adding DMEM containing 10% FBS. 100U/ml DNase I were added to reduce viscosity. Cells were then collected in PCR tube. E8.0-E10.5: Embryos were washed with cold DPBS three times, then incubated in 10U/ml papain for 20 min at 37°C, 5% CO2/air and pipetted gently every 10 min. The digestion was halted by adding DMEM containing 10% FBS. 100U/ml DNase I were added to reduce viscosity. Cells were filtered through 40-μm cell strainers on ice and centrifuged at 4°C, 300g for 5 min and washed once with cold DPBS with 0.04% BSA. For embryo at E10.0 and E10.5, cells were further treated with ACK lysing buffer for 5 min at room temperature to remove red blood cells. Cells were then collected in PCR tube. E11.0-11.5: Embryos were dissected into trunk and head parts, washed twice with cold PBS. The head and trunk parts were digested in 10U/ml papain and 0.05% trypsin for 15 min at 37°C, 5% CO2/air and pipetted gently every 5 min respectively. After digestion, cells were filtered through 40-μm cell strainers on ice and centrifuged at 4°C, 300g for 5min. Cells were treated with ACK lysing buffer for 5min at room temperature to remove red blood cells and washed once with cold PBS with 0.04% BSA once. Cells were then collected in PCR tube. E12.0-15.0: Embryos were washed with cold PBS twice and dissected into three parts: head, trunk(skeleton-skin) and viscera. The head part was digested in 10U/ml papain for 20–30 min at 37°C, 5% CO2/air and pipetted gently every 10-15 min. The trunk part was digested in 0.25% trypsin for 20-30 min at 37°C, 5% CO2/air and pipetted gently every 10-15 min. The viscera was digested in 1mg/ml collagenase I/ II/ IV for 30-60 min at 37°C, 5% CO2/air and pipetted gently every 15-30 min. After digestion, cells were filtered through 40-μm cell strainers on ice and centrifuged at 4°C, 300g for 5min. Cells were treated with ACK lysing buffer for 5min at room temperature to remove red blood cells and washed once with cold PBS with 0.04% BSA once. Cells were then collected in PCR tube. E15.5-E19.0 (Birth): Embryos were washed with cold PBS twice and dissected into four parts: head, skin, skeleton and viscera. The head part was digested in 10U/ml papain for 30 min at 37°C, 5% CO2/air respectively and pipetted gently every 15 min. The viscera was digested in 1mg/ml collagenase I/ II/ IV for 60 min at 37°C, 5% CO2 and pipetted gently every 30–45 min. The skin was digested in 2mg/ml collagenase A and B for 60 min at 37°C, 5% CO2/air and pipetted gently every 30 min. The skeleton was digested in 0.25% trypsin for 20-30 min and afterwards treated by 2mg/ml collagenase II/ D for 60-90 min at 37°C, 5% CO2/air and pipetted gently every 10-15 min. After digestion, cells were filtered through 40-μm cell strainers on ice and centrifuged at 4°C, 300g for 5min. Cells were treated with ACK lysing buffer for 5min at room temperature to remove red blood cells and washed once with cold PBS with 0.04% BSA once. Cells were then collected in PCR tube. ScRNA-seq sampling for lung of Casz1iΔEC Tamoxifen (1 mg) was administered intraperitoneally to pregnant mice daily from E11.5 to E15.5 to activate Cre recombinase. At E18.5, embryonic lung tissues were harvested, digested at 37°C as described aforementioned, and cell suspensions processed for flow cytometry. DAPI⁻CD45(Pacific Blue)⁻Ter119(PE-Cy7)⁻Calcein-AM⁺ lung cells were FACS sorted. Cells were obtained from 14 Casz1iΔEC and 8 littermate control mice; 2.7×10⁴ (Ctrl) and 2.9×10⁴ (Casz1iΔEC, CKO) cells were used for library construction using Chromium Single Cell Reagent Kits V3 (10X GENOMICS) following manufacturer’s instruction. Sequencing was performed on Illumina NovaSeq 6000. Single cell RNA-seq library preparation Single cell suspensions were loaded onto a chromium chip to generate single-cell gel bead-in-emulsions (GEMs) for capturing 500–10,000 single cells per reaction. The single-cell 3′-library was constructed using Chromium Single Cell Reagent Kits V3 (10X GENOMICS) following manufacturer’s instruction. Following cell lysis, first-strand cDNA synthesis and amplification were carried out according to the instruction. Amplified cDNA was purified using SPRIselect beads (Beckman Coulter) and sheared to 250-350 bp. cDNA quality control was performed using Qubit 4.0 Fluorometer and Qsep1 Bio-Fragment Analyzer (Bioptic). The DNA libraries were sequenced by Ilumina Novaseq 6000. Single Cell RNA sequencing analysis Processing of sequencing data The FASTQ files of single-cell libraries generated from Illumina NovaSeq. Original FASTQ files processed by fastp92 which filter out low-quality reads using default parameters: (1) Base quality threshold: Phred quality ≥ Q15 (via -q 15 parameter); (2) Allowed unqualified bases proportion for each read: ≤ 40% (via -u 40 parameter), to get the "Clean" FASTQ files. The clean FASTQ files were aligned to the Mm10 genome with mouse gene annotation of Gencode vM21 version by STARsolo function of STAR (2.7.6a). Low-quality cells were filtered out by the number of unique molecular identifiers (UMIs) and total counts following the pipeline of python package Scanpy (Table S1). We have sequenced a total of 322 single-cell libraries and performed independent quality control (QC) for each library given potential variation in sequencing depth, detailed QC metrics are documented in Table S1. Overall, all cells have passed the following quality control criteria: Minimum threshold for Number of Features: 1000; Maximum threshold for Number of UMIs: 200,000; Maximum threshold for % mitochondrial transcripts: 20%; No filtering was applied to % ribosomal transcripts (Figure S1D). The total count of each cell was normalized to 10,000 using the sc.pp.normalize_total and loge transformation using sc.pp.log1p functions from Scanpy. The gene expression level in the manuscript was calculated by the loge-normalized expression values, which was defined as “mean expression” in the analysis. Some of expression level indicated the smoothing log-normalized expression (by generalized additive model) after 0–1 normalization, which was defined as “Norm. mean expression” to facilitate better visualization. Definition of endothelial cells Unsupervised clustering was applied to the transcriptomic profile of all sequenced cells to obtain distinguishable cluster for consensus gene module scoring and key endothelial marker expression detection. We scored cells from mouse embryos using the average expression levels of 25 endothelium-related marker genes (Cldn5, Tek, Plxnd1, Robo4, Erg, Nos3, Emcn, Cav1, Fabp4, Sox17, Fgd5, Flt1, Flt4, Aplnr, Apln, Nr2f2, Efnb2, Ephb4, Vwf, Eng, Tie1, Plvap, Podxl, Icam1, CD34). The cell cluster with the highest endothelial score at each time point was selected and defined as endothelial cells. For the UO arterial ECs subpopulation scoring, we used an additional 7 marker genes to define the cells scoring: Bmx, Efnb2, Vegfc, Sema3g, Alpl, Gja5, and Gja4. Data visualization and clustering For all the ECs from E7.0-E19.0, we used Scanpy for downstream analysis: step Ⅰ, identify highly variable genes (HVGs) with sc.pp.highly_variable_genes (min_mean=0.0125, max_mean=3, min_disp=0.7); step Ⅱ, perform PCA with 60 principal components; step Ⅲ, calculate the k-nearest neighbors of cells (k=20); step Ⅳ, generate UMAP embeddings based on these dimensionality-reduced features. The cells were clustered using the Leiden algorithm with a resolution of 0.3. No batch effect correction was performed during the process. Organotypic endothelial cell annotation To determine the organ annotation of these endothelial cells, we collected 11 public single-cell sequencing datasets of isolated individual organs, including the brain,93 heart,94 lung,24 liver,9 kidney,25,95 spinal cord,96 gastrointestinal tract,97 bone marrow,72 pancreas,98 spleen, muscle, lymph, and testis.15 These datasets cover embryonic and adult stages. We trained an organ label classifier of endothelial cells using Random Forest implemented in scikit-learn and used it to predict the cell label of STED-EC atlas. We used following steps to annotate the organ label. Step1: Firstly, we collect public organotypic endothelial cell datasets in adult mice.15,16 Step2: The adult endothelial cell datasets were used to train the Random Forest Classifier to predict the E19.0 ECs in different organs using RandomForestClassifier implemented in sklearn (with parameters: n_estimators=100, max_depth=20, min_samples_leaf=2), the organ-specific endothelial DEGs were used as input (with parameters: cells_per_group=500, Wilcoxon test pvalue<0.001, log_fold_change>0.2, minimum difference in the fraction of detection between the two groups>0.2). Step3: The initially-predicted E19.0 endothelial population was further analyzed combining unsupervised clustering, organ-specific molecular markers and anatomical tag during sequencing (head, viscera, skin and skeleton) to refine the cell labelling of E19.0 ECs in each organ. The final E19.0 endothelial cell organ annotation was used for further prediction. Step4: Based on developmental time tag during sequencing (E7.0-E7.5), we defined the population of unorganotypic differentiated ECs. Step5: The ECS in each organ of E19.0 (from step 2) was combined with E7.0-E7.5 early-stage ECs (from step 4) to train the Random Forest Classifier to predict the remaining endothelial cells (with parameters: n_estimators=100, max_depth=20, min_samples_leaf=2). Step6: Refine and confirm the cell labelling. We manually checked if the annotation is correct. The cells of each timepoint from STED-EC atlas were clustering. If the organ marker genes expressed by a cluster were consistent with the results of organ label prediction, the cells of this cluster were all labeled with the organ’s tag. If the cells in a cluster did not specifically express the marker genes of any organ, then this group of cells was defined as unorganotypic ECs. Of note, EndoMT cells are strictly defined as those co-expressing Cdh5, Pecam1, Kdr, and at least one marker from the mesenchymal lineage: Pdgfra, Pdgfrb, or Acta2. The calculation of progenitor score and maturity score The organ-specific maturity state genes were defined as the top 15 enriched genes of cells from E18.0, E18.5, E19.0 relative to the other stages and organs (ranked by loge fold changes). The progenitor state genes were defined as the top 15 enriched genes of cells from unorganotypic ECs relative to other cells (ranked by loge fold changes). The progenitor scores were defined by average expression of progenitor markers, and the maturity scores were defined by the average expression of each organ. The gene list can be found in Figure S3D and Table S3. Lineage tree inference We used Moscot, an optimal transport (OT) based method for modeling time series single cell data, to infer the ancestor-descendant relationship of ECs. In detail, the union of cell type marker genes and highly variable genes were used as input. Data pairs from all adjacent time points were selected and subjected to canonical correlation analysis (CCA).99 Subsequently, the TemporalProblem function in moscot was employed to infer the ancestor-descendant OT scores using the top 20 CCA components (with parameters: epsilon=0.001, tau_a=0.99, tau_b=0.999, scale_cost=’mean’). This analysis resulted in transport scores between adjacent time points, the cell types with the highest average transport score were connected. A lineage tree model was build using Python package Toytree,100 where each node is a cell type in a time point, and lines connect the nodes of the same lineage. We then calculated the gene expression of each lineage node. The gene expression of each node is defined as the weighted average of single-cell gene expression on the transport score. Notably, to reduce the discovery rate of false positive gene expression, the transport score was restricted in the cells of each node, the cells that do not belong to the node will not participate in the calculation. The pathway score was calculated by the average gene expression of each pathway; the pathway gene sets were collected from Gene Ontology (R package org.Mm.eg.db) and Reactome Pathway (R package reactome.db) databases. Score values exceeding the 95th percentile were clipped to the 95th percentile for each pathway. Gene regulatory network (GRN) analysis We performed gene regulatory network (GRN) analysis on all endothelial cells using pySCENIC. We firstly use the GRNboost function in pySCENIC to identify the genes with high correlation together with the expression of transcription factors (TFs). The genes, together with transcription factors, form a regulon. Notably, we used a TF list from the AnimalTFDB database for our calculations, as it is more comprehensive than the TF list provided by the SCENIC database. Genes lacking regulatory relationships with their respective TFs in each regulon were pruned using the SCENIC ranking database; however, regulons containing TFs present in AnimalTFDB but not in the SCENIC database were not pruned. Finally, the regulon score was calculated as the average expression of the genes within each regulon. The top 5 regulons of each organ are shown in Figures 3H and S4H. Integration of human and mouse data We evaluated different integration methods followed BENGAL pipeline.58 This analysis uses two metrics to evaluate integration performance. The species mixing score indicates the mixture of mouse and human cells in integrated space. The biology conservation score reflects the discriminability of different cell types after integration, which is used to evaluate the presence of over-correction. Higher values for both scores represent better performance. Species mixing was assessed by 4 established batch correction metrics for scRNA-seq. This includes the principal component regression (PCR), batch average silhouette width (bASW), graph connectivity (GC) and k-nearest neighbour batch effect test (kBET). The scIB package was used to calculate the metrics.101 All metrics were computed on the latent embedding resulted from integrated methods. We computed these 4 metrics in 9 integration strategies and 1 unintegrated data with homology genes. For each metric, we performed min-max scaling to reflect the relative performance of different strategies in concordance with scIB. We included the unintegrated data in the scaling as a reference, to avoid minor differences in metrics between algorithms that performed similarly well enlarged by scaling. Species mixing score is the average of the scaled 4 metrics. Species mixing score = average ( PCR scaled , bASW scaled , GC scaled , kBET scaled ) Biology conservation was assessed by 3 biology conservation metrics for scRNA-seq. Biology conservation metrics include cell type average silhouette width (cASW), normalised mutual information (NMI), and ARI. We computed these 4 metrics in 9 integration strategies and 1 unintegrated data with homology genes using scIB and perform min-max scaling. Biology conservation score is the average of the scaled metrics. Species mixing score = average ( PCR scaled , bASW scaled , GC scaled , kBET scaled ) After multiple integration methods evaluation, we used Harmony CCA and SeuratV3 CCA for human and mouse data integration with the following steps. Step 1, we aligned mouse gene symbol with human gene symbol according to the human-mouse homologous gene table provided by MGI database (https://www.informatics.jax.org/downloads/reports/HOM_MouseHumanSequence.rpt). Step 2, Seurat canonical correlation analysis99 was performed on the combined mouse and human data, jointly embedding the cells into 40 canonical components with highly variable genes using sc.pp.highly_variable_genes function (min_mean=0.0125, max_mean=3, min_disp=0.7). All components were then used as input for canonical correlation analysis (CCA), resulting in 20 CCA components. Step 3, the Harmony algorithm102 was applied to the CCA components to correct for batch effects. These batch-corrected harmony components were used for visualization with UMAP. The trajectory analysis was then performed in the harmony space using scFates.84 In trajectory analysis, the diffusion components calculated by Palantir83 were used for trajectory inference, the scFates parameters were: method="ppt", Nodes=50, use_rep="palantir", ppt_lambda=100, ppt_sigma=0.1, ppt_nsteps=100. Cell-cell communication analysis We analyzed ligand-receptor interactions using LIANA+ and CellChat, with human-mouse homologous genes as input. Given that both methods utilize their own ligand-receptor databases, each containing unique entries, we integrated the cell-cell interaction analysis results from the two approaches to retain more comprehensive information. We set type = "truncatedMean" and trim = 0.1 when running computeCommunProb of CellChat. To ensure consistent results, we used the same ligand-receptor probability algorithm as CellChat when calculating interactions with LIANA+. The ligand-receptor connection diagram was drawn using the R package iTALK. Calculation of stage similarity We selected out the lung endothelial cells from the E18.5 control and Casz1iΔEC scRNA-seq, and integrated them with the E12.0-E19.0 pulmonary ECs of STED-EC atlas using Harmony. We took the average of harmony corrected principal components of Casz1iΔEC data, and pulmonary ECs of each time point from STED-EC atlas. Then, we calculated the gene expression distance between Casz1iΔEC data and STED-EC atlas pulmonary ECs, d = 1 - r, where r is the Pearson correlation coefficient. We defined the similarity as the exponential transformation of the expression distance. 𝑠 𝑖 𝑚 = exp ( - 𝑑 2 ) Spatial sequencing and analysis Spatial sequencing was conducted following published MISAR-seq, and the method details of MISAR-seq can be found in previous reference26. Only spatial transcriptomic data were analyzed. In brief, the main process includes tissue preparation, permeabilization, reverse transcription, barcode ligation, tissue lysis, library preparation, and Next Generation Sequencing (NGS). Tissue slides are firstly thawed and fixed with formaldehyde, followed by quenching with glycine and washing with DPBS-RI. Permeabilization is then carried out using an Omni-ATAC buffer, followed by washing with ATAC-RSB buffer. For reverse transcription (RT), an RT mixture is used and the tissues are incubated at room temperature and 42°C. For in situ ligation of the first and second barcodes, PDMS chips are covered on the tissue regions of interest, and the PDMS devices are clamped tightly. Ligation mixtures are prepared and loaded into the devices, which are then incubated. Tissue lysis is performed using a reverse crosslinking mixture, and the lysate is collected and incubated. PCR is performed and used for cDNA library construction. The beads are washed and resuspended in a TSO solution and incubated. They are then resuspended in a PCR solution and PCR is performed. The PCR product is purified and used for library preparation with a TruePrep DNA Library Prep Kit V2 for Illumina. The size distribution of the library is determined by Qsep100, and NGS is conducted on an MGI-seq 2000 sequencer in paired-end, 100-base-pair mode. Barcode matrix file was generated for downstream analysis. To filter the data in non-tissue regions, microscope fluoresce images with two channels were used to identify the pixel locations with manual selection using Adobe Photoshop and a mask picture generated in which the tissue region was filled in white while the non-tissue region was filled in with black. Then we used a custom python script to get the filtered barcode location to filter the fragment file and feature barcode matrix file. Bulk RNA-seq Analysis The RNAs of HUVEC were extracted based on a standard TRIZOL extraction protocol. The raw sequence data from Bulk RNA-seq were quality-trimmed using the default options of fastp software v0.23.4. Reads were aligned to the human genome hg19 using Bowtie2 v2.4.4. Transcript abundance was measured with RSEM v1.3.1. Custom scripts written in R v4.2.2 were used to carry out the analysis. Differential gene expression across sample pairs was evaluated using DESeq2 v1.38.0, focusing on Fold Change (FC) and p-values for multiple hypothesis testing. In the overexpression group, 148 genes showed significant differential expression (p-value < 0.05), compared to 96 genes in the control group. Visualization of these differentially expressed genes was done using Pheatmap v1.0.12, and further visualization, including volcano plots, was performed with ggplot2 v3.4.0. Quantification and statistical analysis All results (error bars) are presented as mean ± s.e.m. Number of animals or cell samples represents biological replicates and is indicated in corresponding figure legends. Comparisons between different groups were performed using two-tailed Student's t test unless otherwise indicated in figure legends. p values are indicated in the graphs, and p values below 0.05 were considered to be statistically significant. metadata.title: A new way to express yourself: Gemini can now create music
metadata.summary: The Gemini app now features our most advanced music generation model Lyria 3, empowering anyone to make 30-second tracks using text or images.
metadata.content: Use Lyria 3 to create music tracks in the Gemini app A new way to express yourself: Gemini can now create music Feb 18, 2026 · Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link The Gemini app now features our most advanced music generation model Lyria 3, empowering anyone to make 30-second tracks using text or images in beta. Joël Yawili Senior Product Manager, Gemini app Myriam Hamed Torres Senior Product Manager, Google DeepMind Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Since launching the Gemini app, we've built tools to encourage creative expression through images and video. Today, we're taking the next step: custom music generation. Lyria 3 , Google DeepMind’s latest generative music model, is rolling out today in beta in the Gemini app. Just describe an idea or upload a photo, like “a comical R&B slow jam about a sock finding their match" and in a matter of seconds, Gemini will translate it into a high-quality, catchy track. To push the creative envelope further, you can even ask Gemini to take inspiration from something you upload. Lyria 3 improves on audio generation from our Lyria models in three important ways: No need to provide your own lyrics! They'll be generated for you based on your prompt. You have more creative control over elements like the style, vocals and tempo you want. You can create more realistic and musically complex tracks. Here’s how you can use it: Text to track: Describe a specific genre, mood, inside joke, or memory to create unique tracks with lyrics or instrumental audio that fits your vibe. “I’m feeling nostalgic. Create a track for my mother about the great times we had as kids and the memories of her home cooked plantains. Make it a fun afrobeat track with a true African vibe.” From photos and videos to track: Upload a photo or video and watch Gemini use the content to compose a track with lyrics that fit the mood perfectly. “Use these photos to create a track about my dog Duncan on a hike in the woods.” The Gemini app creates 30-second tracks with custom cover art generated by Nano Banana. This makes it easy to quickly share with friends by downloading or simply clicking the share link. The goal of these tracks isn't to create a musical masterpiece, but rather to give you a fun, unique way to express yourself. Your browser does not support the audio element. Sweet Like Plantain Creators can also explore Lyria 3 on YouTube’s Dream Track . Available in the U.S. and now rolling out to YouTube creators in other countries, Lyria 3 will enhance the quality of each unique Shorts soundtrack. Whether it's creating a lyrical verse or a vibey backing track, being able to better customize the soundtrack will take creators’ Shorts to the next level. New audio verification capabilities All tracks generated in the Gemini app are embedded with SynthID , our imperceptible watermark for identifying Google AI-generated content. We are also giving you more tools to help identify AI content, broadening our verification capabilities in the Gemini app to include audio, along with image and video. Simply upload a file and ask if it was generated using Google AI, and Gemini will check for SynthID and use its own reasoning to return a response. Our commitment to developing generative AI responsibly Since we first launched Lyria in 2023, we've sought to develop this technology responsibly in collaboration with the music community. We've learned a lot through these collaborations and our experiments, like Music AI Sandbox , and have been very mindful of copyright and partner agreements as we've trained Lyria 3. Music generation with Lyria 3 is designed for original expression, not for mimicking existing artists. If your prompt names a specific artist, Gemini will take this as broad creative inspiration and create a track that shares a similar style or mood. We also have filters in place to check outputs against existing content. We recognize that our approach might not be foolproof, so you can report content that may violate your rights or the rights of others. Additionally, in order to use our products, users must adhere to our Terms of Service and Gen AI prohibited use policies , which prohibit violations of others’ intellectual property and privacy rights. Lyria 3 is available in the Gemini app for all users 18+ in English, German, Spanish, French, Hindi, Japanese, Korean and Portuguese, with plans to expand quality and coverage of more languages, rolling out on desktop today and to the mobile app over the next several days. And Google AI Plus, Pro and Ultra subscribers will enjoy higher limits. Our goal with music generation in the Gemini app is to help you add a fun, custom soundtrack to your daily life. Try it out today at gemini.google.com .
