Discussion Complementary imaging and modeling allowed us to resolve the native choreography of the ExHOS and cellular membranes during exocytosis. The stoichiometry and plasticity of the ExHOS within a stepwise tethering mechanism We showed that, on average, 7 exocysts organize in a ring-shaped ExHOS to control vesicle tethering. The number of exocysts is remarkably similar to the Munc13 hexamers that have been proposed to control mammalian synaptic exocytosis,45,46 however, the radius of synaptic vesicles is nearly half as compared with those of secretory vesicles in yeast.47 The similarity in the stoichiometry of related—yet evolutionarily distant—pathways suggests that the number of exocysts might be critical for their function, such as the lateral immobilization of the tethered vesicle. Integrative modeling provides mechanistic clues on tethering initiation Although tethering starts when the vesicle is at ∼45 nm from the PM (Figure 6D), the dimensions of the exocyst structure in isolation cannot account for such a distance (Figure 7; Video S1). Instead, our reconstruction of the initial tethering hypothesizes that the extension of the Sec3’s N terminus (residues 250–611 that were not resolved by cryo-EM) might be critical to determine the longest distance at which vesicles can be tethered (Figure S7B). Indeed, this flexible stretch can link the exocyst with the Sec3 pleckstrin-homology (PH) domain that targets the complex to the PM18 for up to 126 nm (in an ideal full extension). Interestingly, Sec3’s N terminus contains 24 phosphorylation sites, which have been suggested to regulate Sec3 folding and binding to partners.18 The post-translational modification of Sec3’s N terminus would provide a fast mechanism for the regulation of vesicle kinetics along step 1. The role of SNAREs in a stepwise tethering mechanism The coincidence of MS2, step 3, and MS3 with Sec9 and Sec1 clusters opens the possibility that the formation of the trans-SNARE complex plays a role in the stepwise mechanism. Supporting this idea, structural modeling shows that yeast exocytic SNAREs associated with the vesicle and the PM can only start zippering when the two membranes are found at distances under 24 nm (Figure S7C). While first interactions between SNAREs may happen in MS2, the proximity between membranes in step 3 and MS3 suggests that the vesicle displacement involves the zippering of the trans-SNARE complex. Interestingly, reconstitution of vesicle tethering with the isolated human exocyst detected distal tethering (32.1 nm) but could not recapitulate proximal tethering observed in MS2 and MS3,48 further supporting an essential role of the SNAREs in the confinement of secretory vesicles at 18 and 5 nm from the PM. Sec18 promotes ExHOS disassembly to preserve the rate of exocytosis After fusion, the stationary ExHOS, with a radius of 38 nm, remains associated with the PM for 1.9 s. Here, we have shown that Sec18 is required for the native disassembly of ExHOS (Figure 5). Unexpectedly, upon partial depletion of functional Sec18, we could not detect a defect in mNG-Sec9 activation, whose capacity to cluster in exocytic events remained unimpaired (Figure 5G). Instead, the rate of clustering of exocyst-mCh and Bgl2 secretion dropped by more than 40% (Figures 5F and 5H), indicating that the initiation of new exocytic events is limited by the recycling of exocysts rather than the recycling of SNAREs. Thus, our results underscore the functional relevance of ExHOS disassembly: a mechanism that ensures new secretory vesicles are only engaged for tethering if ongoing exocytic events are terminating normally. Although we showed that Exo84 and Sec18 interact in close proximity, the mechanism used by Sec18 to disassemble ExHOS remains unknown. It is unlikely that exocyst release involves the hydrolysis of ATP, as the unwinding of the cis-SNARE complex, known to involve this activity,15 occurs 2.5 s later (Figures 3B and 3C). Indeed, mNG-Sec9 release poorly correlates with exocyst release (r = −0.21), suggesting that ATPase activity is not involved in the disassembly of ExHOS. Instead, we hypothesize that ATP binding by the D2 domain of Sec18 or the action of Sec17 (or other unknown proteins) would provide the energy required to disassemble the ExHOS. Unfortunately, our attempts to resolve this mechanism by using Sec18 mutants or Sec17 constructs resulted in major defects of the exocyst subcellular distribution that prevented us from deriving meaningful data. Overall, this study provides quantitative insights into the biophysical principles that drive tethering of secretory vesicles. Given the exocyst’s central role across multiple cellular processes and diseases, these insights could help advance our understanding of the exocyst’s mechanism of action across biology more generally. Limitations of the study Capturing mechanistic nuances, such as reversibility in dynamics or biological heterogeneity, remains unattainable because of the need for averaging. For example, while the average copy of exocyst subunits is highly homotypic, the exocyst clusters show a broad distribution of brightness and lifetime that suggests larger differences among individual events (Figures 3C and S1D). Although ring-shaped ExHOS suggest a homotypic conformation of the multiple exocysts, no current technique can experimentally resolve individual exocysts. Despite calibration, the estimated radius of ExHOS may have a few nm offsets because SMLM localizes fluorescent tags. Along these lines, the variance in the size and tethering distance of vesicles imaged by cryo-CLEM prevented subtomogram averaging of proteins captured in expectably different conformational states, necessary to adapt to the different geometries found in situ. Resolving how the continuum landscape of ExHOS conformations is linked to the kinetics of the tethered vesicle opens up an avenue for understanding the mechanism of the exocytic machinery as an ensemble. We forecast that the continuum dynamics of proteinaceous higher-order structures and membrane deformation kinetics will be central in the study of other pathways in membrane biology. Quantifoil Micro Tools Cat# Q2100CR1.3 Open table in a new tab Experimental model and study participant details All strains used in this study were derived from Saccharomyces cerevisiae BY4741 and BY4742 backgrounds. A complete list of the strains used in this study can be found in Table S2 and protocols for strain generations are described below. Unless otherwise indicated, yeast cells were inoculated from single colonies in 3 mL of YPD and grown overnight at 30 °C. The next morning, saturated cultures were diluted in yeast extract peptone dextrose (YPD) or low-fluorescence media and grown for a minimum of 5 h until they reached OD600 of 0.8-1. Method details Yeast strain generation Standard PCR-based genetic manipulation methods were used to generate strains with C-terminally tagged proteins.49 Shortly, a DNA cassette containing the tag followed by a selectable marker was amplified using oligos that matched the C-terminal end of the desired protein. This cassette was inserted into the parental stain and transformed colonies were selected according to the proper selection marker. Seamless N-terminal tagging was done as described by Khmelinskii et al.50 Briefly, a DNA cassette containing the first 180 bp of the tag, two I-SceI restriction sites surrounding a selectable marker for the synthesis of uracil (URA3) and the full-length tag was inserted into the desired parental strain. Transformed colonies were plated on plates containing galactose to induce the expression of I-SceI. This causes the excision of the URA3 marker and homologous recombination between the N-terminal fragment of the tag and the full-length tag. Finally, colonies are plated onto 5-FOA plates to test for the successful removal of URA3 marker. For all strains, the correct integration of inserts was validated by colony PCR. Moreover, fluorescent tags were also confirmed by live-cell imaging. Cryo-electron tomography Sample preparation and tomogram acquisition To prepare samples for cryo-ET,23 cells expressing exocyst-mNG or mSc3-Sec9 were grown in YPD at 30 °C and 200 rpm overnight. The next morning, they were diluted and grown until they reached OD600 = 0.6, thereafter glycerol was added to a final concentration of 5%. In the case of the Sec18-FRB depletion strain, cells were incubated with 10μM of rapamycin for 10 to 15 minutes. 4 μL of cells were deposited on glow-discharged Cu 200 mesh R1.2/1.3 grids (Quantifoil), 3.5 μL on the front and 0.5 μL at the back side. The grids were blotted and then plunged frozen into liquid ethane by back-side blotting for 4 s using an automated Plunge Freezer EM GP2 (Leica). Grids were clipped in FIB-compatible autogrid cartridges, loaded into an Aquilos 2 Cryo-FIB (ThermoFisher Scientific) and coated with platinum for FIB-SEM milling.22 Lamellae were prepared with AutoTEM (ThermoFisher Scientific) software to a target thickness of 160-180 nm. Automatic rough milling was performed with 3 steps, with 1 nA, 0.5 nA and 0.3 nA respectively. After rough milling on all sites, automatic polishing was performed with 50 pA and 30 pA. Lastly, manual polishing with 30 pA at 0.5⁰ overtilt was performed to further improve the quality of the lamellae. Cryo-fluorescence Z-stack images of lamellae were acquired with 100X objective (0.75 NA) in AiryScan mode on LSM900 (Zeiss) equipped with a cryo-stage (Linkam). 488 nm and 561 nm lasers were used to acquire exocyst-mNG and mSc3-Sec9 images, respectively. The Z-stacks were aligned with StackReg,51 then maximum intensity projection was done in Fiji52 for later correlation. At EMBL Imaging Centre, grids with lamellae were loaded into a Titan Krios G4 (ThermoFisher Scientific) equipped with SelectrisX energy filter and Falcon4i camera, operated with SerialEM software.53 Medium magnification montages of the lamellae were acquired and blended with Etomo.54 Then medium-mag-montages and their corresponding fluorescence map were registered in ICY with ec-CLEMv2 plugin,55 so that the fluorescence signal could be used to guide the high-magnification tilt series collection. Dose-symmetric tilt-series were acquired in SerialEM with PACE-tomo56 during three sessions with different acquisition parameters. The tilts series were recorded over a tilt range of 108° where possible, starting from the milling angle, with an angular increment of 2° or 3°. The total dose of the tilt series was 140e/A2. The raw frames were acquired and stored in EER format, then later processed to reduce beam-induced motion. Tilt-series were acquired with a pixel size between 1.96 and 3.04 Å, with defocus. Table S3 summarizes and compares the acquisition parameters of the four batches. Tilt series processing A total of 736 tilt series were acquired in four batches. In three of these batches, cells with the exocyst fused to mNeonGreen (exocyst-mNG) were used, while the other batch corresponds to cells where Sec9 has been N-terminally tagged with mScarlet3 (mSc3-Sec9). For batch 1 (exocyst-mNG, pixel size = 3.044 Å, 57 tilt images in angular steps of 2° between -46° and 66°) frame alignment for motion correction was performed with the implementation of the UCSF motioncor2 program in Relion 457 using whole frame correction. For batch 2 (exocyst-mNG, pixel size = 1.968 Å, 37 tilt images in angular steps of 3° between -63° and 45°), batch 3 (mSc3-Sec9, pixel size = 1.968 Å, 37 tilt images in angular steps of 3° between -45° and 63°) and batch 4 (exocyst-mNG, pixel size = 1.968 Å, 41 tilt images in angular steps of 3° between -66° and 54°) frame alignment for motion correction was performed in Relion 457 using 25 patches. Tomographic alignment and reconstruction of each tilt series in batches 1 and 4 was performed with AreTomo 1.2.058 and in batches 2 and 3 with IMOD 4.11.1254 using patch-tracking.59 A total of 76, 112, 220 and 328 tilt series were acquired for batch 1, 2, 3 and 4, respectively. All tomograms were reconstructed using either the SART algorithm provided by the Aretomo package58 or the SIRT-like reconstruction protocol of IMOD.54,59 Tomogram annotation and inspection were done in Dynamo.60 All recorded tilt series have been made public in EMPIAR61 under the accession code EMPIAR-12989. Tomogram analysis Segmentation of membranes Membrain-Seg62 was used to identify pixels potentially belonging to membranes using the pre-trained MemBraine_seg_v10_alpha weights on a version of the tomograms downsampled four times. For each tomogram, the normalized score map produced by Membrain-Seg was binarized (with an intensity threshold of 0). The content of the binarized map was analyzed through Matlab's bwconcomp function to reveal the connected components in the tomogram. Connected parts were divided into coherent supervoxels with an in-house, Matlab based code, aiming at identifying coherent regions of a characteristic volume of about 5000 voxels, assumed to be fragments of membranes. Edge filtering of the corresponding regions in the tomogram allowed for assigning to each supervoxel a normal vector that captured the orientation of the membrane fragment it contained. The centroids of those supervoxels were then clustered by DBSCAN in its Matlab implementation. We used an ad-hoc built distance metrics that promotes grouping supervoxels according to local norm similarity and to mutual positioning in an orthogonal arrangement to both normals. In general, this automatic procedure produces very few classification errors: assignment of supervoxels from different membranes to the same cluster is a rare event. Also rare, but more frequent, is the failure to cluster all fragments of the same membrane into the same class: in some cases, the PM of a yeast cell appears not as a single entity but distributed in a few areas. Such cases were identified and manually curated during visual inspection of results. Finally, in order to generate a smooth representation of each membrane, the centroids in a class were used as input for the alphaShape algorithm63 in Matlab with the smallest alpha radius for which all centroids are connected. This results in a triangulation of arbitrary mesh parameters, allowing for a fine sampling of the membrane geometry. Vesicle radius and distance to PM estimation The initial evaluation of vesicle radius and their distribution in relation to the distance to the plasma membrane (Figure 1A) was performed using tomograms from batches 1 and 2. A two-step procedure was applied to improve the quality of the measurements. The first step consisted in a visual inspection of the tomograms with the goal of removing those tomograms that presented global issues such as problematic vitrification, ice contamination, broken lamellas or similar issues that caused deformations during the alignment procedure. The second step consisted in a second round of visual inspection focusing on the quality of the vesicles and the plasma membrane. The reasons for the exclusion of tomograms in this step were: i) vesicles that were too close to the edges of the tomogram, ii) vesicles damaged by the FIB-milling procedure, and iii) unclear definition of membrane boundaries. This two-step analysis reduced the number of tomograms from 188 to 61, allowing the modelling of 370 vesicles and the computation of the radius and vesicle-PM distances using the method described below. Table S4 summarizes the characteristics of the vesicles used for this measurement. Measurement of vesicle-PM distance The simple geometry of vesicles made it possible to identify them by manual picking using a spherical model followed by fast visual curation. This was done using the dtsmlice GUI of Dynamo.60 Dipoles models were manually created on the tomograms. Then, the correspondences between vesicles in the tomogram and models were inspected visually by representing the model as a super-imposed transparent sphere. As such, the vesicles were described merely by their central point and radius. The distance from each vesicle to the closest point in the PM was computed by searching to the closest barycenter in the smooth triangulation provided in the previous step to the vesicle centers. This information was then compensated by the vesicle radius to give an initial automatic estimation of vesicle-PM distance. A further estimation of the vesicle-PM distance was then done manually. In this approach, for each vesicle, the previous estimation of the vesicle-PM geometry was used to define a plane that sectioned the vesicle and crossed the closest point of vesicle and the closest point of the PM. This plane was used to generate and represent an image that was used to manually select more precise estimations of the closest points on the surface of the vesicle and the surface of the plasma membrane. The relative distance between these points was considered an updated estimation of the vesicle-PM distance. This typically resulted in a change of the estimated distances in the order of the nanometer, as the thickness of the membranes can be taken into account more precisely. Selection of isolated vesicles To select isolated vesicles that correlated with exocyst-mNG or mSc3-Sec9 clusters, the following criteria were used: i) a diffraction-limited fluorescence spot had to be observed close to the PM, ii) the vesicle had to be closer than 70 nm from the PM, iii) the vesicle had to be at the center of the tomogram (i.e., >250 nm from the edge), and iv) no vesicles closer than 250 nm could be observed. The estimation of vesicle-PM distance of vesicles correlating with exocyst-mNG signal was performed on the batches 1, 2 and 4. After applying the filtering described above, the number of tomograms was reduced from 516 to 70, allowing the modelling of 76 isolated vesicles. For tomograms in batch 3 (mSc3-Sec9) an additional filtering step was applied: all isolated vesicles were visually inspected to ensure that the closest membrane to the vesicle was the PM. This procedure reduced the number of used tomograms from 220 to 5, allowing the modelling of 5 isolated vesicles. Table S5 summarizes the characteristics of isolated vesicles used for distance estimation. Measurement of vesicle sphericity To assess possible deformations in the shape of the exocytic vesicles due to the presence of forces that might deform vesicles along tethering, we compared their shape at the metastable states MS1-3. Each vesicle subtomogram in states MS1, MS2 and MS3 was annotated manually with the dtmslice tomogram viewing tool in the Dynamo package,60 marking an average of ∼300 points on each vesicle. The cloud of points annotated on each vesicle was fitted into an ellipsoid through a Matlab script, assigning to each vesicle a set of directions and lengths that define the orientation and semiaxes of the fitted ellipsoid. Because of the missing wedge in tomographic reconstruction, an elongation in the direction close to the electron beam was systematically detected (Figure S6A). Correlations between the two minor axes of each fitted ellipsoid and the metastable state where the vesicle was found in were analyzed with an in-house Matlab script that was not able to detect relevant deviations from sphericity (Figure S6B). Possible correlations of these parameters and membership in the predefined classes were investigated through in-house Matlab scripts. These results agree with a fast fusion event, but do not rule out the existence of forces that might deform the vesicle shape during the short lapse of time that separates the end of MS3 and the estimated fusion. These measurements were done on isolated vesicles that correlated with exocyst-mNG (40 vesicles) or mSc3-Sec9 signal (5 vesicles). Subtomogram Averaging Several approaches were used for subtomogram averaging (STA) experiments. In a first approach we used Dynamo60 for the alignment of the interstitial space of 281 vesicles extracted from 277 tomograms, from the Batches 2, 3 and 4. Those tomograms were processed using the same protocol SART reconstruction with a common pixel size to allow for a fair comparison between all the particles. From these reconstructions, the distance between vesicles and plasma membrane was measured to classify vesicles into their respective metastable states. To increase the number of particles available for STA, all well-reconstructed particles located sufficiently close to the membrane were included, even if the vesicles were not isolated vesicles. We used the vesicles by selecting as center of the extracted subtomograms the approximate found midpoint between vesicle and plasma membrane. Additionally, the vector defining the closest direction between vesicle and plasma membrane was used as initial orientation of the subtomograms for STA. Such experiments used a pixel size of 7.92 Å and 12.18 Å, and an initial lowpass of at least 16 nm and 24 nm, respectively. They were repeated for different parameter combinations such as field of view of the subtomogram box (ranging between 120 and 240 nm), extent and shape of the mask to selectively exclude areas of the membrane and/or vesicle, and selection of subsets of particles with a homogeneous interstitial distance (MS1, MS2 and MS3 in the text). In a second approach, STA was carried towards the alignment of individual exocyst proteins. In order to possibly limit the number of conformations, we selected the 98 vesicles corresponding to the MS2 state with a pixel size of 7.92 Å, and analyzed the interstitial space with template matching64 searching for individual copies of the exocyst using as template a single particle map of the exocyst complex available in the Electron Microscopy Data Bank65 (accession code: EMD-6827) rescaled to a pixel size of 7.92 Å. The search was performed with an angular interval of 5 degrees. Only the peaks located in the interstitial space were selected for the evaluation in order to avoid false positives originated by the plasma membrane or the vesicle. After extraction of a total of 1394 and 2601 particles for a cross-correlation threshold of 0.2 and an angular coherence of 5 and 20 degrees between the normal of the vesicle and the orientation obtained from template matching, respectively. Several STA experiments were performed, varying the initial orientation of the particles for avoiding the template bias (from an azimuthal randomization to a complete perturbation). Such experiments used an initial lowpass of above 10 nm to avoid transmission of template bias into STA computations. Live-cell imaging Sample preparation for live-cell imaging For all live-cell imaging experiments, cells were grown at 30 °C and 180 rpm overnight until saturation. The next morning, cells were diluted in low fluorescence media (Yeast Nitrogen Base Low Fluorescence without Amino acids, Folic Acid and Riboflavin, 2% Complete Supplement Mixture Drop-out without Trp, and 2% glucose), grown for 5 h until OD600 = 1 approximately, and attached to Concanavalin A-coated coverslips. Microscope setups Images were obtained with a Nikon Eclipse Ti2-E inverted microscope configured in 5 different setups: 1) Prime 95B camera (Photometrics), 100X/1.45 NA objective (Nikon), 488 nm 50 mW laser (Coherent, OBIS) with iLas2 controlled by Modular V2.0 software (Gataca Systems) for an homogeneous oblique illumination and a filter cube containing ZET488/561x, ZET488/561m-TRF and ZT488/561rpc as excitation, emission, and dichroic filters, respectively (all from Chroma); 2) sCMOS Zyla 4.2 camera (Andor, Oxford Instruments), SR HP Apo TIRF 100x/1.49 objective (Nikon), 488 nm 50 mW and 561 nm 150 mW lasers (Coherent, OBIS) with iLas2 controlled by Modular V2.0 software (Gataca Systems) and a dual bandpass filter cube (ZET488/561x, ZT488/561rpc and ZET488/561m-TRF as excitation, dichroic and emission filters, respectively), and 3) Prime 95B camera (Photometrics), SR HP Apo TIRF 100x/1.49 objective (Nikon), SpectraX Lumencor LED illumination system, with excitation filters of 475/35 nm (Semrock) for mNG and 575/35 nm (Chroma) for mCh, a FF505/606-Di01-25x36 dual band-pass dichroic mirror (Semrock), and FF01-524/628-25 dual band-pass emission filter (Semrock), 4) sCMOS Zyla 4.2 camera (Andor, Oxford Instruments), SR HP Apo TIRF 100x/1.49 objective (Nikon), 488 nm 50 mW TIRF and 488 nm 150 mW FRAP lasers (both Coherent, OBIS) with iLas2 controlled by Modular V2.0 software (Gataca Systems) and a dual bandpass filter cube (ZET488/561x, ZT488/561rpc and ZET488/561m-TRF as excitation, dichroic and emission filters, respectively), and 5) sCMOS Zyla 4.2 camera (Andor, Oxford Instruments), SR HP Apo TIRF 100x/1.49 objective (Nikon), SpectraX Lumencor LED illumination system, with excitation filters of 475/35 nm (Chroma) for mNG and 575/35 nm (Chroma) for mCh, a FF505/606-Di01-25x36 dual band-pass dichroic mirror (Semrock), and FF01-524/628-25 dual band-pass emission filter (Semrock). In all cases, the microscope was controlled by μManager software.66 Live-cell copy number quantification Cells expressing a target protein endogenously tagged to a fluorescent protein (i.e., Sec3-GFP, Sec5-GFP, Sec6-GFP, Sec8-GFP, Sec10-GFP, Sec15-GFP, Exo70-GFP, Exo84-GFP, Sec2-mNG, mNG-Sec9 or Sec18-mNG) were mixed at a 1:1 ratio with cells expressing Cse4-GFP or Cse4-mNG and attached to a concanavalin A-coated coverslip. Z-stacks of 21 frames separated by 250 nm were acquired using a 100 ms exposure, utilizing microscope setup 1 (see microscope setups section). The average copy number of the reference, Cse4, has been recently quantified by Single Molecule Localization Microscopy (SMLM).25 Cse4 clusters in cells undergoing anaphase were tracked over the Z-stack using TrackMate67 with a spot diameter of 7 pixels. The plane with the highest corrected total intensity (CTI) was determined by 𝐶 𝑇 𝐼 = 𝐼 𝑠 𝑝 𝑜 𝑡 − 𝐼 𝐵 𝐺 ∗ ( 𝐴 𝑠 𝑝 𝑜 𝑡 / 𝐴 𝐵 𝐺 ) , where 𝐼 𝑠 𝑝 𝑜 𝑡 / 𝐵 𝐺 and 𝐴 𝑠 𝑝 𝑜 𝑡 / 𝐵 𝐺 represent the integrated intensity and area of the selected spot and the local background, respectively. The local background is defined as the circular region with twice the diameter of the selected spot and that surrounds this spot. If CTI maximum occurred in the first or last frame, the Cse4 cluster was discarded. Afterwards, PM-associated, isolated and static target protein clusters (fluorescent spots without apparent in-plane movement) were manually chosen. Those events were tracked with a spot-diameter of 3 pixels, and the CTI was calculated as explained before. The target protein copy number ( 𝑛 𝑡 𝑎 𝑟 ) was calculated by the stoichiometry ratio 𝑛 𝑡 𝑎 𝑟 = 𝑛 𝑟 𝑒 𝑓 ∗ ( 𝐼 𝑡 𝑎 𝑟 / 𝐼 𝑟 𝑒 𝑓 ) , where 𝑛 𝑟 𝑒 𝑓 is the number of Cse4 in a cluster (4.8 ± 2.4 Cse4 per kinetochore,25 which leads to 𝑛 𝑟 𝑒 𝑓 = 76.8 ± 9.8 Cse4 per cluster during telophase or anaphase), and 𝐼 𝑡 𝑎 𝑟 and 𝐼 𝑟 𝑒 𝑓 are the median of the CTI values for the corresponding protein target and Cse4, respectively. The error associated to 𝑛 𝑡 𝑎 𝑟 was calculated as described in Picco et al. (2015).24 The average exocyst copy number was obtained by averaging the copy number of all exocyst subunits. Single particle tracking Images were acquired using the microscope setup 2 (see microscope setups section). A cage incubator mounted on the microscope (Okolab) was used to keep a constant 25 °C environment. Simultaneous acquisition was performed with an OptoSplit II Bypass image splitter (Cairn Research). A quadrant of 512x700 pixels centered in the illumination maxima of the camera sensor was used. Movies were acquired at 8.7 frames per second (fps) to a total length of 70 seconds. An exposure time of 80 ms was used, and laser power was manually optimized for each protein. Zyla camera was set to 540 mHz and binning 2. C1 spots were tracked with TrackMate,67 setting the Difference of Gaussians (DoG) method with a particle diameter of 3 pixels. Tracks closer than 10 pixels from the image borders and those with a duration shorter than 10 frames were discarded. The polarized nature of exocytosis challenges the detection of isolated events. To aid the detection of isolated exocytotic events we included three additional features into TrackMate: Track_Quality_Enviroment, Track_Quality_Before and Track_Quality_After. All three are computed over the 32-bits DoG-filtered movie. Track_Quality_Enviroment is defined as the mean intensity of the local background along the track (i.e., pixels at 2 and 3 pixels from the mean track centroid). A value close to zero of this feature indicates a uniform background signal along the track duration (i.e., no track overlapping has occurred). Track_Quality_Before and Track_Quality_After are the mean intensity of those pixels within a distance of 1.5 pixels from the mean track centroid ∼500 ms before the track start and ∼500 ms after the track end, respectively. High values of these features might indicate overlapping with neighboring tracks or a deficient tracking, since the intensity at the exocytic site is expected to be close to background levels just before and after exocyst clustering. The remaining supernatant was removed, and spheroplasts were washed twice in spheroplast washing buffer (50 mM Tris–HCl, pH 7.5, 1.4 M D-Sorbitol, 10 mM NaN3, 10 mM NaF). For intracellular protein extraction, spheroplasts were lysed in 20 mM Tris–HCl, pH 7.5, 100 mM NaCl, 2 mM MgCl2, 0.5% Triton X-100, 1x protease inhibitor cocktail (100 ng/mL of Antipain, Leupeptin, Pepstatin A, in DMSO and 1mM phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride PMSF) and incubated on ice for 10 minutes. Affinity purification-mass spectrometry Affinity purification with crosslinking Yeast cells were grown overnight at 30°C and 180 rpm until saturation. Cultures were diluted in 600 mL YPD and grown at 30°C to an OD600 of 0.8-1. Cells were harvested by centrifugation (1000 x g, 10 min, 4°C), and washed twice with resuspension buffer (50 mM HEPES, 150 mM NaCl, pH 7.4 supplemented with protease inhibitors (100 ng/mL of Antipain, Leupeptin and Pepstatin A in DMSO and 1 mM phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride PMSF). The final pellet was resuspended in 1 mL resuspension buffer and quickly frozen in liquid nitrogen in a drop-by-drop fashion. Cell lysis was performed using Freezer/Mill® model 6775 (1 min pre-cooling, 2 min running, 1 min interval, 1 min cooling, rate: 11, cycles: 3) (SPEX SamplePrep, LLC). Lysates were resuspended in 5 mL resuspension buffer and clarified by centrifugation at 17,000 × g for 10 min at 4°C, and the supernatant was collected for downstream processing. A fresh stock solution of disuccinimidyl suberate (DSS) (100 mM), a cross-linker 11.4 Å in length, was equilibrated at room temperature for 10 min before use. Cross-linking was initiated by adding DSS to the lysate at a final concentration of 0.5 mM, followed by incubation at room temperature for 1 hour with gentle mixing. The reaction was quenched by adding glycine to a final concentration of 100 mM and incubating for 15 min at room temperature. Samples were centrifuged (17,000 × g, 10 min, 4°C), and the clarified supernatant was used for immunoprecipitation. GFP-Trap and blocking agarose beads were equilibrated by washing five times in PBS. For each sample, 90μL of blocking beads were incubated with the lysate for 1 hour at 4°C on an orbital shaker to reduce nonspecific binding. The blocked lysate was collected by centrifugation (7000 rpm, 30 sec, 4°C) and transferred to fresh tubes containing 90μL of GFP-Trap beads. Samples were incubated overnight at 4°C on an orbital shaker. The next day, beads were collected by centrifugation, washed five times with a stringent buffer (2M NaCl, 8M urea, 1% Triton X-100) and five times with PBS, changing tubes after the last wash in each condition. Mass spectrometry Beads used in immunoprecipitation were cleaned three times with 500 μl of 200 mM ammonium bicarbonate and 60 μl of 6M Urea/200mM ammonium bicarbonate were added. Samples were then reduced with dithiothreitol (30 nmol, 37 °C, 60 min), alkylated in the dark with iodoacetamide (60 nmol, 25 °C, 30 min) and diluted to 1M urea with 200 mM ammonium bicarbonate for trypsin digestion (1 μg, 37°C, 8h). After digestion, peptide mix was acidified with formic acid and desalted with a MicroSpin C18 column prior to LC-MS/MS analysis. Samples were analyzed using a Orbitrap Fusion Lumos mass spectrometer (ThermoFisher Scientific) coupled to an EASY-nLC 1200 (ThermoFisher Scientific). Peptides were loaded directly onto the analytical column and were separated by reversed-phase chromatography using a 50-cm column with an inner diameter of 75 μm, packed with 2 μm C18 particles. Chromatographic gradients started at 95% buffer A and 5% buffer B with a flow rate of 300 nl/min and gradually increased to 25% buffer B and 75% A in 52 min and then to 40% buffer B and 60% A in 8 min. After each analysis, the column was washed for 10 min with 100% buffer B. Buffer A: 0.1% formic acid in water. Buffer B: 0.1% formic acid in 80% acetonitrile. The mass spectrometer was operated in positive ionization mode with nanospray voltage set at 2.4 kV and source temperature at 305°C. The acquisition was performed in data-dependent adquisition (DDA) mode and full MS scans with 1 micro scans at resolution of 120000 were used over a mass range of m/z 350-1400 with detection in the Orbitrap mass analyzer. Auto gain control (AGC) was set to ‘standard’ and injection time to ‘auto’. In each cycle of data-dependent acquisition analysis, following each survey scan, the most intense ions above a threshold ion count of 10000 were selected for fragmentation. The number of selected precursor ions for fragmentation was determined by the “Top Speed” acquisition algorithm and a dynamic exclusion of 60 seconds. Fragment ion spectra were produced via high-energy collision dissociation (HCD) at normalized collision energy of 28% and they were acquired in the ion trap mass analyzer. AGC and injection time were set to ‘Standard’ and ‘Dynamic’, respectively and isolation window of 1.4 m/z was used. Digested bovine serum albumin was analyzed between each sample to avoid sample carryover and to assure stability of the instrument and QCloud74 has been used to control instrument longitudinal performance during the project. Acquired spectra were analysed using the Proteome Discoverer software suite (v2.5) and the Mascot search engine (v2.6).75 The data were searches against a Saccharomyces Genome database (as in April 2022, 6049 entries) plus a list76 of common contaminants and all the corresponding decoy entries. For peptide identification, a precursor ion mass tolerance of 7 ppm was used for MS1 level, trypsin was chosen as enzyme and up to three missed cleavages were allowed. The fragment ion mass tolerance was set to 0.5 Da for MS2 spectra. Oxidation of methionine and N-terminal protein acetylation were used as variable modifications whereas carbamidomethylation on cysteines was set as a fixed modification. False discovery rate (FDR) in peptide identification was set to a maximum of 1%. Peptide quantification data were retrieved from the “Precursor ions quantifier” node from Proteome Discoverer (v2.5) using 2 ppm mass tolerance for the peptide extracted ion current (XIC). The obtained values were normalized with the median of EXO84 and have used to calculate protein fold-changes and their corresponding p-value and adjusted p-values. The raw proteomics data have been deposited to the PRIDE77 repository with the dataset identifier PXD061766. Single Molecule Localization Microscopy Sample preparation for SMLM Sample preparation for SMLM26 was performed as previously described.78 Briefly, yeast cells were grown at 30 °C and 180 rpm overnight until saturation. The next morning, the cultures were diluted and grown at 30°C to an OD600 = 0.8. 2 ml of culture was pelleted (2500 rpm), resuspended in 100 μl of YPD and pipetted onto a Concanavalin A-coated coverslip. After 15 minutes in a humidified atmosphere, the non-attached cells were removed by decantation. For the Sec18 anchor-away, after 5 minutes of attachment, rapamycin was added to a final concentration of 10 μM and incubated for 10 more minutes. Coverslips were then submerged into a freshly prepared fixation solution (4% paraformaldehyde and 2% sucrose in PBS). After 15 minutes of gentle shaking, they were removed from the fixation solution and submerged into a quenching solution (100 mM NH4Cl in PBS) for 15 minutes with gentle shaking. Quenching was repeated twice. Finally, coverslips were washed three times in PBS for 5 min. SMLM imaging All Single Molecule Localization Microscopy (SMLM) images were acquired on a custom-built, fully automated microscope, which was built for stable long-term automated image acquisition, and featured homogeneous high-power illumination as described previously.79 The free-space output of a commercial LightHUB laser box with 405 nm, 488 nm, 561 nm and 638 nm laser lines was focused on a speckle reducer and coupled into a multimode fiber. The output of the fiber was then imaged into the sample to homogenously illuminate a circular area of ∼1000 mm. Fluorescence was collected through a 160x NA 1.43 TIRF objective (Leica), filtered by a bandpass filter (for GFP: 525/50; for mMaple: 600/60), and focused onto an Evolve512D EMCCD camera. The z focus was optically stabilized by total internally reflecting an additional IR laser off the coverslip onto a quadrant photo diode, which was coupled into an electronic feedback loop with the piezo objective positioner. Z focus stability was typically better than 5 nm/h. All microscope components are controlled by a custom-written plugin for μManager.80 Samples were mounted in 1 mL of imaging buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 8 in 95% D2O) and sealed with parafilm to prevent evaporation. The back focal plane was imaged and visually inspected to make sure no air bubbles were present in the immersion oil. Then, videos of 15000-50000 frames were acquired using the 561 nm laser at 7-9 kW/cm2 with an exposure time of 30 ms, and a camera EM gain and readout rate of 200 and 10 MHz, respectively. During acquisition, mMaple was slowly photoconverted to its red state by 405 nm illumination. The 405 nm pulse duration was controlled through an automatic feedback loop to maintain the number of blinks constant. When all mMaple was photoconverted and no more blinking was observed, acquisition was stopped. Photoconversion parameters were optimized so that no overlapping point spread functions (PSFs) were observed. After acquiring SMLM data, a diffraction-limited snapshot of GFP or mNG signal was collected using a 488 nm laser and the same camera parameters as previously described. To automatically image multiple regions of one sample, the stage position list of μManager was used to define a grid of 80-100 positions. There was a separation of 200 μm in each X and Y direction between positions to avoid undesired photoactivation and photobleaching due to scattered light. A waiting time of 3 s was established between positions to allow for mechanical equilibration of the stage after its movement. SMLM data processing and analysis Super-resolution microscopy analysis platform (SMAP) was used to reconstruct SMLM data.81 All images were automatically fitted during acquisition. For the reconstruction, all localizations found in consecutive frames within a range of 75 nm were grouped into one localization. Localizations with a PSF standard deviation greater than 160 nm and a localization precision that exceeded 25 nm were discarded. To visualize the images, localizations were rendered using Gaussian kernels with a standard deviation proportional to their localization precision. A minimum Gaussian standard deviation of 6 nm was used. To correct for chromatic aberrations between SMLM and diffraction-limited (DL) images, a predetermined transformation was used to align red (photoconverted mMaple) and green (GFP or mNG) images. The transformation was created by imaging and localizing more than 1000 TetraSpeck beads in both channels. Then, a projective transformation was created from their positions. This correction was also done using SMAP. To select isolated exocytic sites, cells were first automatically segmented by the “SegmentCellsCME” plugin from SMAP. Each cell was visualized using SMAP ROI manager, from where individual clusters (correlating to isolated DL GFP or mNG spots) were identified. Exocyst clusters were only segmented at the center of the cell surface to avoid tilted structures. Those DL spots that were not in the central region of the cell surface or that did not colocalize with mMaple signal were manually discarded. Finally, just those selected sites containing more than 30 localizations –which correspond to 3 exocysts on average- were considered for further analysis. SMLM copy number quantification Nuclear pore complex (NPC) proteins can be used as reference standards for assessing molecular counting in SMLM experiments.28 Following this idea, yeast cells expressing Nup188, an NPC subunit, labeled with mMaple (Nup188-mM), were imaged using the optical settings previously described. The segmentation of Nup188-mM clusters was done manually using the ROI Manager interface of SMAP. The mean ( 𝐿 𝑅 ) and standard deviation ( 𝜎 𝑅 ) of the distribution of localizations per Nup188-mM cluster was used to estimate the number of exocysts ( 𝑁 𝑇 ) , by computing the ratio 𝑁 𝑇 = ( 𝐿 𝑇 / 𝐿 𝑅 ) ∗ 𝑁 𝑅 / 3 , where 𝐿 𝑇 is the mean number localizations per exocyst-mM or exocyst-mM-GFP cluster, 𝑁 𝑅 = 16 is the average number of Nup188 per NPC28 and the factor 3 accounts for each exocyst being labeled with 3 mMaples. The error associated with 𝑁 𝑇 is calculated as 𝑁 𝑇 ∗ ( 𝜎 𝑅 / 𝐿 𝑅 ) 2 + ( 𝜎 𝑇 / 𝐿 𝑇 ) 2 . All code is available at https://github.com/GallegoLab. SMLM analysis Modeling the conformational space of ExHOS We aimed to model the space of possible higher-order structures in which multiple exocysts can bind the vesicle and the PM simultaneously. To do this, the exocyst was represented as a rigid cylinder with a height ( 𝐿 𝑒 ) of 32 nm and a diameter ( 𝑊 𝑒 ) of 13 nm, based on the overall exocyst dimensions in the cryo-EM structure (PDB82: 5YFP). Note that this is likely an underestimation of the exocyst dimensions as 18% of the exocyst amino acids, mostly Sec3 and Exo84 N-termini, could not be resolved. The vesicle was represented as a sphere of radius ( 𝑟 𝑣 ) of 41.2 nm (this value was derived from the cryo-ET experiments, see Figure 1). Additionally, the effective radius ( 𝑟 𝑒 𝑓 𝑓 ) of the vesicle was increased by 4 nm to account for the minimal space that the Sec4-Sec2 complex occupies on the vesicle surface (PDB: 2OCY). Assuming (i) the exocyst-vesicle and exocyst-PM binding sites are located at the extreme of the axial axis of the cylinder and (ii) the exocysts are bound radially outwards to the vesicle, the allowed configurations can be parametrized with an angle 𝜃 varying in the range [ 0 , 𝜋 / 2 ] , where 𝜃 = 0 when the longest axis of the exocysts are orthogonal to the PM, and 𝜃 = 𝜋 / 2 when the longest axis of the exocysts are parallel to the PM. For a given exocyst, we defined the coordinates of the contact point with the PM { 𝑥 0 , 𝑦 0 , 𝑧 0 } and the coordinates of the contact point with Sec4-Sec2 complex at the vesicle surface { 𝑥 1 , 𝑦 1 , 𝑧 1 } as follows: { 𝑥 0 , 𝑦 0 , 𝑧 0 } = { 𝑟 𝑒 𝑓 𝑓 cos 𝜃 , 0 , 𝑑 𝑉 − 𝑃 𝑀 + 𝑟 𝑣 − 𝑟 𝑒 𝑓 𝑓 sin 𝜃 } { 𝑥 1 , 𝑦 1 , 𝑧 1 } = { 𝑥 0 ± 𝐿 𝑒 2 − 𝑧 0 2 , 0 , 0 } , where 𝑑 𝑉 − 𝑃 𝑀 is the vesicle-PM distance. We were particularly interested in the radial position (respect to the shortest axis between the vesicle and the PM) of the exocyst centroids (ρ), that can be computed as ( 𝑥 0 + 𝑥 1 ) / 2 . This parameter served us as descriptor of the ExHOS. The underlying organization of the ExHOS highly depends on the conformational relationship among the exocysts present. For example, a heterogeneous ExHOS where the multiple exocysts are positioned in random locations, but always fulfilling the condition of binding the vesicle and the PM simultaneously. On the other hand, a homotypic ExHOS where the exocysts adopt the same conformation relative to the vesicle and the PM leads to ring-shaped ExHOSs (all ρ’s values would be equal). In this case, the maximum number of exocysts ( 𝑁 max ) can be approximated as 𝑁 max = 𝑥 0 / 𝑊 𝑒 and the coordinates for jth exocyst can be obtained by applying a rotation with angle 2 𝜋 / 𝑁 max ∗ 𝑗 around the Z-axis. In the homotypic situation, the radius of the resulting ring-shaped ExHOS depends on the 𝑑 𝑉 − 𝑃 𝑀 and 𝑁 𝑚 𝑎 𝑥 . By imposing 𝑁 max ≥ 6 (since the average number of exocysts determined by live-cell imaging was 7 ± 1 exocysts in each cluster; Figures 1B and S1D), the distal tethering ( 𝑑 𝑉 − 𝑃 𝑀 = 31 nm) leads to exocyst configurations of radius within 15-22 nm. Instead, for the proximal tethering ( 𝑑 𝑉 − 𝑃 𝑀 = 4 nm ), radii in the range 28-50 nm are possible (Figure 1D). All code is available at https://github.com/GallegoLab. Synthetic SMLM datasets We simulated a set of SMLM images for all the possible higher-order structures modeled for distal and proximal tethering. Firstly, between 6 and 8 exocyst centroids were distributed uniformly along a ring (or randomly inside a patch) of radius 𝑟 for a homotypic (or the heterotypic) ExHOS. For each exocyst, three mMaple were positioned randomly, with their centroids following a two-dimensional Gaussian distribution with zero mean and a standard deviation of 10 nm along each direction. Each mMaple had a probability of emitting of 0.55, as previously determined.28 The number of blinking events, 𝑛 , per emitting mMaple was simulated using a log-normal distribution with parameters obtained from the fit of the number of localizations per cluster of the Nup188-mM (Figure S2). Finally, the localizations were distributed around each mMaple centroid position following a two-dimensional Gaussian distribution with zero mean and a standard deviation corresponding to an average localization precision of 20 nm along each direction. The resulting set of XY-coordinates from the generated localizations was used for image rendering and subsequent analysis. For Compact and Expanded ExHOS, synthetic images were randomly selected from 𝑟 values in the range from 15 to 22 nm and from 28 to 50 nm, respectively. All code is available at https://github.com/GallegoLab. SMLM data classification For a given synthetic SMLM image containing the set of N localizations with coordinates { 𝑥 𝑗 , 𝑦 𝑗 } , with j=1,···,N, a ring center { 𝑐 𝑥 , 𝑐 𝑦 } and radius 𝑅 𝑇 estimated using the Taubin algorithm83 implemented in the Python library circle_fit that aims to minimize the algebraic function 𝐹 ( 𝑐 𝑥 , 𝑐 𝑦 , 𝑅 𝑇 ) = ∑ 𝑗 = 1 𝑁 [ ( 𝑥 𝑗 − 𝑐 𝑥 ) 2 + ( 𝑦 𝑗 − 𝑐 𝑥 ) 2 − 𝑅 𝑇 2 ] 2 / ∑ 𝑗 = 1 𝑁 [ ( 𝑥 𝑗 − 𝑐 𝑥 ) 2 + ( 𝑦 𝑗 − 𝑐 𝑦 ) 2 ] 2 Taubin’s center estimation achieves the lower Kanati-Cramer-Rao bound,84 which establishes a limit of the precision of the parameter estimation given the average SMLM resolution. In addition to 𝑅 𝑇 and its associated error, a series of geometrical features were computed for all the synthetic images based on the Taubin center, including the first and second circular moment and the inner radius. The gyration radius, which does not rely on the Taubin center, was also considered. The mathematical expressions for all these geometrical features are provided in Figure S4. A matrix containing the values of the geometrical features for all the synthetic images was generated. This matrix served as input for training a random forest classifier to classify the synthetic SMLM images into the categories Compact and Expanded ExHOS, implemented using the ensemble.RandomForestClassifier library from Scikit Learn 1.3.2.85 We performed a randomized grid search to tune the model's hyperparameters. The optimal configuration utilized 100 decision trees, a maximum tree depth of 5, and considered the square root of the total features at each split (max_features=”sqrt”), with bootstrap sampling. This model achieved an average accuracy of 0.90 in classifying the synthetic data. The relative importance of the geometrical features in the random forest model and the average images of the predicted classes are shown in Figure S4. Finally, after computing the described geometrical features for the experimental set of images of isolated exocyst-mM (or exocyst-mM-GFP) clusters, the optimized random forest classifier was applied to predict the ExHOS class (Compact or Expanded). This prediction was repeated 30 times with randomizations of the training dataset, and the average prediction result was reported (Figure S4A). All code is available at https://github.com/GallegoLab. SMLM averaging and ExHOS radius estimation Those images belonging to a class (Compact or Expanded) were aligned to their Taubin’s center and weighted-averaged, i.e., 𝐼 𝑎 𝑣 𝑔 ( 𝑥 , 𝑦 ) = ∑ 𝑖 𝜔 𝑖 𝐼 𝑖 ( 𝑥 , 𝑦 ) / ∑ 𝑖 𝜔 𝑖 , where 𝜔 𝑖 is the random forest-score for the i-th image. Then, from the average radial density 𝑔 ( 𝑟 ) , the mean distance-to-center was computed: ∫ 0 ∞ 𝑟 ∗ 𝑔 ( 𝑟 ) 𝑑 𝑟 . Because of the existence of estimation bias of the underlying ExHOS radius,84 a bias-correction was implemented by creating a calibration curve between the underlying radii of the ExHOS and the corresponding localizations mean distance-to-center in the synthetic dataset. Note that, as SMLM localizes tags, potential few-nm systematic offsets may remain despite calibration. All code is available at https://github.com/GallegoLab. Estimation of ExHOS conformational dynamics The transition from Compact to Expanded classes of ExHOS was modeled as a first-order reaction process, according to an effective rate 𝑘 . The relative population of the Compact ExHOS at a given time t after exocyst clustering, 𝑝 𝐶 𝑜 𝑚 𝑝 𝑎 𝑐 𝑡 ( 𝑡 ) , is governed by the differential equation: 𝑑 𝑑 𝑡 𝑝 𝐶 𝑜 𝑚 𝑝 𝑎 𝑐 𝑡 ( 𝑡 ) = 𝑘 ∗ 𝑝 𝐶 𝑜 𝑚 𝑝 𝑎 𝑐 𝑡 ( 𝑡 ) , with 𝑝 𝐶 𝑜 𝑚 𝑝 𝑎 𝑐 𝑡 ( 𝑡 ) + 𝑝 𝐸 𝑥 𝑝 𝑎 𝑛 𝑑 𝑒 𝑑 ( 𝑡 ) = 1 . Based on the trend observed in the Sec2-GFP and mNG-Sec9 correlative SMLM experiments (Figure 4A), it is reasonable to assume that exocysts are organized exclusively in a Compact structure during the initial time-point of the tethering, leading to the condition 𝑝 𝐶 𝑜 𝑚 𝑝 𝑎 𝑐 𝑡 ( 0 ) = 1 . Therefore, the solution for 𝑝 𝐶 𝑜 𝑚 𝑝 𝑎 𝑐 𝑡 is given by 𝑝 𝐶 𝑜 𝑚 𝑝 𝑎 𝑐 𝑡 = exp ( − 𝑘 ∗ 𝑡 ) (Equation 1). The reported errors of 𝑘 and predicted frequency of ExHOS classes were calculated using an error-propagation scheme based on the previous equation. Estimation of the vesicle kinetics Assuming the images obtained by cryo-CLEM provide a uniform sampling of the exocytic event lifetime and that the likelihood that multiple exocysts cluster before the arrival of the vesicle is negligible (which is supported by the enrichment of tomograms without vesicle or PM deformation in the cryo-CLEM of cells expressing mSc3-Sec9), it is reasonable to estimate the fusion time based on the frequency of exocyst-mNG correlated-tomograms with and without vesicles. Then, the likelihood to find a tomogram without a vesicle can be modeled with a binomial distribution with a successful probability pfusion. The error associated to the fraction of no-vesicles tomogram is given by 𝑛 ∗ 𝑝 𝑓 𝑢 𝑠 𝑖 𝑜 𝑛 ∗ ( 1 − 𝑝 𝑓 𝑢 𝑠 𝑖 𝑜 𝑛 ) / 𝑛 , where n is the number of sampled tomograms. Considering n = 95, 𝑝 𝑓 𝑢 𝑠 𝑖 𝑜 𝑛 = 0.2 (from the 19/95 observed no-vesicles tomograms; Figure 6A), and the exocyst cluster lifetime is 9.4 s on average, we estimated vesicle fusion occur 1.9 ± 0.4 s before exocyst release (or similarly, 7.5 ± 0.4 s after exocyst clustering), on average. The related error can be estimated by modeling the likelihood to find a tomogram without a vesicle. A similar analysis of the cryo-CLEM of cells expressing mSc3-Sec9 estimated the fusion time to be 3.2 ± 1.1 seconds after Sec9 clustering which yields 6.2 ± 1.1 s after exocyst clustering. This result is in concordance with exocyst-based estimation given the relatively smaller sampling. Importantly, the lack of detected vesicles in our tomograms might happen when the ExHOS is captured in the lamella, but the vesicle is cut relatively peripherally. Thus, the missing wedge might hinder the vesicle detection resulting in “false negative” (i.e. tomograms correlated to diffraction-limited fluorescent clusters but devoid of vesicles because the vesicle detection is prevented by technical limitations). To estimate the upper limit for the fusion time, we assumed that all 19 tomograms devoid of vesicles in the exocyst-mNG dataset (19/95 = 20%) represent the maximum “false negative” rate of our approach. Under this assumption, only 6 of the 14 tomograms in the mSc3-Sec9 dataset would be really devoid of vesicles. Consequently, following the same approach as before, the fusion time would correspond to 8.1 ± 1.1 s after exocyst clustering. Per definition, a fusion time of 8.1 s after exocyst clustering implies that a dataset of 95 tomograms should have about 13 tomograms truly devoid of vesicles. Therefore, we used the fusion time estimated from the exocyst-mNG dataset for further analysis, as the assumption that all tomograms devoid of vesicles in the exocyst-mNG dataset are false negative overestimates the fusion time, while estimations based on small dataset as the mSc3-Sec9 might lack accuracy. Additionally, to model the continuous average vesicle approaching to the PM, we mapped the xth quantiles (x = 1/95,···,76/95) of the exocyst-mNG cryo-CLEM distances to the exocyst lifetime interval (0-9.4 s), (Figure 6D). An interval confidence of this approximation was estimated using a bootstrap strategy, i.e, by randomizing repeatedly the selected measured distances and reapplying the same quantile-to-time mapping. Integrative modelling of exocytosis We integrated key experimental data into a cohesive model of exocyst-mediated vesicle tethering in exocytosis (Figure 7; Video S1). This integrative model combines the continuous ExHOS conformational dynamics (Equation 2, based on SMLM-DL), the vesicle kinetics (Figure 6D, based on cryo-CLEM), the average radius of secretory vesicles (Figure 1A), the average stoichiometry of exocyst clusters and other proteins involved in exocytosis (Figures 1B, S1D, and S3A) and the clustering/disassembly of Sec2, Sec9 and Sec18 from live-cell imaging (Figures 3C and 3D). Modeling the yeast cis-SNARE complex The structure of the yeast cis-SNARE complex was predicted with AlphaFold3 Server86 using the fasta sequences of Sec9 (Uniprot87 ID P40357), Sso1 (Uniprot ID P32867) and Snc1 (Uniprot ID P31109) proteins. The top ranked prediction was used for analysis of the AlphaFold3 metrics86,88 and posterior visualization. Only the confident regions (pLDDT >70) were taken into account to represent the ribbon silhouette of the cis-SNARE complex (Figure S7A, top). Modeling the exocytic trans-SNARE complex Modeling of the trans-SNARE complex conformation was based on the mammalian trans-SNARE complex simulated previously.89 To identify the juxtamembrane linker (L) and the transmembrane region (TMR) of Sso1 and Snc1 proteins we performed a multiple sequence alignment with the mammalian homologs Syntaxin1 (Uniprot ID P32851) and Synaptobrevin2 (Uniprot ID P63045) (Figure S7A). The multiple sequence alignment was performed with Clustal Omega.90 We used MODELLER91 to predict, by comparative modeling, the yeast trans-SNARE complex using the simulated mammalian trans-SNARE complex as template structure. Finally, we used ChimeraX92 to represent the yeast trans-SNARE complex with a density map of 10 Å resolution (Figure S7A, bottom). Quantification and statistical analysis All particle tracking and SMLM experiments were acquired in three biological replicates. More detailed information regarding the number of replicates used in each experiment can be found in figure legends. Error bars in plots indicate the standard deviation (SD) unless otherwise indicated. To compare differences between groups, unpaired Student’s t-tests were performed using the SciPy package. Results were considered significant if p < 0.05. Significance levels are indicated as follows: not significant (ns), p-value < 0.05 (∗), p-value < 0.01 (∗∗), p-value < 0.001 (∗∗∗). metadata.title: Structural decoding of reversible covalent linkage of odorants in human olfactory receptor OR6A2
metadata.summary: The human olfactory receptor OR6A2, re-engineered to be functional, demonstrates the mechanism by which it detects aldehydes. Using this approach, Wang, Wu, et al. uncovered a broadly conserved activation switch in class II odorant receptors. This work also outlines a practical approach to decode smell, with potential uses in fragrance design and inflammation therapy.
metadata.content: Skip to Main Content Skip to Main Menu Outline Get Access Cite Share Set Alert Get Rights Reprints Previous article Next article Highlights • Cryo-EM structures of consOR6 reveal distinctive features of the OR6 subfamily • Back-mutated OR6A2 regains odorant responses seen in wild-type OR6A2 • Reversible covalent Schiff base linkages for odorants recognition are uncovered • A simplified activation mechanism and native Golf protein binding mode for ORs are elucidated Summary Olfactory receptors (ORs) are a diverse superfamily of G protein-coupled receptors responsible for odor detection that are also implicated in non-olfactory physiological functions. OR6A2, a class II OR, selectively senses medium-chain aldehydes and belongs to a cluster of ORs genetically associated with the “soapy” perception of cilantro. It also modulates macrophage-mediated inflammatory responses. Structural studies of ORs have long been challenging. Using a back-mutation strategy, we engineered a functional OR6A2 variant (bmOR6A2) from a consensus OR6 (consOR6). Structures of bmOR6A2 in complex with aldehydes reveal a novel ligand-recognition mechanism involving a reversible Schiff base linkage with residue K4.60, validated by mass spectrometry. By integrating structures of consOR6, molecular dynamics simulations, and functional assays, we identified a conserved D45.51Y6.55Y7.41 triad critical for activation in class II ORs. These findings establish a practical strategy for decoding odorant recognition, offering new insights into olfaction signaling and applications in fragrance and therapeutic development. metadata.title: MYC binding to nascent RNA suppresses innate immune signaling by R-loop-derived RNA-DNA hybrids
metadata.summary: RNA-binding-mediated multimerization of MYC concentrates RNA-degrading factors around double-stranded RNAs and R-loops. This prevents aberrant RNAs from accumulating and leaking into the cytosol. Through RNA binding, MYC suppresses innate immune signaling and promotes tumor growth.
metadata.content: Skip to Main Content Skip to Main Menu Outline Download PDF Cite Share Set Alert Get Rights Reprints Previous article Next article Highlights • MYC is an RNA-binding protein that binds to nascent, intronic RNAs in cells • MYC moves from DNA to RNA under stress and multimerizes around dsRNAs and R-loops • MYC multimers concentrate RNA-degrading factors to limit the buildup of aberrant RNAs • RNA binding of MYC suppresses TLR3-pTBK1 signaling and promotes tumor development Summary In response to perturbed transcription elongation, the MYC oncoprotein multimerizes and undergoes a phase transition. Here, we demonstrate that MYC globally relocalizes from its canonical positions on DNA to nascent RNA upon accumulation of intronic RNA. Upon binding to RNA, MYC forms multimers that concentrate the nuclear exosome, an RNA exonuclease, and its targeting complexes around double-stranded RNA and R-loops. MYC harbors four RNA-binding regions (RBRI–IV). RBRIII promotes MYC multimerization and is necessary for recruiting the exosome to R-loops. RBRIII is dispensable for transcriptional activation and pancreatic tumor cell proliferation in culture, but it is indispensable for sustaining tumor growth in vivo. Via RBRIII, MYC suppresses the accumulation of R-loop-derived RNA-DNA hybrids and prevents them from activating the innate immune kinase TBK1 via the TLR3 pattern recognition receptor. Our data demonstrate that the phase transition of MYC is an RNA-driven stress response that suppresses the accumulation of immunogenic RNA-DNA hybrids. Graphical abstract Keywords MYC RNA binding TLR3 TBK1 R-loop exosome innate immune signaling pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma PDAC Introduction The MYC protein is an oncogenic driver in many tumor entities.1 Relative to normal tissues, MYC expression is enhanced in human tumors due to mutations in the MYC gene or as a downstream consequence of a plethora of alterations in signaling pathways that collectively control MYC expression. Wherever tested, tumors depend on elevated MYC expression throughout their lifetime, prompting numerous attempts to target MYC for tumor therapy.2,3 MYC forms a DNA-binding complex with MAX that associates with most active promoters and enhancers.4,5 The complex exerts both positive and, in conjunction with additional partner proteins, negative effects on the expression of large sets of genes, resulting in a characteristic expression profile of MYC-driven tumors.4,5 Increased MYC expression stimulates cell growth and proliferation and reprograms cellular metabolism. These cell-autonomous effects correlate with the altered expression of the respective MYC target genes.5 However, not all oncogenic effects of MYC can be explained by changes in gene expression.6 For example, MYC establishes an immunologically “cold” microenvironment and allows tumors to escape from immune surveillance.7,8,9,10 Depletion of MYC in a p53/KRAS-driven (“KPC”) model of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC)11 results in tumor regression in immunocompetent mice but has little effect when cells are transplanted into immunodeficient mice.12,13 Mechanistically, MYC suppresses the activity of the TANK-binding kinase 1 (TBK1), which activates nuclear factor κB (NF-κB) and interferon-dependent genes.13,14 Deletion of TBK1 abrogates the dependence of tumor growth on MYC, demonstrating that suppression of TBK1 is the critical function of MYC in this model.12 Activation of TBK1 in MYC-depleted cells depends on Toll-like receptor 3 (TLR3), a pattern recognition receptor,12 which recognizes double-stranded (ds)RNA and RNA-DNA hybrids derived from nuclear R-loops,15,16 arguing that MYC suppresses their accumulation on TLR3 and that this is critical for its oncogenic function. Consistently, MYC represses the transcription of genes that are required for TLR3 function,8,12 but whether MYC directly affects dsRNA or R-loop metabolism is unknown. Both MYC and MYCN directly bind RNA in addition to DNA.17,18,19 In MYC, a short motif (KRR), which is contained in the basic region, interacts with both DNA and RNA and enhances MYC binding to promoters and transcriptional activation of its target genes.19 MYCN harbors a distinct RNA-binding domain in the amino terminus, which is not required for transcriptional activation.17 Rather, MYCN binds RNA as part of the nuclear exosome targeting (NEXT) complex, which targets the nuclear exosome to non-polyadenylated RNAs and promotes the degradation of intron-derived nascent RNAs.20 In MYCN-driven neuroblastoma cells, MYCN RNA binding enhances stress resilience during S-phase, suggesting that it attenuates transcriptional activation in response to transcriptional or replication stress.17,20 A fraction of MYC exists in a multimeric state, and perturbing transcription elongation by inhibition of the spliceosome or the FACT (facilitates chromatin transcription) histone chaperone causes MYC proteins to undergo a phase transition and form large sphere-like structures.21 This transition has little effect on gene expression but protects stalled replication forks from RNA polymerase and prevents transcription-replication conflicts.21 Here, we show that MYC multimerization reflects the transition from a DNA- to an RNA-bound form of MYC. MYC harbors four RNA-binding regions (RBRs), of which RBRIII has no role in transcriptional activation by MYC. Rather, RBRIII promotes MYC multimerization and the recruitment of the nuclear exosome to R-loops. In pancreatic tumor cells, RBRIII suppresses the activation of TBK1 by RNA-DNA hybrids that are derived from nuclear MYC-bound R-loops, directly linking RNA binding of MYC to its ability to suppress innate immune signaling. Results MYC binds nascent RNA To investigate whether MYC is bound to RNA in cells, we performed cross-linking and immunoprecipitation (CLIP) experiments in K562 chronic myeloid leukemia cells, which express elevated levels of MYC.22 SDS-PAGE of immunoprecipitations (IPs) of MYC from UV-crosslinked cells stained positive for RNA, with the signal being sensitive to RNase I (Figure 1A). Control immunoglobulin G (IgG)-IPs and MYC-IPs from cells that were not UV-cross-linked contained no RNA, confirming the specificity of the signal. Analysis of single-end enhanced CLIP (seCLIP) sequencing23 of immunoprecipitated RNA identified 11,077 reproducible enriched windows in MYC-IPs versus 72 reproducible enriched windows in IgG controls using the Skipper algorithm24 (Figure 1B). Heatmaps as well as inspection of individual genes confirmed the specificity of the MYC signal (Figures 1C and 1D). Around 70% of MYC-bound sites were localized in intronic RNA, and about 10% were adjacent to splice sites, indicating that MYC binds to nascent or unprocessed transcripts, consistent with findings for MYCN17 (Figure 1E). Normalizing the number of MYC-bound sequence windows to the total number of windows assigned to different RNA features revealed that MYC RNA binding is distributed evenly across multiple sequence elements (Figure S1A). Direct comparisons suggested that the promoter-distal RNA-binding sites of MYC were not identified in previous analyses mainly due to the use of MACS2, an algorithm developed for identifying short binding sites on chromatin.19 The distribution of MYC binding sites was similar to that of other intron-binding proteins (Figure S1B). Many introns contained multiple MYC-bound windows, suggesting that individual introns are potentially bound by multiple MYC molecules (Figure S1C). GO term analysis did not reveal any enrichment of a functional class of transcripts among MYC-bound genes. De novo motif analysis of MYC-bound RNA windows using either the Skipper or the PureCLIP25 algorithm showed a moderate enrichment of several UG-rich motifs (Figure S1D), similar to MYCN RNA binding.17 MYC RNA-binding sites were not enriched for E-box sequences, to which MYC/MAX complexes bind on DNA. Figure 7 TLR3-bound RNA-DNA hybrids are derived from nuclear R-loops bound by MYC Show full caption Discussion Here, we demonstrate that the MYC protein is a multivalent RNA-binding protein that harbors four RBRs (RBRI–IV). Of these, RBRIV corresponds to the basic region, which also binds DNA.19 The three additional RBRs overlap with evolutionary highly conserved domains termed “MYCBoxes.”6 MYC binds broadly to nascent and intronic RNAs independently of DNA binding at promoters, and mutation of RBRIII compromises this ability. In cells, MYC globally relocalizes from DNA to nascent RNA when RNA processing or transcriptional elongation is perturbed. Stress conditions that enhance MYC RNA binding coincide with the formation of MYC multimers with condensate-like properties.21,45,46 Point mutations that disable RNA binding by RBRIII or the removal of RNA-DNA hybrids by the ectopic expression of RNase H1 compromise the ability of MYC to multimerize in cells, arguing that MYC binding to RNA promotes multimerization. Most likely, MYC multimerization involves the binding of multiple MYC molecules to the same or adjacent RNA molecules, similar to other RNA-protein interactions that compartmentalize RNA metabolic processes.47 Since MYC proteins form droplet-like condensates,21,46 and incubation with RNA moderately enhances condensate formation in vitro, MYC proteins are also likely to have an inherent capacity to multimerize, which is enhanced by their interaction with RNA or other RNA-binding proteins. MYC multimers concentrate the nuclear exosome, a 3′–5′ RNA exonuclease complex, and its targeting complexes around dsRNA and R-loops, arguing that MYC multimers compartmentalize the nuclear RNA degradation machinery. RBRIIIMUTMYC shows reduced binding to multiple introns that can harbor R-loops. In PDAC cells, RNA-DNA hybrids from these R-loops accumulate in cells expressing RBRIIIMUTMYC, but not in cells expressing WTMYC. To suppress RNA-DNA hybrid accumulation, MYC recruits the nuclear exosome to RNA sequences that otherwise form RNA-DNA hybrids and R-loops. In PDACs, RBRIIIMUTMYC promotes cell proliferation in culture but is deficient in sustaining tumor growth in vivo, arguing that RBRIII contributes a critical function to tumorigenesis. MYC suppresses the accumulation of both dsRNAs and R-loop-derived RNA-DNA hybrids on TLR3, which recognizes both nucleic acid species.16,48 While RBRIIIMUTMYC retains the ability to suppress dsRNA accumulation on TLR3, a class of MYC-bound, intron-derived R-loops accumulates on TLR3, and TBK1 is highly active in cells expressing RBRIIIMUTMYC. R-loops can be cleaved from the genome, and R-loop-derived RNA-DNA hybrids can be exported from the nucleus to activate TLR3.16 We propose that RNA binding by RBRIII is critical in tumors since it enables MYC to suppress the accumulation of RNA-DNA hybrids on TLR3, downstream TBK1 activation, and the subsequent TBK1-dependent eradication of tumor cells by the immune system.12 Our data establish that MYC has mechanistically distinct functions in transcription and RNA metabolism. While MYC multimers21 and RNA-bound pools of MYC are detectable in unstressed cells, levels of both greatly increase in response to transcriptional stress. Intriguingly, MYC multimers are present in human colon tumors and PDACs, and depletion of MYC in PDAC cells increases the accumulation of misprocessed RNAs and R-loops in the absence of exogenous stress. Both observations suggest that tumor cells experience endogenous stresses, such as transcription-replication conflicts, that perturb transcription elongation. MYC mutants that are unable to bind RNA retain their mitogenic potential, suggesting that they maintain physiological functions. We therefore propose that targeting the ability of MYC to bind RNA will disrupt the immune-evasive functions of MYC and open a wide therapeutic window. Limitations of the study While RBRIIIMUTMYC shows a substantial decrease in RNA binding, it is not completely deficient, suggesting that other RBRs contribute to RNA binding in cells. Hence, the functions of RNA-bound MYC may extend beyond R-loop metabolism. The mechanisms by which RNA-DNA hybrids are excised from chromatin and exported to the cytosol and how the tumor microenvironment is shaped by RNA binding of the MYC remain to be clarified. Finally, the role of RNA binding in MYC-driven oncogenesis likely differs between tumor entities.
