A number of such combinations have shown better efficacy than monotherapy and current standards of care in a series of late phase clinical trials of patients with renal, lung, hepatocellular, and endometrial cancers, leading to clinical approvals. However, similar trials with different regimens or different drugs from each class in these and other cancer types failed to demonstrate sufficient benefit for clinical approval, indicating the need for further refinement in trial designs. An example of such refinement is the promising development of bispecific monoclonal antibodies (mAbs)—ideal drugs, in principle, for hallmark co-targeting—that concomitantly block VEGFA and PD1 (or PD-L1). Bispecific anti-VEGFA/PD1 mAbs are showing demonstrable efficacy in late-stage clinical trials, though none have yet attained FDA approval, and widely varying responses are being observed in different tumor types. Figure 5 A rationale for therapeutic co-targeting of cancer hallmarks Show full caption The second example involves an anti-VEGFA mAb (bevacizumab) in combination with an inhibitor (olaparib) of the poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) DNA repair enzyme, which targets a vulnerability presented by the enabling characteristic of genome instability consequent to mutationally impaired DNA damage repair pathways. This dual therapy has shown added benefit in certain patients with ovarian cancer, leading to clinical approval (Figure 5B). Another clinically approved example, in certain patients with acute myeloid leukemia (not shown), involves co-targeting resistance to cell death with the BCL-2 inhibitor venetoclax along with epigenetic reprogramming using azacytidine or decitabine, which inhibit DNA methylation and thereby disrupt hallmark-enabling gene expression. The third example, which is intended to illustrate the logic of formulating new conceptual designs, ones that have yet to be clinically validated, involves the lack of generality for immunotherapy of solid tumors. While ICIs have demonstrated historic efficacy in patients with select tumors and subsets thereof, many tumor types do not show responses to monotherapy, or rather, respond transiently. As discussed above, one prominent mechanistic basis for intrinsic and adaptive resistance to ICIs and other immunotherapies involves a multiplicity of cells in the TME that elaborate potent immunosuppressive activities. Therefore, a logical strategy is to block immune checkpoints on T cells concomitant with pharmacological reprogramming of CAFs, TAMs, TANs, cancer cells, and other accessory cells, or subsets thereof, to obviate their immunosuppressive capabilities (Figure 5C). While the first two examples are demonstrably beneficial, albeit not transformative in terms of enduring survival benefit, the results encourage further investigation of hallmark co-targeting trial designs involving logical combinations of these and other cancer drugs—e.g., KRAS inhibitors—that disrupt different, quasi-independent hallmark parameters. Future hallmark co-targeting strategies may prove to have transformative value for cancer patients, not only in improved therapeutic benefits but also in their endurance, by raising the bar for relapse and progression, which would require the induction of multi-faceted adaptive resistance mechanisms for each of the distinctive mechanisms being targeted.48,186,196,197,198,199,200,201,202,203,204,205 In conclusion The conceptual premise set forward in January of the year 2000 has endured, remarkably and unexpectedly, for 26 years, namely that there is a logical underpinning to the complexity and diversity of human cancer. From this foundation, refinements and embellishments have been put forward in a series of publications in the last decade and the current one that have expanded the landscape, albeit complicating the elegant simplicity of the original synthesis. This synopsis has sought to integrate many but not all of the various facets into a new framework, one that hopefully restores some of the conceptual clarity. By considering distinctive parametric classes as different dimensions (Figure 2), the various topical parameters are organized and distilled to crystallize in essence their individual and interactive contributions to cancer. Thus, here and now, there are nine acquired functional capabilities, the hallmarks of cancer, five enabling phenotypic characteristics, and seven classes of hallmark-facilitating cells in the tumor microenvironment, along with a number of instrumental systemic interactions, of which two hallmark-influencing examples are presented. Looking beyond the here and now, to the future, two clear opportunities are discussed, namely (1) to elucidate and illuminate the involvement of the various hallmark parameters in different cancers throughout multi-step tumor development and tumor evolution to states of heightened malignancy and therapy resistance and (2) to investigate the hypothesis that “hallmark co-targeting” of mechanisms underlying quasi-independent parameters could result in more enduring therapeutic responses and impaired adaptive resistance to hallmark-targeting therapies. Certainly, multi-targeting tumors with drug combinations looks to be the future for many forms of human cancer, and perhaps this refined design principle could add impact to such strategies, as two case studies suggest. Finally, this synthesis has not sought to address the question: will there prove to be additional functional capabilities, enabling phenotypic characteristics, and hallmark-facilitating cells in the TME that have demonstrable generality across the spectrum of human cancers and hence become conceptually incorporated? Time will tell. enrichment.normalized_title: Hallmarks of cancer—Then and now, and beyond
enrichment.normalized_summary: Hanahan revisits the evolving framework of cancer hallmarks, synthesizing 25 years of conceptual refinement into a multidimensional view of tumor biology. This review highlights how aberrant capabilities, enabling traits, microenvironmental players, and systemic interactions converge to drive tumorigenesis and proposes that mechanism-guided co-targeting of hallmarks may offer promising therapeutic strategies.

Jane Halpern | Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science Publication Date : February 4, 2026 Press Inquiries Press Contact : Jane Halpern Email: jhalpern@mit.edu Phone: (617) 324-4081 Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science Close Caption : Antonio Torralba is the faculty head of artificial intelligence and decision-making within MIT's Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science. Credits : Photo: Lillie Paquette/School of Engineering Previous image Next image Antonio Torralba, Delta Electronics Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science and faculty head of artificial intelligence and decision-making at MIT, has been named to the 2025 cohort of Association for Computing Machinery (ACM) Fellows. He shares the honor of an ACM Fellowship with three MIT alumni: Eytan Adar ’97, MEng ’98; George Candea ’97, MEng ’98; and Gookwon Edward Suh SM ’01, PhD ’05. A principal investigator within the Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, Torralba received his BS in telecommunications engineering from the Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya, in Spain, in 1994, and a PhD in signal, image, and speech processing from the Institut National Polytechnique de Grenoble, in France, in 2000. At different points in his MIT career, he has been director of both the MIT Quest for Intelligence (now the MIT Siegel Family Quest for Intelligence) and the MIT-IBM Watson AI Lab. Torralba’s research focuses on computer vision, machine learning, and human visual perception; as he puts it, “I am interested in building systems that can perceive the world like humans do.” Alongside Phillip Isola and William Freeman, he recently co-authored “Foundations of Computer Vision,” an 800-plus page textbook exploring the foundations and core principles of the field. Among other awards and recognitions, he is the recipient of the 2008 National Science Foundation Career award; the 2010 J. K. Aggarwal Prize from the International Association for Pattern Recognition; the 2017 Frank Quick Faculty Research Innovation Fellowship; the Louis D. Smullin (’39) Award for Teaching Excellence; and the 2020 PAMI Mark Everingham Prize. In 2021, he was awarded the inaugural Thomas Huang Memorial Prize by the Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence Technical Committee and was named a fellow of the Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence. In 2022, he received an honorary doctoral degree from the Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya. ACM fellows, the highest honor bestowed by the professional organization, are registered members of the society selected by their peers for outstanding accomplishments in computing and information technology and/or outstanding service to ACM and the larger computing community. enrichment.title: Makers Are Building Back Against ICE
enrichment.summary: In hacker spaces and at their homes, creative protesters are laser-cutting and 3D-printing tools to resist an occupation.
enrichment.content: Makers Are Building Back Against ICE | WIRED Skip to main content Save this story Save this story As the US government’s immigration crackdown expands across the country , anxious residents have mobilized to look out for each other. One way they’re doing that is by finding ways to build the tools they need to be resilient against the surge of Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents empowered to kill with impunity . All over the country, makers are 3D-printing thousands of whistles to help people on the ground alert others to nearby ICE activity. But the whistles are far from the only tools being used to respond to the surge of federal agents. Protesters are DIY-ing a wide array of gadgets like camera mounts, mobile networking gear, and handheld eye washers to clear away pepper spray, tear gas, and irritants used to quell protests. Many of these efforts are coming from individual makers. Many of these projects are being made in hacker spaces. Hacker spaces, also called maker spaces, are community centers or warehouse spaces that contain workbenches, 3D printers, laser engravers, power tools, and just about anything somebody might need to build whatever project—digital or analog—they have in mind. They’re also meeting points for like-minded tinkerers and focal points for the hacker community. You can find one near you pretty easily just by searching for it online or using directories . “There is a constant level of inherent stress and anxiety,” says B, a maker who uses hacker spaces in the Midwest and who also asked not to be identified out of fear of retribution from federal agents. “There's like a base level of concern that will not go away for the foreseeable future.” It has been a month since federal agents shot and killed Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis and uprooted life across Minnesota as part of the Trump administration’s Operation Metro Surge. Last week, Trump border czar Tom Homan announced that it would withdraw its forces from Minnesota. It isn’t yet clear how long that process will take, what the scope of the withdrawal is, or whether Department of Homeland Security forces will return. ICE is also looking to extend its reach, secretively leasing spaces for new facilities across the US. Maker spaces are providing the tools to help people push back. Builders are cranking out those whistles, but also 3D-printed tourniquets and mounts for bodycams that observers can wear to free up their hands while filming ICE activity . They’ve become spaces for community readiness meetings and conversations about how to build resilience. They’re also serving as venues for fix-it clinics where folks can get help repairing the damages that occur as people’s tech is broken during protests or after federal agents break doors down while bursting into people’s homes. “Resistance is actually pretty practical,” says a maker who also asked not to be named for fear of retribution. “Anybody can 3D-print a whistle. Anybody can fix a door or laser-cut stencils.” Individually and in communities, people are utilizing techniques and technologies that have been available for years. Meshtastic is a community that uses low-power mesh routers as nodes in an expansive off-grid network that lets people send text messages. Individual routers can be placed on trees or roofs and create expansive networks for communication without having to connect to the internet or cell towers. (The security isn’t perfect, as anyone who happens to have the password for a channel can see the messages within.) If everything works as planned, the setup offers a pretty clear use case for people looking to monitor and communicate about ICE movements without being found out. People can buy and repurpose routers online, or build their own. Woody Poulard, a Meshtastic advocate in New York City who participates at the hacker space NYC Resistor and has distributed a zine about how to use mesh routers, says he has worked with ICE watch volunteers to establish a broader network of mesh communications in New York. In January, he participated in a workshop for people building small router nodes into their phone cases, so they would have an immediately available connector wherever they went. “If there's a natural disaster, it's good for that too,” Poulard says. “But it's perfect for the situation that we're in right now, where you have people you might not want to join a conversation.” Beyond the makers meeting the moment are those preparing for what is likely to come. Artist and crafter Claire Danielle Cassidy has been at the resistance art game for a while in Portland, Oregon, a city that is currently suing ICE over its use of tear gas . She builds solar-panel power banks to charge people’s devices at demonstrations and protests and advocates for joy and “weaponized cuteness,” because “girly culture is going to save us, like it always does.” She spoke to me from her neon-soaked home in Portland, wearing a pair of her own laser-cut earrings that spell out “FUCK ICE.” (You can download the file to make your own.) “Being effective in activism, you don't need to be upset, stressed out, and have an adrenaline response for you to be caring,” Cassidy says. “This is the whole pipeline of fascism: sucking people into shame and fear cycles and trying to take power over the situation. Things can be gentle even in the middle of all of this. And you can still be effective.” The trick to doing that, Cassidy says, is to make it a habit. She runs a pop-up camp called There U Glow , a queer- and femme-led workshop that aims to teach people how to modify LED lights as a fun way to get participants into technical tinkering. “If you learn about how to set up an LED coat, you actually know 75-ish percent of how to set up an off-grid solar array,” Cassidy says. “I can tie that together for people.” Despite the Trump administration’s increasingly aggressive push into cities and communities around the country, Cassidy says crafters and makers are preparing for the worst without sacrificing what makes them human. “We’re not fucking around in the dream space anymore,” Cassidy says “This is a particularly fucking fraught time. But we are still going to live our lives.” Comments Back to top You Might Also Like In your inbox: Sign up for our new Tracker: ICE newsletter The math on AI agents doesn’t add up Big Story: We are witnessing the self-immolation of a superpower Apple finally upgraded the AirTag Marhaba, world! enrichment.title: ArtSci Roundup: March
enrichment.summary: Come curious. Leave inspired. The UW offers an exciting lineup of in-person and online events. From thought-provoking art and music to conversations on culture, history, and science, the UW community invites you to explore, learn, and connect across disciplines throughout the University. And you don’t have to wait until March—take a look at everything still happening this February. In addition, sign up to receive a monthly notice when the ArtSci Roundup has been published. ArtSci On Your Own Time Exhibition |...
enrichment.content: ArtSci Roundup: March – UW News Skip to content All the UW Current site Search scope All the UW Current site Enter search text UW NEWS Come curious. Leave inspired. The UW offers an exciting lineup of in-person and online events. From thought-provoking art and music to conversations on culture, history, and science, the UW community invites you to explore, learn, and connect across disciplines throughout the University. And you don’t have to wait until March — take a look at everything still happening this February. In addition, sign up to receive a monthly notice when the ArtSci Roundup has been published . ArtSci On Your Own Time Exhibition | 2026 Jacob Lawrence Legacy Residency | indira allegra: The Book of Zero (School of Art + Art History + Design) Death is a fundamental first step toward rebirth—but this transition can feel daunting without a compassionate guide. In The Book of Zero, our 2026 Jacob Lawrence Legacy Resident indira allegra presents a multimedia, meditative experience shaped by their research into doula work, death care, and the cyclical nature of bodies and environments. Free. Recorded Lectures | 2026 History Lecture Series – Powers & Punishment: Histories of Incarceration (History) Incarceration is a hotly debated topic in the United States, a country that has one of the highest rates of incarceration in the world. Looking at the practice from a historical perspective, what can incarceration teach us about who we were and who we are now? What might histories of incarceration, and the histories of those who have been incarcerated, tell us about power dynamics, belonging, exclusion, struggle, and hope across societies in the past and present? The 2026 History Lecture Series explores the practice of incarceration, tracing its change over time from antiquity to our modern world. Recordings are available online. Free. by Geena Powa Haiyupis Recorded Lectures | 2025 Living Breath of wǝɫǝbʔaltxʷ Indigenous Food Systems (American Indian Studies) People come together to share knowledge on topics such as traditional foods, plants and medicines; environmental and food justice; food sovereignty/security; health and wellness; and treaty rights. Indigenous peoples in the Northwest have maintained a sustainable way of life through a cultural, spiritual, and reciprocal relationship with their environment. This symposium serves to foster dialogue and build collaborative networks as we, Native peoples, strive to sustain our cultural food practices and preserve our healthy relationships to the land, water, and all living things. Save the date: The 14th Annual Living Breath of wǝɫǝbʔaltxʷ Indigenous Foods Symposium, “Healing Hands – Healing Lands,” will take place from May 1 – 2. Free. Book Club | Chronicles from the Land of the Happiest People on Earth by Wole Soyinka (UW Alumni) Readers’ Choice! A mix of mystery and political satire, this novel takes aim at corruption in modern Nigeria. Two old friends decide to investigate a local cartel that traffics in human body parts. But in a country where religious charlatans and dishonest officials abound, can they trust anyone in their search? Free. Week of March 2 Photo by Michael B Maine February 26 – March 1 | Dance Majors Concert 2026 (Dance) Presenting seven original student-choreographed works. This platform gives students the opportunity to express their creative voices through choreography and costume design, as well as collaborating with lighting designers and mentors. March 2 | Campus and Concert Bands (School of Music) The Campus Band (Solomon Encina, conductor) and Concert Band (Yuman Wu, conductor) present their Winter Quarter concert, performing music by Julie Giroux, John Philip Sousa, Percy Grainger, Johan de Meij, Frank Ticheli, Aaron Perrine, and others. Online – March 2 | Trump in the World 2.0 Winter Lecture Series 2026: What was Intelligence and What Comes Next? (Jackson School of International Studies) Presented by Kelly McGannon, current World Affairs Council Fellow, and Jeff Hovenier, U.S. Ambassador (ret.). Trump in the World 2.0 is an online series of talks and discussions featuring guest speakers and faculty exploring global perspectives on a second Trump administration. Free. March 3 | Ethnomusicology Visiting Artist Concert: Ramón Gutierrez: Son Jarocho music (School of Music) Winter Quarter Ethnomusicology Visiting Artist Ramón Gutierrez hails from Xalapa, Veracruz in Mexico and specializes in playing the requinto (a small melodic guitar). He is the leader of the group Son de Madera, and has performed and recorded with musicians in other traditions, including the Chicano rock band Quetzal from Los Angeles and Antonio Corona, a performer of early music in Mexico. In this concert concluding his UW residency, he performs music from the Son Jarocho tradition with his UW students and special guests. Free. March 3 | UW Choirs and Seattle University Choirs: “Considering Matthew Shepard” (School of Music) The UW Chamber Singers and University Chorale collaborate with Seattle University Choirs (Leann Conley-Holcom, director) in performing Craig Hella Johnson’s Considering Matthew Shepard, a profound tale of discrimination, cruelty, death, yet with themes of hope. Online option – March 4 | Primary: Alma Thomas, Sisterhood, and the Revolutionary Quality of Light (Public Lectures) Based on Alexis Pauline Gumbs’ forthcoming book of poetic indexes, this interactive poetic lecture explores the life, teaching, and artwork of color theorist Alma Thomas. Engaging themes of audience, intimacy, abstract expressionist art, and the dynamic relationship between Black women’s creativity and the process of being Earth, the lecture invites participants into a rhythmic dialogue of form, meaning, and presence. Free. March 5 | Collections Open Doors (Burke Museum of Natural History and Culture) Part of Burke’s Free First Thursday series, the museum opens its collections spaces from 4:30 to 7:30 PM. Visitors can explore behind‑the-scenes labs and storage, and speak with researchers, staff, and volunteers about their work. Free. Online – March 6 | Nicholas McLeod | Raising The Black Star: West Indian Pan-Africanists and The Politics Of Nation Building In Kwame Nkrumah’s Ghana (Jackson School of International Studies) Raising The Black Star presents a historical restoration of Kwame Nkrumah’s contributions to the Pan-African movement, as well as the transnational nature of post-colonial Ghana’s nation-building process. Dr. McLeod’s richly-textured narrative highlights the startling and continued relevance of Pan-Africanism in both historical and contemporary discussions of transnational solidarities and visions of a completely liberated African continent. Free. March 6 | Opera Workshop: Alice Tierney (School of Music) UW Opera Workshop presents Melissa Dunphy’s 2023 opera Alice Tierney. With stage direction by Kelly Kitchens; music direction by Andrew Romanick. Commissioned by the Oberlin Opera Commissioning Program through the generosity of Elizabeth and Justus ’71 Schlichting, Melissa Dunphy’s opera Alice Tierney was premiered at Oberlin Conservatory in 2023, and at Opera Columbus in April 2023. Dunphy was one of seven winners of a 2020 OPERA America Discovery Grant, presented to female composers with the intention of increasing gender parity across the opera industry. That grant supported the development of Alice Tierney at Oberlin. Online – March 6 | Palestine to Iraq with Adam Hanieh (Public Lectures) Explore how World War I reshaped the Middle East. This lecture traces anti-colonial movements, Palestine’s pivotal role, and the shift from British to American power—linking regional upheaval to the global rise of fossil capitalism and reimagined imperial hierarchies. Free. March 7 | Composition Studio Concert (School of Music) Emerging and established composers explore unconventional sonic landscapes in this concert of music by students, faculty, alumni, and guests of the UW Composition program. Free. Week of March 9 Online – March 9 | Trump in the World 2.0 Winter Lecture Series 2026: The China Question(s) (Jackson School of International Studies) Presented by David Bachman, UW Professor, International Studies; James Lin, UW Associate Professor, International Studies and Taiwan historian; Tabitha Grace Mallory, Founder and CEO, China Ocean Institute; and Susan H. Whiting, UW Professor, Political Science. Trump in the World 2.0 is an online series of talks and discussions featuring guest speakers and faculty exploring global perspectives on a second Trump administration. Free. March 10 | Liberation Book Club: Movie Night (School of Art + Art History + Design) This year-long program series hopes to honor our commitment to social justice and to gather our community to think about the work of liberation through shared texts, art, film, music, conversation, and workshops. Unlike your traditional book club all the reading and study happens together, so no need to prepare. Join us monthly as we approach the topic of liberation from a number of perspectives. Free. March 10 | Chamber Music Showcase (School of Music) Students of John Popham present a chamber music showcase. Free. March 10 | Modern Music Ensemble (School of Music) The Modern Music Ensemble (Cristina Valdés, director) performs music by John Cage, Hilda Paredes, Sofia Gubaidulina, and Salvatore Sciarrino. March 10 | Book Launch: Sasha Senderovich’s “In the Shadow of the Holocaust: Short Fiction by Jewish Writers from the Soviet Union” (Stroum Center for Jewish Studies) The short fiction collected in In the Shadow of the Holocaust, translated by Senderovich and Harriet Murav, recovers a range of compelling voices that had been scarcely known or translated, with particular emphasis on the work of women writers. Jewish authors from Ukraine, Lithuania, Russia, and Belarus—some writing in Yiddish and others in Russian—tell stories of ordinary people living on after the massive devastation of the Holocaust on Soviet territory, depicting memory, conflict, love, and loss. Writers in this collection offer especially powerful perspectives on survival in the aftermath of genocide. These are not stories only about how people died, but about how they continued to live and make meaning. Free. March 12 | Digital/Data Humanities Lecture: Tonia Sutherland, “Resurrecting the Black Body: Race and the Digital Afterlife (Simpson Center for the Humanities) Tonia Sutherland examines the consequences of digitally raising the dead. Attending to the violent deaths of Black Americans–and the records that document them–from slavery through the present, Sutherland explores media evidence, digital acts of remembering, and the rights and desires of humans to be forgotten. Free. March 12 | Wind Ensemble and Symphonic Band: Mystic Threads (School of Music) The Wind Ensemble and Symphonic Band (Erin Bodnar, director) presents Mystic Threads, featuring music by Victoriano Valencia, Jodie Blackshaw, Reena Esmail, Florent Schmitt, Luigi Zaninelli, and others. With guest composer Simon Alami. March 12 – 21 | Bunny (School of Drama) For most of Sorrel’s high school career, she was friendless and quietly weird. She didn’t even seem to fit in with the geeky kids. When she turned seventeen, and late puberty produced a supermodel physique, she became seen as a “hot dork”. Bunny spans twenty years of Sorrel’s life. Unencumbered by the burden of shame, she journeys through the complex social expectations surrounding female sexuality. MFA student, Ren, directs this intimate and thought-provoking play. March 13 | UW Symphony Orchestra with Rachel Lee Priday (School of Music) David Alexander Rahbee leads the UW Symphony in a program of music by Mieczyslaw Karlowicz and Sergei Prokofiev. Faculty violinist Rachel Lee Priday is featured soloist with the orchestra for Karlowicz’s Violin Concerto in A major, op. 8. Bird’s signature whistling, looping and lyrical finesse meet Poor’s expressive, boundary-pushing rhythms. Cady Endowed Lectureship in Chemistry was established in memory of Prof. Cady by his family and many friends and colleagues in 1994. George H. Cady earned his bachelor’s degree from the University of Kansas and Ph.D. from the University of California, Berkeley, in 1930 under the direction of Joel H. Hildebrand. Cady held positions at the University of South Dakota, M.I.T., U.S. Rubber Company, and Pittsburgh Plate Glass before joining the UW as assistant professor in 1938. He worked on the Manhattan Project (1942-43), chaired the Department of Chemistry (1961-65), and became professor emeritus in 1972. Prof. Cady was a distinguished inorganic chemist who, among many honors, shared the first Prix Moisson, a prestigious prize named after the father of fluorine chemistry. Free. March 16 | ‘The Neighborhood: Space, State, and Daily Life in a Manchurian City’ with Nianshen Song (Jackson School of International Studies) What can one neighborhood reveal about the making of a modern nation? This talk deciphers the unexpected significance of Xita, a half-square-mile quarter in Shenyang, in Northeast China. It shows that over nearly four centuries, Xita has been shaped and reshaped by empire, war, migration, and urban transformation. The history of this small area mirrors large-scale changes, including and especially China’s metamorphosis from a multi-ethnic Eurasian empire to a postindustrial society. By studying how global and local forces play out in everyday spaces, the talk reveals a perspective for understanding China’s past—not from the top down, but through the streets and people who lived it. Edwards. The event will conclude with a Q&A session followed by a reception. Hosted by Sheri Mizumori. Free. enrichment.title: The neuronal clock network in the polar key species Antarctic krill (Euphausia superba)
enrichment.summary: Organisms are exposed to predictable daily and seasonal environmental oscillations. Biological clocks enable organisms to anticipate these changes and coordinate physiology and behaviour accordingly. While circadian mechanisms are well studied in terrestrial model organisms, little is known about the neuronal organisation of biological clocks in ecologically important species, especially in the marine environment. Antarctic krill (Euphausia superba) is central to the functioning of the Southern Ocean ecosystem and relies on precise timing to cope with the extreme, high-latitude fluctuations in photoperiod, food availability, and sea-ice cover in its habitat. Despite evidence for circadian and seasonal rhythms in krill behaviour and physiology, the neuronal architecture underlying these timing processes has remained unresolved. In this study, we use in situ hybridisation and antibody staining to characterise the circadian clock in the krill brain. Immunostaining with an antibody against crustacean {beta}-Pigment-dispersing hormone ({beta}-PDH) reveals distinct clusters of PDH-positive neurons in the optic lobes and dorsal central brain, along with an extensive PDH-positive fibre network. We further localise transcripts of the core clock genes cryptochrome-2 (cry2) and period (per) in cell clusters in the optic lobes, which also include the PDH-positive neurons. More specifically, PDH-positive neurons are a subgroup of the cry2 and per-positive cells. Together, these findings provide the first description of the neuronal architecture of the circadian clock in Antarctic krill and establish essential groundwork for future studies on biological timing, environmental adaptation, and the resilience of this key species in a rapidly changing Southern Ocean.

enrichment.title: Nanoparticles hijack calvarial immune cells for CNS drug delivery and stroke therapy
enrichment.summary: Drug-loaded albumin NPs hijack calvarial immune cells to bypass the BBB via skull-meninges microchannels for CNS drug delivery and stroke therapy, establishing skull-based delivery and immune-assisted transport as a clinically translatable strategy for neurological therapeutics.
enrichment.content: Skip to Main Content Skip to Main Menu Outline Download PDF Cite Share Set Alert Get Rights Reprints Previous article Next article Highlights • Drug-loaded albumin NPs hijack calvarial immune cells in vivo via ICO injection • The NP-loaded cells migrate toward the CNS via skull microchannels, bypassing the BBB • The NP-loaded cells promote targeted drug delivery to CNS lesions • The NP-loaded cells relieve stroke injury, showing clinical feasibility and safety Summary The rapid accessibility of calvarial immune cells to the brain, in principle, may offer transformative opportunities for overcoming drug delivery barriers in central nervous system (CNS) disorders. Here, we hijacked calvarial immune cells using drug-loaded nanoparticles (NPs) and leveraged their unique migration mechanism through skull-meninges microchannels to bypass the blood-brain barrier (BBB) for CNS drug delivery. We constructed NP-loaded immune cells in situ via intracalvariosseous (ICO) injection, validated their prompt migration in response to CNS perturbation, and targeted therapeutic delivery to CNS lesions. Compared with conventional delivery approaches, this strategy achieved promising therapeutic efficacy in improving both short- and long-term outcomes in preclinical stroke models. Our prospective clinical trial further supports the translational feasibility of ICO immune access in treating malignant stroke. These findings establish skull-based delivery as a promising, clinically translatable route for CNS drug delivery and highlight immune-assisted transport as a potentially transformative strategy for improving therapeutic outcomes in neurological disorders. Graphical abstract Keywords central nervous system disorders blood-brain barrier cell-based drug delivery nanomedicine brain-bordering immunity skull-meninge microchannels calvarial immune cells acute ischemic stroke brain-machine interface Introduction Development of effective medications for central nervous system (CNS) disorders has long been plagued by a high failure rate in clinical trials.1,2,3 One major obstacle is the restrictive permeability of the blood-brain barrier (BBB) to most drugs, thereby leading to insufficient brain accumulation and unsatisfactory therapeutic outcomes.1,2,3 At the same time, the lack of specificity in drug targeting often leads to adverse effects, which are particularly problematic in the CNS due to the region-specific vulnerabilities in most neurological disorders.1,2,3 Despite recent advancements in multiple drug delivery platforms proposed in the open literature, efficacious drug delivery to the CNS remains a daunting challenge. Immune cells, which are actively involved in the pathogenesis of most CNS disorders, have emerged as promising vectors for CNS drug delivery due to their innate ability to traverse the BBB and target CNS lesions.4,5,6 Nevertheless, clinical translation of immune cell-based drug delivery strategies still faces several challenges. One primary limitation is that current strategies rely on systemic administration of drug-loaded cells, which are prepared ex vivo and typically isolated from either actual patients or healthy donors.7,8,9,10 Off-target effects during systemic circulation, along with the low expression of leukocyte adhesion molecules on the BBB, often result in limited infiltration of drug-loaded immune cells into the brain parenchyma.7,8,9,10 Additionally, the infusion of large numbers of immune cells may raise safety concerns, including the risk of graft-versus-host diseases and graft immune rejection.11,12,13 The possibility of immune rejection may also diminish the persistence of infused cells and undermine their therapeutic benefits.12,13 Finally, the complexity and expertise required for ex vivo manipulation procedures render the accessibility and scalability of these therapies barely possible.6,8 These hurdles underscore the need to develop alternative cell-based delivery strategies that can achieve efficient CNS delivery while minimizing the associated risks. More recently, the skull bone marrow and the meninges encasing the brain have been recognized as critical immune niches for CNS surveillance.14,15,16,17,18,19 These niches continuously monitor changes in the brain’s immune environment and dynamically adjust immune responses to maintain CNS homeostasis. Under homeostasis, the skull bone marrow replenishes the meninges with a repertoire of immune cells through skull-meninges channels (SMCs).18,20 In CNS disorders, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), laden with disease-specific biomarkers, engages directly with these cells through SMCs and prompts their chemotactic infiltration into the brain parenchyma.19,21,22,23 Distinct from peripheral circulating immune cells, the calvaria-derived immune cells are in immediate proximity to the brain and further exhibit a unique migration mechanism that can bypass the BBB through the brain-bordering immune gateway (i.e., SMCs), thus enabling rapid targeting of CNS lesions.14,19 Additionally, populated immune cells and relatively low liquidity in the skull bone marrow provide a favorable setting to facilitate drug-loaded cells in vivo, thereby circumventing the introduction of high numbers of cells or the inefficiencies associated with intravascular in vivo loading methods.4,5,6,24 Therefore, an alternative approach that can construct drug-loaded immune cells in these brain-adjacent immune niches, exploit their immune specificity, and use the brain-targeted immune gateway to bypass the BBB for enhanced CNS drug delivery, has recently attracted considerable attention in research communities.1,14 Here, we propose to hijack the calvarial immune cells with drug-loaded nanoparticles (NPs), leveraging their unique brain-targeted migration through SMCs for CNS drug delivery (Figure 1A). We employed albumin NPs because of their tropism for immune cells via complement opsonization.25,26,27 We observed rapid internalization of the albumin NPs by the immune cells following intracalvariosseous (ICO) injection. Using a lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced neuroinflammation model and an experimental stroke model induced by middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO), we discerned a substantial migration of NP-loaded cells toward the brain via the SMCs, with a subsequently markable accumulation of albumin NPs in the target neurons at CNS lesions rather than the unlesioned tissues. To validate the therapeutic potentials of this strategy, we loaded nerinetide (Tat-NR2B9c and NA1), a clinically validated neuroprotective eicosapeptide, onto albumin NPs via electrostatic interaction and evaluated their efficacy in treating acute ischemic stroke using the MCAO mouse model.28 Comparative evaluation revealed that ICO administration of NA1-loaded NPs not only significantly alleviated ischemic infarction and cerebral edema during the acute phase but also mitigated brain atrophy and neurological deficit in long term. Remarkably, these effects, achieved with only 1/15 of the conventional dosage, greatly exceeded those from clinical intravenous (i.v.) administration, direct ICO injection of free NA1,29 or i.v. injection of the NA1-loaded NPs that may have peripheral immune cell-mediated brain targeting as reported.24 Moreover, to assess clinical translation, we conducted a prospective, randomized, open-label clinical trial, SOLUTION (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05849805), to treat patients with malignant middle cerebral artery infarction (mMCAI). Real-world data from this trial demonstrates the feasibility and safety of our approach, underscoring its translational potential. Together, these findings establish a clinically translatable platform for CNS drug delivery, harnessing unique brain-bordering immune mechanisms to bypass the BBB and achieve lesion-specific targeting, thereby unlocking considerable potential for CNS disorder treatments. Figure 1 NPs target calvarial myeloid cells in vivo Show full caption Results NPs target calvarial myeloid cells in vivo through ICO injection Calvarial immune cells, particularly those of the myeloid lineage, possess a distinct transcriptomic and proteomic profile for CNS immune surveillance.30 Compared with the peripheral immune cells, the calvarial myeloid cells (monocytes and neutrophils) exhibit a mature phenotype with upregulated genes related to migration and phagocytosis.30 We therefore hypothesized that injecting NPs into the skull bone marrow could directly load them into calvarial myeloid cells in vivo. High-resolution ex vivo X-ray computed tomography (CT) revealed highly interconnected marrow cavities in the mouse interparietal bone and numerous microchannels extending to the meninges, identifying this site as optimal for ICO injection (Figures S1A and S1B).23 Following injection, radiographic data of the harvested mice skulls confirmed both the accessibility of the bone marrow and the integrity of the compact inner table (Figure S1C). The data indicate that NPs firstly distribute within the marrow cavity, interact with resident myeloid cells, and then enter the CNS via microchannels, rather than direct meningeal diffusion. Complete skull healing was observed within 5 weeks (Figure S1C). Figure S1 Characterization of mouse skulls and albumin NPs, related to Figure 1 Show full caption To target calvarial myeloid cells in vivo, we developed albumin NPs, a clinically approved material with known myeloid tropism via complement-mediated opsonization.25,26,27 Dynamic light scattering (DLS) and scanning electronic microscopy (SEM) show uniform diameters and good stability of the albumin NPs (Figures 1B, 1C, and S1D–S1F). To confirm phagocytosis of the albumin NPs by calvarial myeloid cells, we grafted the NPs with fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC) and used a combination of confocal microscopy, flow cytometry, and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) for characterizations. In vitro co-incubation with skull and tibial bone marrow cells shows up to 90% uptake efficiency (Figures S2A–S2C). In vivo, 2 h after ICO injection, confocal imaging reveals clear colocalization between FITC-NPs and granulocyte receptor-1 (Gr1+) cells (Figure 1D), confirming phagocytosis by calvarial myeloid cells (Figure 1D). Flow cytometry experiments further quantified the in vivo phagocytosis by myeloid cell subsets, with the proportion of FITC+ neutrophils and Ly6Chi monocytes at 29.7% and 49.4%, respectively (Figures 1E and 1F). By contrast, i.v. administration resulted in 12.6% of peripheral neutrophils and 8.3% of peripheral Ly6Chi monocytes being FITC-labeled (Figure S2D), further supporting the enhanced targeting efficiency of the ICO route. Figure S2 Immune cell targeting efficiency and biodistribution of albumin NPs administered via ICO versus i.v. routes, related to Figures 1 and 3 Show full caption To investigate whether the CNS perturbation enhances NP uptake, we employed an LPS-induced neuroinflammation model for verification.31,32 Compared with the naive control, flow cytometry analysis reveals a significant increment of calvarial myelocyte subsets co-stained with the NPs in the neuroinflammatory group, with FITC+ neutrophils and Ly6Chi monocytes rising to 70.1% and 76.1%, respectively (Figures 1E and 1F). It is noteworthy that the proportion of FITC+ neutrophils demonstrated a more pronounced increase than that of Ly6Chi monocytes, which may be attributed to their mature late-stage phenotype and rapid immune responses.30,33 Moreover, TEM images clearly demonstrated the presence of a large number of NP-loaded cells inside the bone marrow (Figure 1G).34 After in vitro co-incubation or in vivo injections of the albumin NPs, no decrease in the viability of the myeloid cells was observed, indicating good biocompatibility of the NPs (Figure S2E).25 Systemic leakage following the ICO administration was also assessed. Flow cytometry of peripheral blood at multiple time points revealed minimal presence of FITC+ myeloid cells (Figure S2G). Ex vivo imaging at 24 h further demonstrated negligible NP accumulation in peripheral organs, in sharp contrast to the widespread distribution observed with i.v. delivery, highlighting low systemic exposure via the ICO route (Figure S2F). Collectively, these results establish ICO injection as a feasible strategy to construct NP-loaded calvarial myeloid cells at brain boundaries, offering high efficiency and minimal systemic leakage under both homeostatic and pathological conditions. NP-loaded calvarial myeloid cells migrate toward CNS border through the skull-meninges immune gateway To determine whether the NP-loaded calvarial myeloid cells would subsequently migrate toward the CNS through the skull-meninges immune gateway,18,19 we performed ex vivo immunofluorescence (IF) imaging on mouse interparietal skulls after ICO injection. Consistent with the TEM findings (Figure 1G), optically cleared skulls showed successful in vivo labeling of myeloid cells, evidenced by colocalization of Gr1+ cells and FITC-NPs in the bone marrow of both sham and LPS-treated mice (Figure 1H). Based on the optically cleared skulls, the skull-meninges microchannels could be distinctly identified as the discontinuities of the inner table of the skull created by CD31-labeled blood vessels (Figures 2A, S3A, and S3B). In the sham control, occasional Gr1+ cells were seen traversing microchannels (Figure 2A, left). By marked contrast, however, LPS-treated mice showed pronounced accumulations along these pathways (Figure 2A, right). Quantification analysis further revealed a significant increase in both density and proportional distribution of Gr1+ signals along microchannels of the LPS-treated mice, as compared with the sham control (Figures 2B and 2C). These findings align with the early studies that show the distinct supply of the immune cells under homeostatic and pathological conditions by the adjacent skull bone marrow niches,18 suggesting feasibility to utilize these cells for responsive drug delivery to the CNS in disease settings. Figure 2 Calvarial myeloid cells mediate NP delivery to CNS border via skull-meninges immune gateway Show full caption Figure S3 Migration of NP-loaded calvaria immune cells toward CNS through the skull-meninge vascular microchannel, related to Figure 2 Show full caption Furthermore, we confirmed that the Gr1+ cells distributed along the microchannels were extensively colocalized with the NPs in both the LPS-treated mice and the sham control (Figures 2D–2F and S3C; Video S1). TEM further revealed the widespread presence of NPs inside these cells (Figure 2G), consistent with the high cell loading efficiency observed after ICO NP injections (Figure 1F). Although some NPs were observed dissociating outside cells (Figure S3D), the finding suggests that chemotactic cell migration represents an alternative naturally evolved pathway for delivery of the NPs to the CNS, complementing their simple diffusion to the brain surface via the physical microchannels.18,19 In the majority of cases, these NP-loaded cells were observed to migrate toward the CNS through the perivascular space (Figures 2E and 2G).19,23 Occasionally, these cells were also observed entering the intravascular space (Figure S3E), which would get access to the systemic circulation.35 Whole-mount dura imaging further confirmed the wide presence of NP-loaded Gr1+ cells within the dura mater following LPS-induced inflammation (Figures 2H, 2I, and S3F), providing direct evidence that calvarial immune cells can deliver NPs to CNS borders when responding to CNS perturbations. Video (42.96 MB) Video S1. NP-loaded Gr1+ cells migrate toward CNS through the vascular microchannels, related to Figure 2 Collectively, these findings reveal a CNS-targeting paradigm in which NPs leverage calvarial myeloid cells and skull-meninges trafficking pathways to reach CNS borders, representing an alternative to conventional systemic strategies limited by the BBB. Calvarial myeloid cells promote targeted delivery to CNS lesions Having confirmed that the NP-loaded myeloid cells could migrate to CNS borders through the skull-meninges microchannels in response to CNS perturbations, we then ask whether they would deliver the NPs into the deep brain parenchyma. Flow cytometry of brains collected 6 h after ICO NP injection in LPS-induced neuroinflammatory mice revealed robust NP loading in brain-infiltrating myeloid cells, with a markedly higher proportion of NP-carrying cells compared with sham controls (Figures 3A–3C). By 24 h after LPS injection, this response became more pronounced. The numbers of neutrophils and CD45hi leukocytes were markedly elevated compared with sham mice (Figures 3D and 3E), resulting in a substantially increased ratio of NP-loaded myeloid cells to resident microglia (Figures 3F and 3G). These results together support the feasibility of leveraging calvarial myeloid cells to transport therapeutic cargos into the inflamed brain parenchyma. Figure 3 Calvarial myeloid cells promote targeted delivery to CNS lesions Show full caption To investigate whether these myeloid cells may achieve targeted delivery to CNS lesions, we employed an experimental MCAO model to simulate acute ischemic stroke and performed a combination of IF analysis and flow cytometry for validation. 24 h after ischemia onset, the decreased fluorescent signals of neuron-specific nuclear protein (NeuN) or microtubule-associated protein 2 (MAP-2) clearly delineated the ischemic region in the ipsilateral hemibrain (Figure S4A). Within these lesions, a substantial accumulation of the Gr1+ cells was observed, markedly higher than that of the contralateral side (Figures 3H and S4A). Similarly, FITC-NPs were observed more frequently concentrated in the ipsilateral cerebral cortex instead of the contralateral side (Figures 3H and 3I). By marked contrast, in sham-operated mice, both the Gr1+ cells and FITC-NPs exhibited minimal infiltration into the brain parenchyma, with no significant difference in their distributions between the two hemibrains (Figures S4B and S4C). Flow cytometry further confirmed these observations, revealing a significantly higher accumulation of the NP-loaded Ly6G+ neutrophils and CD45hi cells in the ipsilateral side (Figures 3J and 3K). The data indicate a strong correlation between the targeted delivery of NPs and the tropism of myeloid cells for the CNS lesion. Figure S4 Enrichment of immune cells, NPs, and therapeutics in ischemic brain lesions, related to Figures 3 and 4 Show full caption In these brain lesions, we further confirmed the effective delivery of the NPs into the affected neurons, as evidenced by the presence of abundant NPs within the NeuN-labeled cells (Figure 3I). Concurrently, Gr1+ cells were observed in immediate contact with neurons (Figure 3L). To further explore whether the immune cells may facilitate this neuronal uptake, we co-cultured NP-loaded neutrophils with mouse primary neurons in vitro. These experiments recapitulated the in vivo phenomena, showing close contact between neutrophils and neurons and the presence of the NPs within neurons (Figures 3M and S4D). A time course analysis further shows that co-culturing neurons with NP-loaded neutrophils could lead to neuronal internalization of NPs within a few hours (Figure S4D), comparable to that observed under conditions of direct exposure to higher NP concentrations (Figure S4E). Together, these observations suggest a potential role of neutrophils in facilitating NP transfer to neurons; however, the underlying mechanisms remain uncertain and require more investigation. Collectively, these findings demonstrate the important role of calvarial myeloid cells in the targeted delivery to neurons in the CNS lesions. Therapeutic calvarial myeloid cells alleviate acute ischemic stroke We next sought to investigate whether the BBB-bypassing drug delivery strategy, which leverages the skull-meninges immune gateway and the chemotactic migration of calvarial myeloid cells, could be utilized to alleviate CNS disorders. We selected eicosapeptide nerinetide (Tat-NR2B9c or NA1), a promising i.v.-administered neuroprotectant in a phase 3 clinical trial, which may reduce infarct volume and preserve neurological function after stroke, as a test drug to verify the delivery and therapeutic efficacy in MCAO mice.28,36 NA1 was surface-loaded onto albumin NPs via electrostatic interaction between its positive charge and the negatively charged NP surface (Figure S1G). High-performance liquid chromatography showed encapsulation efficiencies above 85% across doses (Figure S1I), and DLS confirmed minimal size change and stable surface potential (>−20 mV) after loading, indicating good colloidal stability (Figure S1H). To evaluate both the therapeutic efficacy and dose-response relationship of NA1 NPs delivered via ICO injection, we administered the formulations immediately after ischemia-reperfusion (Figure 4A). As a positive control, NA1 was given i.v. at a validated effective dose of 10 nmol/g in mice.37 Additionally, to compare the cell-mediated delivery strategy with direct ICO injection (diffusion-based delivery), free NA1 was administered at an optimized dose equivalent to one-half of the i.v. dose.29 For the NA1 NPs group, the administered doses were adjusted to 1/30 to 1/3.75 of the i.v. dosage. Figure 4 Therapeutic calvarial myeloid cells alleviate acute ischemic stroke Show full caption Before stroke induction, physiological parameters did not differ among the groups. At 24 h after the ischemia onset, 2,3,5-triphenyltetrazolium chloride (TTC) staining revealed a marked reduction in infarct volume in mice treated with either NA1 or NA1 NPs compared with the placebo, with decreases of at least 25.6% (Figures 4B, 4C, S5A, and S5B). Notably, all cohorts administered with the NA1 NPs via ICO injection showed greater reductions in infarct volume compared with those receiving i.v. NA1, with the 1/15 dosage group achieving the highest efficacy, exhibiting an additional 26.7% decrease in infarct size and improved neurological functions (Figures 4B, 4C, and S5A–S5C). Thus, the 1/15-dose regimen was selected for subsequent studies. Figure S5 Dose dependence, timing, and efficacy of ICO-NA1 NPs versus other delivery routes and formulations, related to Figure 4 Show full caption To evaluate the therapeutic time window, we administered NA1 NPs at delayed time points of 4.5 and 6 h after the stroke onsets. Strikingly, while ICO delivery of NA1 NPs at 6 h conferred no therapeutic benefit, administration at 4.5 h still yielded significant neuroprotection (Figures S5D and S5E). By contrast, i.v. administration of NA1 did not achieve significant efficacy at either delayed time point, likely due to limited drug penetration across the BBB and insufficient accumulation at the ischemic site.29 These findings highlight the advantage of the ICO route in maintaining efficacy within a clinically relevant therapeutic window (Figures S5D and S5E). For long-term evaluation, we performed continuous magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) analysis and behavioral observations over a period of up to 28 days. Notably, TTC staining at 24 h showed comparable infarct volumes between ICO-NA1 NPs and free NA1 administered via ICO injection, consistent with the prior reports highlighting the hyperacute neuroprotective effect of NA1.29,36,37 By 72 h, however, T2-weighted MRI and TTC staining revealed markedly smaller ischemic regions in the ICO-NA1 NP group compared with all other treatments (Figure S5F). Apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) imaging further demonstrated the improved therapeutic efficacy of the ICO-administered NA1 NPs in relieving infarct cores over free NA1, regardless of the delivery route (Figure 4F). Moreover, ICO-NA1 NPs significantly alleviated stroke-induced cerebral edema compared with other groups (Figures 4D and 4G), underscoring their multifaceted neuroprotective capabilities during the acute phase. By contrast, i.v.-NA1 and ICO-NA1, while effective at 24 h, failed to confer these protections at 72 h, likely reflecting the transient nature of free NA1 due to rapid clearance rather than sustained release from NPs.29,38,39 To assess this, we quantified the NA1 concentration in the brain with liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) 24 h after stroke induction. The results show that the NA1 NPs delivered by ICO route achieved the highest NA1 concentrations in the brain even at substantially lower dosages, along with markedly higher accumulation in the ipsilateral hemibrain compared with the contralateral side (Figure S4F), confirming both the efficiency and targetability of ICO-delivered NA1 NPs. In addition, brain-to-organ ratios, particularly brain-to-spleen, brain-to-lung, and brain-to-kidney, were markedly higher with ICO-NA1 NPs than with other treatments (Figures S4G–S4J), further indicating enhanced CNS selectivity and reduced systemic exposure. In the follow-up imaging observations up to 28 days, these beneficial effects persisted, collectively highlighting their durable therapeutic efficacy in ameliorating ischemic stroke (Figure 4D). To estimate the long-term neuroprotective effect on tissue damage, we assessed brain atrophy and white matter integrity up to 28 days post-stroke (Figures 4H–4K). We quantified brain atrophy by measuring volumetric reduction of tissues on the T2-weighted images on 14, 21, and 28 days after stroke. The data indicate that ICO administration of NA1 NPs alleviates brain atrophy more effectively than free NA1 administered intravenously or intracalvariosseously, suggesting its long-term histological neuroprotective effects (Figure 4H). More impressively, 35 days after the stroke induction, the mouse brains in the NA1 group administered either intravenously or intracalvariosseously showed severe brain atrophy on the lesional side, akin to those in the placebo group. By marked contrast, ICO delivery of the NA1 NPs significantly reduced stroke-induced brain atrophy, with some cases even demonstrating brain integrity indiscernible from that of the healthy control (Figures 4I and 4J). Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) further showed that ICO-NA1 NPs preserved corpus callosum integrity, maintaining continuous fraction anisotropy (FA) signals and fiber tracts, in contrast to the disrupted architecture seen in saline or free NA1 groups (Figure 4K). Ultimately, 35 days after stroke induction, NA1 NP-treated MCAO mice demonstrated an improved survival rate compared with the MCAO mice treated with either i.v. or direct ICO injection of free NA1 (Figure 4L). Throughout the 28-day observation period, we also conducted neurological assessments using neurological severity scores (NSSs) and behavioral evaluations, including the rotarod test, water maze test, and object recognition test. Animals treated with ICO-NA1 NPs demonstrated improved NSS scores from the initial 24 h after ischemia onset and throughout the 28-day period (Figure 4M). This group also presents significantly better performance in the rotarod task than other groups during the continuous observations (Figure 4N). We also confirmed that NA1 NPs administered through skulls significantly improved the performance of mice in the water maze and object recognition tasks (Figures 4O and 4P). Improvements in learning, memory, and object discrimination indicated an evident overall enhancement in cognitive ability (Figures 4O and 4P). Given that peripheral circulating myeloid cells can infiltrate the brain after stroke and serve as potential carriers for cell-mediated drug delivery,5,6,40 we also evaluated the therapeutic efficacy of i.v. administered NA1 NPs. Notably, the ICO group received only 1/15 of the NA1 dose used in the i.v. group. Despite the lower dosage, animals in the ICO-NA1 NPs group exhibited markedly smaller infarct volumes compared with the i.v.-NA1 NPs group, as shown by TTC staining (Figure S5F). MRI analyses corroborated these findings, revealing significantly smaller infarct volumes and reduced perilesional edema as early as day 3, confirming a more effective neuroprotective response (Figures S5G and S5H). These advantages persisted up to 28 days, with the ICO group showing consistently reduced secondary tissue loss and improved survival rates compared with the i.v.-treated animals (Figures S5I and S5J), likely owing to the high and sustained drug accumulation in the ischemic brain during the early acute phase (Figure S4F). Taken together, these data demonstrate the promising potential of the ICO administration of drug-loaded NPs for CNS drug delivery and disease alleviation. Clinical feasibility and safety of ICO drug administration in mMCAI patients To assess the translational potential of ICO delivery, we conducted the first-in-human SOLUTION trial (ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05849805), a prospective, randomized, investigator-initiated pilot study designed to assess the feasibility, safety, and exploratory efficacy of ICO administration in patients with mMCAI. Between April 14, 2023, and November 6, 2023, 20 patients with mMCAI were enrolled and randomized 1:1 to receive either best medical treatment (BMT) alone or BMT plus ICO injection of Y-3, a neuroprotective agent approved by the China National Medical Products Administration, for 3 days (Figure 5A). The demographic characteristics of the two groups were mostly the same (Table S1), and both groups received similar treatments aside from ICO injection. The primary outcome was set to evaluate the feasibility and safety of ICO injection. Secondary outcomes encompassed exploratory efficacy outcomes such as the score on the modified Rankin scale (mRS) at 90 days or the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score at multiple time points. Figure 5 Clinical feasibility, safety, and exploratory efficacy of ICO drug administration in mMCAI patients Show full caption The procedural workflow for ICO injection is illustrated in Figure 5B. The operation consists of five sequential steps: (1) positioning and preoperative marking, (2) skin incision and skull exposure, (3) drilling through the outer table to access the diploic space, (4) drug administration using a syringe, and (5) sealing of the cranial opening with bone wax. The second- and third-day injections utilized the pre-drilled holes. The median duration of the entire procedure with drilling was 32 min, while follow-up injections required only 22 min, indicating its acceptable procedure duration for time-sensitive treatment (Table S2). Representative intraoperative and radiographic images confirmed precise drilling limited to the outer table, with an intact inner plate verified by CT and 3D reconstruction (Figures 5C–5E). The procedure was well-tolerated, with no intraoperative complications such as inner plate penetration or drug leakage throughout the study (Table S2). Safety outcomes over the 90-day follow-up period were comparable between groups. One ICO-treated patient was diagnosed with meningitis at day 75, considered secondary to decompressive craniectomy by the clinical event committee. Symptomatic and non-symptomatic intracranial hemorrhages were reported in 7 cases in the BMT group and 4 in the ICO group (relative risk, 0.57; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.24–1.35; p = 0.37) (Table S3). All patients completed follow-up, while two fatal cases were reported in the BMT group and three fatal cases were reported in the ICO group due to stroke-related or other causes. No statistically significant differences in safety events and serious adverse events of various organ systems were observed between the two groups (Tables S3, S4, and S5). In terms of exploratory efficacy outcomes, the ICO group demonstrates a reduction in NIHSS score at day 14 compared with the BMT group under the last observation carried forward (LOCF) analysis, which includes all patients (median −5 versus −2, p = 0.65) (Figure 5F; Table S6). Only one patient in the BMT group shows a reduction in NIHSS score greater than 4 points, whereas this proportion reached 60% in the ICO group (relative risk, 6.0; 95% CI, 0.87–41.21; p = 0.057). The mRS scores at 90 days are presented in Figure 5G and Table S6, showing no statistically significant difference but providing exploratory data for evaluating potential efficacy. These findings provide evidence regarding the feasibility and safety profile of ICO administration, thereby establishing a foundation for its further clinical translation. Discussion Efficacious drug delivery to the CNS remains a daunting challenge due to the restriction of the BBB. This study tackled the challenge by hijacking calvarial immune cells and leveraging their unique migration mechanism to bypass BBB for enhanced and targeted drug delivery. We identified the feasibility and efficacy of the in situ construction of NP-loaded calvarial immune cells and their unique brain-targeting delivery mechanism through the skull-meninges microchannels. This mechanism enables direct delivery to brain lesions without crossing BBB. The model payloads, delivered using this approach, were confirmed to be able to target the lesion sites and led to clear improvement in both short- and long-term outcomes after acute ischemic stroke. Furthermore, the clinical feasibility and safety of the ICO procedure were validated in a pilot clinical trial, supporting its translational potential. Together, these findings establish a clinically translatable platform that harnesses brain-bordering immune pathways to bypass the BBB and achieve enhanced CNS therapy. A clear advantage of this drug delivery strategy is the complete circumvention of the need to cross the BBB, combined with the rapid responsiveness and active tropism for brain lesions of calvaria-derived immune cells. Compared with conventional cell-mediated delivery methods reported in the open literature,4,5,6 the proposed approach can reduce off-target effects and safety concerns associated with systemic administration through a minimally invasive, local delivery strategy and does not require complex ex vivo cell preparation.10,11,12 While i.v. infusion of the cell-targeted NPs can construct drug-loaded cells in vivo,40 the fluid dynamics and dilution effect during systemic circulation significantly limit the delivery efficiency (Figures S4F–S4J) and therapeutic efficacy (Figures S5F–S5J). By contrast, our approach constructs drug-loaded cells in situ by directly injecting drug-loaded albumin NPs into the skull bone marrow, a low-liquidity environment enriched with immune cells in the brain borders.14,30 These immune cells, which are entrusted for CNS surveillance, respond specifically to the CNS perturbation and deliver the drugs to the lesion site. Importantly, this method avoids the introduction of exogenous immune cells, potentially reducing the risk of immune-related complications.11,12,13 Although the current therapeutic validation focuses on acute ischemic stroke and primarily engages myeloid cells, the underlying delivery strategy—based on the BBB-bypassing and lesion-targeted mobilization of skull-derived, brain-bordering immune cells—is mechanistically conserved and flexibly extensible. Whether similar immune-cell-mediated delivery dynamics occur in other neurological conditions remains to be determined.14,18,30,41 Additionally, our strategy lies in utilizing NPs for cell hijacking, which may enhance the applicability of this method for various therapeutic agents. While direct ICO drug injection can enhance cerebral drug accumulation when compared with systemic administration,29,38,39 its therapeutic efficacy remains limited by two major factors: meningeal barriers that restrict drug entry into the brain parenchyma29,38,39 and the reliance on glymphatic diffusion, which suffers from limited penetration depth and poor lesion specificity.15,17,42 By contrast, our approach utilizes NPs not only as carriers of therapeutic payloads but also as key mediators to guide the phagocytic process by calvarial immune cells in order to leverage their active tropism for brain lesions to ensure effective drug delivery into the deep brain and reduce off-target effects on healthy tissues. In the case of acute ischemic stroke, we demonstrated that the ICO route enabled targeted accumulation of NPs and therapeutic payloads within ischemic lesions, achieving robust therapeutic efficacy with only 1/15 of the i.v. dose (Figures 5 and S5). This underscores the efficiency of the approach and suggests its potential for other drugs with limited BBB permeability. In addition, the sustained-release properties of NA1 NPs enable prolonged drug exposure in the brain throughout the acute phase of ischemic stroke (Figure S4F), which may mitigate reperfusion-induced secondary injury and ongoing neuroinflammatory damage. This extended CNS bioavailability, together with targeted delivery mediated by skull marrow-derived immune cells, likely contributes to enhanced and more durable neuroprotection compared with free NA1, underscoring the advantage of ICO-NA1 NPs in maintaining therapeutic efficacy during the critical early post-stroke period (Figures S4E and S4F). This NP-guided technique may also offer a unique platform for a promising spectrum of pharmaceuticals, with potential for multiple drug delivery or stimuli-responsive release to cater to different clinical demands. Several strategies could be explored in the future to improve the brain accumulation and lesion-targeting effects of drugs by these therapeutic calvarial immune cells. One approach could involve specific modifications of the NPs to optimize selective cellular loading and improve drug payload efficiency.4,26 In addition, these calvarial immune cells could be engineered in situ to enhance their specificity for pathological sites.43,44 External field-responsive mechanisms could also be explored to enable controlled migration or drug release, providing greater precision in therapeutic delivery.5 In summary, this study demonstrates the promising strategy that hijacks calvarial immune cells and the skull-meninges immune shortcut for targeted CNS drug delivery and stroke alleviation. Although we focused here on drug delivery to the brain, this approach may be applied to deliver functional nanotransducers for future-generation neuro-interfacing45,46 or engineered immune cells, such aschimeric antigen receptor T cell (CAR-T),11 for immunetherapy. The approach may also be extended to advanced therapeutic modalities, such as closed-loop feedback regulation devices that respond to neurological or pathological signals, for timely, sustained, or controlled CNS therapy.47,48 These qualities prompt further exploration of hijacking calvaria immune cells to circumvent the CNS delivery barrier, potentially opening a paradigm for targeted delivery for CNS disorders. Limitations of the study While this study demonstrates a promising strategy for CNS drug delivery via skull marrow-derived immune cells, several limitations warrant further investigations. First, this study focuses on myeloid cell-mediated delivery in acute stroke and neuroinflammatory models. The involvement of other immune cell types and the generalizability of this mechanism across different CNS diseases remain to be determined. Second, the mechanism underlying the neutrophil-mediated NP transfer to neurons remains to be further defined. Our findings demonstrate intimate interactions between neutrophils and neurons and support the possibility that immune cells facilitate neuronal NP access; however, the precise route of transfer remains elusive. Future studies employing real time, high-resolution imaging and molecular tracing will be crucial to delineate these dynamic processes and clarify how the immune cells contribute to neuronal NP delivery. Third, although our histological and imaging analyses confirmed a clear discrepancy in neuroprotective outcomes between i.v. NA1 and ICO NA1 NP administration at 24 h and later time points, and our tissue drug quantification suggests that this divergence may stem from distinct acute-phase pharmacokinetic behaviors of free NA1 versus NA1 NPs in metabolically active mice, the underlying mechanisms may still require further elucidation. In addition, while ICO injection has proven safety and effectiveness in both preclinical models and clinical studies,29 technical improvements are required to enhance procedural precision, reduce invasiveness, and enable repeated dosing. The current clinical approach requires drilling through the skull, which is feasible but still invasive. Future work may therefore prioritize the development of minimally invasive injection devices to support wider clinical usages. In parallel, optimizing dosing protocols and conducting comprehensive risk-benefit assessments will be essential. Finally, interspecies differences in skull marrow anatomy and immune responses may affect translation. Thus, validation in large-animal models with long-term follow-up is needed to better evaluate safety, biodistribution, and efficacy under clinically relevant conditions.
