Method details Nanoparticle preparation and characterization The albumin nanoparticles (NPs) were prepared using a desolvation method as previously described.25 Briefly, 7.5 ml of ethanol was continuously added into 3 ml 10 mg/ml of bovine serum albumin solution under magnetic stirring (1000 rpm). After 1 hour of stirring, 80 μL of 2.5% glutaraldehyde was introduced to crosslink the NPs. The reaction was allowed to proceed for 10 hours under stirring, after which the NPs were washed three times with deionized water to remove excess ethanol and unreacted albumin. The purified NPs were then redispersed in saline for subsequent use. The size distribution and surface zeta potential of the NPs were determined by dynamic light scattering instrument (Malvern). The morphology was observed by scanning electron microscopy (HITACHI, SU8600). To produce NPs for fluorescent observation, the prepared albumin NPs were grafted with fluorescein-N-hydroxysuccinimide (FITC-NHS) through NHS-amine chemistry. After incubated with FITC-NHS for 2h, the fluorescent NPs were washed three times with deionized water to remove excess free dye molecules. To prepare NA1-loaded NPs, NA1 of different concentrations were added into the albumin solution under magnetic stirring. The electrostatic interaction between the NA1 molecules and albumin NPs enables the surface loading of drug. After 1 hours of stirring, the NPs suspension was centrifuged to remove free NA1 and resuspended in saline for further use. The concentration of free NA1 in the supernatant was tested to determine the encapsulation efficiency of NA1 by high performance liquid chromatography (Agilent). ICO injection in mice All procedures were conducted on mice anesthetized with tribromoethanol (Avertin, 300 mg/kg). Body temperature was maintained at 37°C throughout the surgery using a heating pad. The head was shaved, a midline skin incision was made, and the interparietal skull was exposed. The injection procedure followed a previously described method with modifications.19 Briefly, an electric drill (RWD, 78001) was carefully used to thin the compact bone overlying the bone marrow in the interparietal bones aided by a dissecting microscope, leaving only a thin layer of periosteum intact. A Hamilton syringe mounted with a 34G blunt needle was then used to puncture the periosteum manually, creating a small hole for injection. All injections were performed manually, with each injection consisting of a maximum volume of 10 μl and taking approximately 60 seconds. After each injection, the needle was kept in place for 15 seconds to minimize leakage of the injected solution. After sacrifice, skulls were dissected from mice for 3D X-ray characterization (Zeiss, Xradia620 Versa). The results were evaluated to determine the accessibility of the bone marrow, the integrity of the inner table of the skull, and the time required for the skull to recover after injection. In situ construction of NP-loaded myeloid cells To construct NP-loaded myeloid cells in situ, ICO microinjection of NPs was performed under anesthesia. For each ICO spot, 10 μl of NP solution was injected using a 5 μl Hamilton syringe mounted with a 34G blunt needle. To validate in situ construction of NP-loaded calvarial myeloid cells, the skull bone marrow was isolated for fluorescent imaging and flow cytometry. Briefly, mice were sacrificed by cervical dislocation 2 hours after ICO injection of NPs, and their interparietal bones were dissected and cut into small pieces. Because the bone marrow cavities of the interparietal bone are highly interconnected, a 32G needle containing RPMI 1640 medium can flush most of the bone marrow cells out of the interparietal fragments to obtain a single-cell suspension. After washing thrice with ice-cold PBS or RPMI 1640 medium, free NPs were removed by centrifugation and cells were redispersed for further characterization. To visualize the phagocytosis of NPs, the cells were stained with Hoechst 33342 (nucleus, blue) and DiD (membrane, red), and observed by a 3D confocal laser scanning microscope (Zeiss, LSM980 Airyscan2). Flow cytometry (Cytek Biosciences, Cytek Aurora) was used to quantify the NP phagocytosis efficiency. After stained with an antibody cocktail, the myeloid cells were screened as Zombie NIR- or Fixable Viability Dye eFluor506-, CD45+ and CD11b+. Subpopulations including neutrophils and Ly6Chi monocytes were identified as Ly6G- and Ly6G-Ly6C+, respectively. Skull bone marrow cells without ICO injection of NPs or fluorescent labelling were served as blank control. The myeloid cells co-stained with FITC-NPs were identified as the NP-loaded myeloid cells. In situ NPs targeting efficiency of myeloid cells and each subset were calculated from the resulting fluorescence signals. LPS induced neuroinflammation The delivery of NPs into the brain parenchyma was evaluated using a neuroinflammation model induced by lipopolysaccharide (LPS).31 In this model, animals received an intraperitoneal (i.p.) injection of LPS at a dose of 5 mg/kg body weight (Escherichia coli O111:B4, Sigma–Aldrich), prepared in sterile, nonpyrogenic 0.9% saline solution. The injection volume was standardized at 10 μL per gram of body weight. For the control group, animals were injected intraperitoneally with an equivalent volume (10 μL per gram of body weight) of sterile saline solution. 1 hour after LPS or saline injection, fluorescence-labelled NPs were intracalvariosseously injection, followed by the collection of calvaria bones 2 hours after NP injected. For brain tissue analysis, mice were sacrificed 24 hours after LPS or saline injection, and their brains without meninges were dissected, dissociated and stained for flow cytometry analysis. Ischemic stroke induction Experimental stroke was induced using the filament middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) model for transient and focal brain ischemia. Under anesthesia (isoflurane), a silicon coated 6/0 filament was inserted from the external carotid artery (ECA) of mice until it obstructed the middle MCA. The ECA was then ligatured with the occluding suture for 60 minutes before reperfusion. Sham-operated mice received the same surgery procedure without filament insertion. 24 hours after onset of MCAO or sham operation, mouse brains without meninges were dissected, dissociated and stained for flow cytometry analysis. Tissue harvest and processing Mice were deeply anesthetized by intraperitoneal injection of tribromoethanol (Avertin, 300 mg/kg) and transcardially perfused with 1X PBS to remove the blood before fixation. Following perfusion, mice were decapitated immediately posterior to the interparietal bone, and all excess skins, muscles and mandibles were trimmed to remove from the skull. Skull was trimmed bilaterally from the interparietal bone towards the olfactory bulb to be released from the mouse head. The skull cap was then incubated in 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) at 4°C for 24 hours and decalcified in 10% EDTA in PBS for 10 days at room temperature. Brains were fixed in 4% PFA for additional 24 hours and placed in PBS until used. To harvest meninges, the mouse head whole mounts were fixed in 4% PFA for 8 hours, the brain tissue was removed, and the dura mater was gently dissected with fine surgical forceps from the intracranial surface and placed in 4°C PBS until further use. Transmission electron microscopy Tissues were fixed via cardiac perfusion with 4% PFA, followed by overnight post-fixation in a solution containing 2% PFA and 2.5% glutaraldehyde. Dissected skulls were decalcified in 10% EDTA in PBS at 4°C, with the solution changed daily for 10 days. After decalcification, the tissues were washed 4 times with PB buffer (0.1 M). The tissue underwent post-fixation with Osmium tetroxide (1%) and Tetrapotassium hexacyanoferrate trihydrate (1.5%) for 1h at 23°C, followed by ethanol dehydration in graded solutions (50%, 70%, 80%, 90%, 100%, 100%, 100%) for 15 min each. Then, 1, 2-Epoxypropane twice for 15 min each and gradient infiltration with mixture of 1, 2-Epoxypropane and Epon 812 resin for 8 h (SPI, America). Subsequently, Pure Epon 812 twice and polymerizing in oven (60°C). Blocks of polymerized resin were sectioned using a Leica EM UC7 ultramicrotome (Wetzlar, Germany). Ultra-thin sections (80 nm) were mounted and dried on coated copper grids. Sections were stained on-grid with 2% uranyl acetate (25 min) and lead citrate (5 min). Imaging was carried out using transmission electron microscope (Hitachi, HT7800). Immunofluorescence staining and imaging To obtain fixed brain tissue, mice underwent transcardial perfusion using 0.9% normal saline followed by 4% PFA. For immunofluorescence staining, tissues were rinsed in PBS and washed by 0.1% PBST for 10 min followed by incubation in blocking buffer (Beyotime, QuickBlock) for 10 min with gentle agitation. Autofluorescence quencher was used to reduce the background signals following the manufacturer’s instructions. Tissue slices were then incubated with diluted primary antibodies overnight at 4°C, washed thrice and incubated with secondary antibodies for 2 hours at room temperature. After rinsing in PBST thrice, mounted on slides, dehydrated, and immersed in antifade reagent with DAPI, the tissue slices were stored at 4°C until imaging using widefield microscopy at 10x objective (Olympus Slideview VS200) and confocal microscopy at 63x objective (Zeiss, LSM980 Airyscan2). Tissue clearing and imaging For cleared mouse head whole-mount or skull imaging, the fixed tissues were cleared using the iDISCO method.51 After decolorization, samples were decalcified by 20% EDTA in PBS for 4 days at room temperatureand then dehydrated, permeabilized, stained and cleared using the iDISCO methods as described. Cleared samples were incubated in dibenzyl ether for optical matching and 3D imaging using light-sheet microscopy (Zeiss, Lightsheet 7) or confocal laser microscopy (Zeiss, LSM 980 airyscan2). Images were stitched and reconstructed using Imaris software. Single cell harvest for flow cytometry For blood analysis, blood was collected before perfusion from the retroorbital sinus. Blood was centrifuged at 350 g for 5 min. Red blood cell lysis was then performed by resuspending the cell pellet in the red blood cell lysis buffer (Biolegend) for 10 min. After centrifugation at 350 g for 5 min, the pellet was resuspended in FACS buffer (1X PBS with 2% fetal bovine serum) until use. For brain analysis, 24 hours after LPS injection or stroke induction, mice were anesthetized and perfused to remove the intravascular leukocytes. Sham-operated mice were set as control. Tissues were harvested as described above. Skull bone marrow cells were isolated by flushing using FACS buffer. Brains were triturated into single cell suspensions by a tissue dissociator (Miltenyi, gentleMACS) with tissue dissociation kits (Miltenyi) according to the provided protocols. The ischemic ipsilateral brain hemisphere and the contralateral brain hemisphere were analyzed separately. Cell debris were removed before test using a debris removal solution (Miltenyi). Single cell suspensions were obtained by filtrating through a 70-μm cell strainer and kept in FACS buffer on ice until use. The antibody list is provided in key resources table and the gating strategy is provided in Figures 3A and S2. Zombie NIR or Fixable Viability Dye eFluor506 was used to select living cells. Unstained controls and single-stained controls were prepared for negative/positive determination and color compensation. Cells isolated from mice that did not receive administration of FITC-NPs were used as negative controls for NP-loaded cells to eliminate potential interference of cell autofluorescence. After stained with an antibody cocktail, the calvaria-derived myeloid cells were screened as Zombie NIR- or Fixable Viability Dye eFluor506-, CD45+ and CD11b+. Subpopulations including neutrophils and CD45hi cells were identified as Ly6G+ and Ly6G-CD45hi, respectively. Microglia were identified as Ly6G-CD45mid. Samples were acquired with Aurora spectral flow cytometer (Cytek) and data were analyzed by Flowjo. In vitro co-incubation of neurons and NP-loaded neutrophils On the co-culture day, neutrophils are isolated from C57BL/6 mice by collecting blood through orbital puncture, followed by immunomagnetic bead sorting. Neutrophils are seeded at 1×106/ml in serum-free RPMI-1640 medium and co-incubated with fluorescent NPs for two hours. After centrifugation at 1500 rpm for five minutes and removal of the supernatant, the neutrophils containing fluorescent NPs are resuspended in 1 ml of medium. Neutrophils are stained with DiD membrane dye (working concentration 1:1000) at 37°C for 20 minutes, followed by Hoechst 33342 nuclear dye (working concentration 1:2) for 10 minutes at 37°C. After staining, cells are washed twice with PBS to remove excess dyes and resuspended in 1 ml of medium. Neurons are stained with MitoTracker mitochondrial fluorescent probe (working concentration 1:2500) and Hoechst 33342 nuclear dye at 37°C for 10 minutes. After washing twice with PBS, 500 μl of neuronal culture medium is added. For co-culture, 500 μl of the neutrophil suspension is evenly added to the neuron culture dish and incubated at 37°C for different times before imaging. Imaging is performed using a HIS-SIM super-resolution structured illumination microscope at 100× magnification. Multiple fields of view are captured for ultra-high-resolution imaging. The acquired super-resolution images were sequentially processed using Wiener reconstruction and Sparse deconvolution, followed by further analysis with Fiji. In vitro co-incubation of neurons and fluorescent NPs To assess whether neurons can uptake fluorescent NPs directly, the primary mouse neurons were directly co-incubated with fluorescent NPs. On day 7 of primary mouse neuronal culture in confocal dishes, the neurons were first stained with MitoTracker and Hoechst 33342 to label mitochondria and nuclei, respectively, using previously optimized concentrations and incubation times. Following staining, the neurons were washed twice with PBS and maintained in 1 mL of neuronal complete medium. NPs were then introduced into the culture medium at a 1:20 dilution ratio, and the co-culture system was incubated at 37°C. To investigate the temporal dynamics of NPs internalization, neurons were co-cultured with NPs for 2, 4, 6, and 12 hours, respectively. After each incubation period, high-resolution structured illumination microscopy (HIS-SIM) was employed for super-resolution imaging, with consistent imaging parameters and post-processing methods as previously described. LC-MS/MS Tissue samples were accurately weighed and flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen, followed by pulverization. The homogenized tissue was resuspended in 200 μL of 0.1% formic acid in water and vortexed thoroughly. A 100 μL aliquot of the suspension was then mixed with 300 μL of acetonitrile containing 0.1% formic acid and the internal standard (aniline-suc-KLVFFC, Molecular weight: 931.18 Da, 20 ng/mL). The mixture was vortexed for 3 min and centrifuged at 13,000 rpm for 10 min at 4 °C. The resulting supernatant was transferred to a clean vial for UPLC-MS/MS analysis. Calibration standards were prepared by spiking blank tissue homogenates with known concentrations of the analyte and internal standard. Chromatographic separation was performed using a Thermo Hypersil GOLD C4 column (2.1 × 150 mm, 3 μm) on an Exion LC UPLC system. The column temperature was maintained at 40 °C and the autosampler was set at 8 °C. The mobile phases consisted of solvent A (acetonitrile containing 0.4% formic acid) and solvent B (water containing 0.4% formic acid), delivered at a flow rate of 0.3 mL/min. The injection volume was 3 μL. The elution gradient was as follows: 0-2 min, 5% A; 2-4 min, 90% A; 4-4.1 min, 5% A; 4.1-10 min, 5% A. The mass spectrometric analysis was conducted on a SCIEX Triple Quad™ 7500 system equipped with an electrospray ionization (ESI) source operating in positive ion mode with multiple reaction monitoring (MRM). The source parameters were as follows: source temperature, 400 °C; curtain gas, 40 psi; ion spray voltage, 3000 V; nebulizer and auxiliary gases, 35 and 60 psi, respectively. The following MRM transitions were monitored: m/z 504.65 → 601.1 for the analyte (RT 1.54 min, Q1: 45 V, CE: 23 V) and m/z 931.53 → 516.23 for the internal standard (RT 2.90 min, Q1: 70 V, CE: 45 V). Quantification was performed using a calibration curve constructed with matrix-matched standards. Data acquisition and processing were carried out using SCIEX OS software (version 3.1.6). Histological and MRI therapeutic evaluation Mice received MCAO surgery were intravenously or intracalvariosseously administered with NA1 or NA1 NPs after 60-min occlusion. Control mice were treated with PBS. Eicosapeptide NA1, or Nerinetide (YGRKKRRQRRRKLSSIESDV) with 99% purity was purchased from Nanjing Aite Biotechnology Co., Ltd. For dose-response relationship studying, mice received different dose of NA1 were assessed for neurological deficit scoring 24 hours after MCAO and then sacrificed to quantify the brain infarct volume using 2,3,5-triphenyltetrazolium chloride (TTC) staining. For long-term evaluation, in vivo MRI imaging was performed on a 9.4T BioSpec 94/30 USR animal scanner (Bruker BioSpin, Germany) using a quadrature transmit/receive volume coil of inside diameter of 35 mm. Animals were kept under isoflurane anesthesia (1.2–1.8% in 80% air and 20% oxygen) during the entire data acquisition period. Physiological signals included heart rate, body temperature and respiratory frequency were monitored throughout the experiment. Temperature was maintained around 37°C with a hydrothermal pad. Anatomical images were acquired with a T2 turboRARE, Diffusion-weight-EPI-sat and Diffusion-Tensor-EPI-sat sequences in a coronal plane. Analysis was finished using ITK-Snap contouring software (Pittsburgh). Stroke volumes were calculated on TTC and T2 images as 𝐼 𝑛 𝑓 𝑎 𝑟 𝑐 𝑡 𝑣 𝑜 𝑙 𝑢 𝑚 𝑒 = 𝑉 𝑐 𝑜 𝑛 𝑡 𝑟 𝑎 − ( 𝑉 𝑖 𝑝 𝑠 𝑖 − 𝑉 𝑖 𝑛 𝑓 𝑎 𝑟 𝑐 𝑡 ) where 𝑉 𝑐 𝑜 𝑛 𝑡 𝑟 𝑎 , 𝑉 𝑖 𝑝 𝑠 𝑖 , 𝑉 𝑖 𝑛 𝑓 𝑎 𝑟 𝑐 𝑡 are the volume of contralateral hemisphere, ipsilateral hemisphere and infarct zone, respectively. Infarct core volumes were calculated on ADC map with severely reduced ADC < 620. Brain edema and brain atrophy was assessed by calculating the percentage ratio of the volume of the ipsilateral hemibrain to the volume of the contralateral hemibrain. 35 days after MCAO, the mice were sacrificed and the brains were harvested for section and Nissl staining. Behavioral assessments A modified Garcia score test was used to evaluate sensorimotor function at 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 14, 21, and 28 days after MCAO. Seven tests were conducted, including body proprioception, vibrissae touch, limb symmetry, lateral turning, forelimb walking, motor test and spontaneous activity. The scores of each test ranged from 0 to 3, with a total maximum possible score of 21. The rotarod test was conducted to assess motor function at 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 14, 21, and 28 days after ischemia. Briefly, the mice were trained on a rotarod apparatus (Panlab, Barcelona, Spain) for 3 successive days (speed from 4 to 40 rpm). The time for each mouse to fall onto the platform was recorded, with a maximum time of 300 seconds per trial. To investigate learning and memory/recognition in mice, the novel object recognition test was performed. Briefly, this two-trial test consisted of a training and a testing phase. During the training phase, the animal was allowed to explore two identical objects for 10 minutes. After a 6-hour interval, one of the training objects was replaced with a novel object, and the animal was allowed to explore the two different objects for another 10 minutes during the testing phase. Mice which did not reach a minimum exploration time (20 s) in the training phase were excluded from the analysis. The recognition index was calculated as the time spent exploring the novel object divided by the total time spent exploring the novel object and the familiar object. The objects were cleaned between mice using 75% ethanol. The Morris water maze test is used to assess spatial learning and memory abilities in mice. The apparatus consists of a circular pool with a diameter of 109 cm, a circular platform with a diameter of 11 cm that is elevated 2 cm above the water surface, and spatial cues placed around the pool. A camera is positioned above the setup for monitoring. Prior to sample collection, mice undergo spatial learning training for an appropriate duration each day: each mouse is placed into the pool from four different locations (northwest, north, east, southwest), and their ability to locate the platform within 60 seconds is observed. The time taken for the mouse to reach the platform is recorded. After each trial, the mouse is allowed to remain on the platform for 15 seconds. Training is conducted for four consecutive days. On the day following the completion of training, a spatial memory test is performed. The circular platform is removed, and the mouse is released into the pool from the location farthest from the original platform. The time spent in the target quadrant (where the platform was previously located) within 60 seconds and the average swimming speed are recorded. Randomization and Interventions of clinical trial Patients with potential mMCAI were continuously screened in the emergency room (ER). Those enrolled were randomly assigned to the ICO group or the best medical treatment group at a 1:1 ratio through simple random allocation. The randomization code was obtained from the Statistics and Data Centre at the China National Clinical Research Centre for Neurological Diseases. All the patients received active treatment and care according to the Evidence-Based Guidelines for the Management of Large Hemispheric Infarction, and the European Stroke Organization (ESO) guidelines for the management of space-occupying brain infarction. Additionally, the ICO group received ICO Y-3 injections, with a dosage calculated as 32 μg/kg (The dosage is calculated from preclinical studies29). All the participants were admitted to the neurointensive care unit (NICU) prior to ICO injection operation. The ICO injection procedure was performed at the bedside in the ICU and required an isolated aseptic operating space. Referring to stereotactic aspiration surgical procedures, we designed a specific operational protocol. Operations in the ICO group were carried out under the monitoring, with salvage equipment and professional medical personnel available. During hospitalization, patients routinely underwent CT scans, and laboratory tests to detect existence of cerebral edema, hemorrhagic transformation, or potential infectious events and other adverse events. Patients were transferred to general wards for rehabilitation training if out of danger. ICO injection in patients Patients were positioned with the shoulder on the affected side elevated and the head tilted toward the contralateral side for ease of operation. The injection site was selected at the region of the ipsilateral parietal bone where the diploe was most prominent. A 2-3 cm longitudinal scalp incision was made at this location. After standard disinfection, draping, and local lidocaine infiltration, the scalp was incised, hemostasis achieved, and the temporal muscle retracted to expose the skull. Using a surgical drill, a 2-3 mm-deep hole was created in the outer plate to expose the diploe. In most cases, slow oozing of dark red blood indicated successful access to the skull marrow cavity. If no bleeding is observed, the drill bit can be changed to grind open the barrier until bleeding occurs. A 5 mL needleless syringe was prepared by wrapping three layers of foam dressing around the syringe cone and screw thread. After pressing the syringe firmly against the bone hole, the therapeutic agent was slowly injected into the skull bone marrow. Upon completion, the bone opening was immediately sealed using bone wax. The scalp incision was then closed with sutures. On postoperative days 2 and 3, additional doses were administered through the same bone access point by repeating the injection process, followed by resealing with bone wax and scalp closure. After each procedure, the surgical site was dressed according to standard sterile technique, and the wound was regularly monitored for healing and signs of infection. Clinical outcomes The primary outcomes of our clinical study were set to evaluate feasibility and safety of ICO Y-3 injection for mMCAI patients. Feasibility outcomes were defined as drilling through the internal plate of skull; terminated due to drug leakage during the injection; the patient’s refusal to continue; and failure for other reasons during the 3-day ICO injection treatments. Safety outcomes included infection events (skin infection, osteomyelitis, or intracranial infection), symptomatic and asymptomatic intracalvarial hemorrhage, moderate to severe bleeding (defined by the GUSTO), hepatic insufficiency, renal insufficiency during the treatment, severe or extremely severe anemia (hemoglobin < 60g/L), mortality, incidence of other adverse events/serious adverse events. Secondary efficacy outcomes included: Changes in NIHSS scores from baseline values to 14 ± 2 days or at discharge; NIHSS score increase of ≥ 4 at 14 ± 2 days compared to baseline; mRS score of 0-3 points at 90 ± 7 days. NIHSS score and mRS score were evaluated by two specialized neurologists. In instances of discordant assessment outcomes, adjudication was performed by a senior clinician to ensure the accuracy and reliability of the diagnostic evaluation. Prior to scoring, the physicians ensured that the heads of the patients in both groups were covered and appearance of medical dressings were consistent. The neurologists validating the scoring and the CEC members were blinded to the patients' group assignments. Quantification and statistical analysis All in vitro experiments were conducted independently at least three times. For preclinical study, sample or replicate numbers (n) are provided in the figure legends. Data are presented as mean values ± standard deviation (SD), mean values ± standard error (SEM) or median (minimum, maximum). For comparisons between two groups, unpaired t-test was applied. Multiple group comparisons were analyzed using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), followed by Dunnett’s post hoc test to compare each group to the ICO-NA1 NPs group, or Tukey’s post hoc test for pairwise comparisons among treatment groups. For time-course data, such as lesion volume change, brain volume change, sensorimotor and cognitive functions, two-way repeated measures ANOVA was used, with subsequent Šídák test to calculate p-values, enabling comparisons between each treatment group and the control, or among all pairs of treatment groups all time points, respectively. Statistical significance was defined as ∗p < 0.05, ∗∗p < 0.01 or ∗∗∗p < 0.001. GraphPad Prism 10 was used for data analysis. Details of statistical analysis conducted are included in the Figure legends. For clinical study, all numeric variables were analyzed by the Shapiro-Wilk test to determine whether they followed normal distributions. Normally distributed data are described as means ± standard deviations (SD), while non-normally distributed data were described as median (interquartile range, IQR) values. Categorical variables were expressed as counts and frequencies. Feasibility measures were only statistically described. All safety measures were compared between groups using Fisher’s exact test. The primary effectiveness measures were compared using the Mann-Whitney U test. Since NIHSS score and GCS score are not applicable for mortality cases, relevant score was treated as missing values and assigned by last observation carried forward (LOCF) which meant the values were assigned by the most recent valid scores. Among the secondary effectiveness measures, rates of NIHSS improvement, NIHSS motor limbs score improvement and mRS 0-3 in 90 days were compared using Fisher’s exact test. Statistical analyses were performed using SAS software, version 9.4 (SAS Institute). All statistical tests will be two-sided, with p < 0.05 considered statistically significant. enrichment.title: Multi-gene biomarkers reveal spatial organization and subpopulation-specific damage response in intrahepatic biliary epithelial cells
enrichment.summary: Background & Aims: Intrahepatic biliary epithelial cell (BEC) heterogeneity remains challenging to define. Here, we sought to identify BEC subpopulations and biomarkers in mouse liver. Methods: We performed scRNA-seq on Sox9EGFP+ liver epithelium from mice subjected to bile duct ligation (BDL) and sham controls. A machine learning algorithm, NSForest, identified minimal, multi-gene signatures for BEC subpopulations. These metagenes and were validated using hybridization chain reaction (HCR) FISH in tissue sections from wild-type mice and on primary BECs expanded in vitro. Metagenes were used to match BDL subpopulations to their corresponding sham subpopulations for differential gene expression (DGE) analysis. Results: We identified 4 BEC subpopulations in sham controls, each associated with 1-2 gene metagenes. Spatial localization of metagene-defined BEC subpopulations by HCR FISH revealed heterogeneous cellular composition of intrahepatic bile ducts. BECs belonging to a given subpopulation were most likely to have neighbors of the same identity, forming homogenous cellular compartments within ducts. BDL downregulated subpopulation-specific genes and upregulated a damage-associated gene set. BDL samples also included a proliferative subpopulation not found in sham controls, which contained populations enriched for three of the four metagenes. All BEC subpopulations were also found in monolayers in vitro, where they clustered spatially with BECs of the same subtype. Conclusions: Novel metagene biomarkers of BEC subpopulations facilitated spatial localization of BECs in situ, identified subpopulation specific injury responses, and confirmed that BEC heterogeneity is preserved in vitro. The presence of locally homogenous BEC neighborhoods in vitro suggests some degree of BEC organization may be epithelial-autonomous.

enrichment.title: Empty drops in scRNA-seq uncover the surprising prevalence of sequestered neuropeptide mRNA and pervasive sequencing artifacts
enrichment.summary: The empty drops in single-cell sequencing experiments are an underexplored resource. As such, they present a substrate to ask questions orthogonal to standard single-cell sequencing workflows, calibrate statistical models using simple internal controls, and detect technical outliers which would be otherwise challenging to distinguish from real biology. In this case study, we report a relatively simple procedure to detect sequencing artifacts and make recommendations to reduce the risk of erroneous quantifications. In addition, we report the surprising abundance and co-expression of mRNA coding for neuropeptide-related genes in the empty drops, possibly reflecting underlying physiology.

enrichment.title: Kennedy announces new vaccine advisory committee members after meeting rescheduled
enrichment.summary: Kennedy adds two new members to the CDC's vaccine advisory committee
enrichment.content: Kennedy adds two new members to ACIP | STAT Skip to Main Content Politics Kennedy announces new vaccine advisory committee members after meeting rescheduled The new appointments come during an unstable time for ACIP Manage alerts for this article Email this article Share this article Members of the CDC Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices at their December meeting in Atlanta, Ga. Elijah Nouvelage/Getty Images By Chelsea Cirruzzo Feb. 27, 2026 Washington Correspondent Chelsea Cirruzzo [email protected] Chelsea Cirruzzo is a Washington correspondent at STAT, where she covers HHS. You can reach Chelsea on Signal at chelseacirruzzo.42. WASHINGTON — Health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced two new members of his handpicked panel of vaccine advisers on Friday, ahead of a meeting rescheduled for March . Kennedy said in a statement that Sean G. Downing, a primary care doctor licensed in Florida, and Angelina Farella, a pediatrician in Texas, would join the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, a group that advises the federal government on which vaccines to recommend to the public. Advertisement The new appointments come during an unstable time for ACIP. The group, whose members were selected by Kennedy after he dismissed its original members, was supposed to meet in February. However, that meeting was rescheduled to March, though the Department of Health and Human Services hasn’t provided a reason. A federal judge is also weighing whether the meeting should take place at all, as part of a lawsuit filed by a major medical group. Meanwhile, HHS has been undergoing a shakeup in recent days in an effort to shift the department’s focus towards politically popular issues like food and drug policy. That shakeup included the exit of Deputy Secretary Jim O’Neill, who was serving as acting Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Director. The new acting director, National Institutes for Health Director Jay Bhattacharya praised the new members in a press release on Friday. “These appointments strengthen ACIP with experienced clinicians who understand how immunization guidance matters for patients and families,” he said. Advertisement According to an HHS press release, Downing is a primary care doctor who works in concierge medicine, meaning his Sarasota clinic is membership-based. According to his website, members of his practice can receive personalized medical care, same-day appointments, and “adult and pediatric vaccination.” Per HHS, Downing completed his residency at Brown University and has worked as a physician for uninsured patients. Farella is a pediatrician and owner of a Texas pediatric clinic, per HHS. She completed her residency at the University of Texas Medical Branch. Farella appeared on NewsMax in 2021 , pushing back against another doctor calling for people to get the Covid-19 shot. “You know how you fight a pandemic, and you know how you fight disease? You treat it,” she responded, before suggesting some drugs, like steroids, as well as vitamins. Credits : Credit: Christine Daniloff, MIT; iStock Previous image Next image Hydrogen sits at the center of some of the world’s most important industrial processes, but its production still comes with a heavy environmental cost. Today, most hydrogen is produced through high-emissions processes like steam methane reforming and coal gasification. But hydrogen can also be made by splitting water molecules using renewable electricity, eliminating fossil fuel emissions and other toxic byproducts. Such “green hydrogen” is made by running an electric current through water in an electrolyzer. Green hydrogen won’t scale through decarbonization alone. It also has to be cost-competitive with the traditional methods of production. 1s1 Energy thinks it has the technology to finally make green hydrogen go mainstream. The company says its boron-based membrane material unlocks previously unachievable performance and durability in electrolyzers. In tests with partners, 1s1 says, electrolyzers with its membranes needed just 70 percent of the energy to produce each kilogram of hydrogen, compared to incumbent devices. “Green hydrogen has been a hard industry to have success in so far,” acknowledges 1s1 co-founder Dan Sobek ’88, SM ’92, PhD ’97. “The difference with us is we’ve done very targeted customer discovery. We have a very strong value proposition that’s not just about decarbonization. We have a pipeline of potential customers that see around a 60 percent reduction in operating costs with our technology. That’s a nice point of entry.” Although 1s1 is focused on hydrogen production now, its technology could also be used in fuel cells and solid-state batteries, and to extract critical metals from mining waste. The company is beginning trials in some of those applications, and it is working with a large materials company to scale up production of its membranes for hydrogen production. “We’re at an inflection point for the company,” Sobek says. “The plan is, by 2030, to have a solid business in several segments: electrolyzers, mineral extraction, and in collaborations with several large companies. But right now, we have to be judicious and focused.” Improving electrolyzers Sobek was born and raised in Argentina, but he also grew up at MIT over the course of three degrees and more than a decade. He first studied aeronautics and astronautics at MIT, then jumped to mechanical engineering as a graduate student, then moved to the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, where he worked under PhD advisors and MIT professors Martha Gray and Stephen Senturia. His thesis focused on a technique for quickly measuring optical properties of large numbers of biological cells. “A lot of my learnings around microfabrication and materials chemistry ended up being really relevant for 1s1,” Sobek says. “A class that was very important to me was taught by Professor Amar Bose . I was a teaching assistant for him for a couple of semesters, and that had an incredible influence on my thinking.” Following graduation, Sobek worked in microelectronics and microfluidics before founding his own company, Zymera, in 2004. The company developed deep-tissue imaging technology for detecting cancer and other serious diseases. Around 2013, Sobek started talking to his Zymera co-founder, Sukanta Bhattacharyya, about making electrolysis more efficient, focusing on “proton exchange membrane” electrolyzers. Such electrolyzers employ a large amount of electricity to split water into hydrogen and oxygen ions. At their center is a membrane that can lose efficiency through voltage resistance. On top of the efficiency challenge, electricity is often more expensive than fossil fuels in many parts of the world. Traditional hydrogen production also has the benefit of existing infrastructure, making it that much more difficult for green hydrogen production to scale. Sobek and Bhattacharyya knew the most important part of such electrolyzers is their proton-conducting membrane, which shuttles hydrogen ions from the anode to the cathode in the electrolyzer’s electrochemical cell. “I asked Sukanta how we could improve the efficiency and durability of that element,” Sobek recalls. “He gave me a one-word answer: boron.” Boron can be given a negative charge, which makes hydrogen ions, or protons, bond to it more quickly. The hydrogen ions can then be filtered through the membrane and released as they move through the cell. Boron-based materials are also more stable and resistant to corrosion, further improving the long-term performance of electrolyzers. The company was officially founded in late 2019. After years of development, today 1s1 attaches a chemically tailored version of boron onto polymer materials to create its membranes for exchanging protons. “These are first-of-a-kind membranes with stable and durable, super-acid proton exchange groups that do not poison catalysts,” Sobek says. Tiny membranes with big impact In 2021, the U.S. Department of Energy set a goal for proton exchange membrane electrolysis to achieve 77 percent electrical efficiency by 2031. Sobek says 1s1 is already reaching that milestone in tests. “It’s not just the technology, but the way we’re applying it,” Sobek says, “We’re making hydrogen viable for use in the production of different industrial chemicals.” 1s1 is currently conducting pilots with partners, including an electrical utility owned by a large steel company in Brazil. The company is also actively exploring other applications for its technology. Last year, 1s1 announced a project to produce green ammonia with the company Nitrofix through joint funding from the U.S. Department of Energy and the Israeli Ministry of Energy and Infrastructure. It’s also working with a large mine in Brazil to extract a material called niobium, which is useful for high-strength steel as well as fast-charging batteries. A similar process could even be used to extract gold. “We can do that without using harsh chemicals, because the standard processes used to extract niobium and gold use extremely strong acids at high temperatures or extremely toxic chemicals,” Sobek says. “It’s gratifying for me because my home country of Argentina has had a lot of problems with the use of toxic chemicals to extract gold. We’re trying to enable low-cost, responsible mining.” As 1s1 scales its membrane technology, Sobek says the goal is to deploy wherever the technology can improve processes. “We have a large number of potential customers because this technology is really foundational,” Sobek says. “Creating high-impact technologies is always fun.” Share this news article on: X Facebook LinkedIn Reddit Print Related Links 1s1 Energy Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics Department of Mechanical Engineering Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science School of Engineering Related Topics Energy Startups Cleaner industry Renewable energy Sustainability Chemical engineering Materials science and engineering Energy efficiency Emissions Batteries Innovation and Entrepreneurship (I&E) Alumni/ae Aeronautical and astronautical engineering Mechanical engineering Electrical engineering and computer science (EECS) School of Engineering Related Articles Taking the heat out of industrial chemical separations Unlocking ammonia as a fuel source for heavy industry New lightweight polymer film can prevent corrosion Previous item Next item More MIT News Electrons in moiré crystals explore higher-dimensional quantum worlds MIT physicists have discovered 3D “moiré crystals” that simulate four-dimensional quantum materials to a T. enrichment.normalized_title: Toward cheaper, cleaner hydrogen production
enrichment.normalized_summary: Co-founded by Dan Sobek ’88, SM ’92, PhD ’97, 1s1 Energy has developed electrochemical cell materials for hydrogen electrolyzers that it says reduces energy use by 30 percent.
